question: Avery attacks with a [Guile] that was turned face-down by [Ixidron], and Nelson blocks with [Jerrard of the Closed Fist]. Does Avery shuffle?
answer:
No — Avery doesn't shuffle. The face-down Guile is a 2/2 with no name, no abilities, and no other characteristics at all: a face-down permanent has only the characteristics granted by the effect that turned it face down (here, Ixidron's "they're 2/2 creatures"), and those are its copiable values [708.2b]. Because the face-down permanent has no abilities on the battlefield, there is no "When Guile is put into a graveyard from anywhere, shuffle it into its owner's library" ability to trigger when lethal damage from Jerrard of the Closed Fist kills it. It simply stays in Avery's graveyard (turned face up there, but too late to matter, since the trigger would have had to exist while it was on the battlefield).

Combat math, assuming Jerrard of the Closed Fist is face up as a 6/5: it deals 6 damage to the 2/2 face-down Guile (lethal) and takes 2, so Jerrard of the Closed Fist survives.

Two notes:
- If Jerrard of the Closed Fist was on the battlefield when Ixidron entered, it too would have been turned face down as a 2/2 [708.2b], and then the two 2/2s would trade. I'm assuming Jerrard of the Closed Fist arrived after Ixidron and is face up.
- Contrast with a face-up Guile: there, the ability does trigger, and per [701.24c] the library gets shuffled even if Guile is removed from the graveyard before the ability resolves.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the same result holds in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.400.7: An object that moves from one zone to another becomes a new object with no memory of, or relation to, its previous existence. This rule has the following exceptions.
gold_text.603.10: Normally, objects that exist immediately after an event are checked to see if the event matched any trigger conditions, and continuous effects that exist at that time are used to determine what the trigger conditions are and what the objects involved in the event look like. However, some triggered abilities are exceptions to this rule; the game “looks back in time” to determine if those abilities trigger, using the existence of those abilities and the appearance of objects immediately prior to the event. The list of exceptions is as follows:
gold_text.603.6c: Trigger events that involve objects changing zones are called “zone-change triggers.” Many abilities with zone-change triggers attempt to do something to that object after it changes zones. During resolution, these abilities look for the object in the zone that it moved to. If the object is unable to be found in the zone it went to, the part of the ability attempting to do something to the object will fail to do anything. The ability could be unable to find the object because the object never entered the specified zone, because it left the zone before the ability resolved, or because it is in a zone that is hidden from a player, such as a library or an opponent’s hand. (This rule applies even if the object leaves the zone and returns again before the ability resolves.) The most common zone-change triggers are enters-the-battlefield triggers and leaves-the-battlefield triggers. Leaves-the-battlefield abilities trigger when a permanent moves from the battlefield to another zone, or when a phased-in permanent leaves the game because its owner leaves the game. These are written as, but aren’t limited to, “When [this object] leaves the battlefield, . . .” or “Whenever [something] is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, . . . .” (See also rule 603.10.) An ability that attempts to do something to the card that left the battlefield checks for it only in the first zone that it went to. An ability that triggers when a card is put into a certain zone “from anywhere” is never treated as a leaves-the-battlefield ability, even if an object is put into that zone from the battlefield.

cited_text.708.2b: Face-down spells and face-down permanents have no characteristics other than those listed by the ability or rules that allowed the spell or permanent to be face down. Any listed characteristics are the copiable values of that object’s characteristics. (See rule 613, “Interaction of Continuous Effects,” and rule 707, “Copying Objects.”) A face-down permanent can’t be turned face down. If a spell or ability attempts to turn a face-down permanent face down, nothing happens and that effect doesn’t change any of its characteristics or their copiable values.
cited_text.701.24c: Shuffle If an effect would cause a player to shuffle one or more specific objects into a library, that library is shuffled even if none of those objects are in the zone they’re expected to be in or an effect causes all of those objects to be moved to another zone or remain in their current zone. Guile says, in part, “When Guile is put into a graveyard from anywhere, shuffle it into its owner’s library.” It’s put into a graveyard and its ability triggers, then a player exiles it from that graveyard in response. When the ability resolves, the library is shuffled. Black Sun’s Zenith says, in part, “Shuffle Black Sun’s Zenith into its owner’s library.” Black Sun’s Zenith is in a graveyard, has gained flashback (due to Recoup, perhaps), and is cast from that graveyard. Black Sun’s Zenith will be exiled, and its owner’s library will be shuffled.

answer_gold:
Yes. By default, triggered abilities are checked immediately after the event in question to see if they should trigger. At that point, the Guile is face-up in the graveyard and has that ability.

(Guile's trigger does not fit the exception for "leaves-the-battlefield" triggers because it is a "from anywhere" trigger.)

question: Archer attacks with a [The Scarab God] that was turned face-down by [Ixidron] and Nia blocks with [Scathe Zombies]. Does The Scarab God trigger?
answer:
No. Nothing about The Scarab God triggers from being blocked by Scathe Zombies.

Two independent reasons:

1) Even face up, The Scarab God has no combat trigger at all. Its printed abilities are an upkeep trigger ("At the beginning of your upkeep, each opponent loses X life and you scry X"), an activated ability ({2}{U}{B}: exile a creature card from a graveyard and make a 4/4 black Zombie copy), and a dies trigger. None of these has a trigger condition of attacking, becoming blocked, or dealing combat damage, so when Nia declares Scathe Zombies as a blocker and abilities that trigger on blockers being declared would trigger [509.1i], The Scarab God has nothing to contribute. Abilities like "whenever this creature becomes blocked" [509.3c] or "attacks and isn't blocked" [509.3g] simply aren't on the card.

2) On top of that, Ixidron's effect turned The Scarab God face down. A face-down creature is a 2/2 with no name, no mana cost, and no abilities, so even if it had a combat trigger, that ability isn't there to trigger while it's face down. (Also note the "attacks and isn't blocked" style trigger wouldn't apply here anyway, since Scathe Zombies did block.)

Timing note: I'm assuming Ixidron turned The Scarab God face down before combat, as stated. If instead The Scarab God were somehow turned face up before blockers were declared, it would still not trigger, because it has no blocking-related trigger.

Player count doesn't matter here — with two players or more, the defending player (Nia) declares blockers the same way and no ability of The Scarab God triggers. Note only that its upkeep ability says "each opponent loses X life," which hits every opponent in a multiplayer game, but that's an upkeep trigger unrelated to combat.

The list of exceptions is as follows:
gold_text.603.10a: Normally, objects that exist immediately after an event are checked to see if the event matched any trigger conditions, and continuous effects that exist at that time are used to determine what the trigger conditions are and what the objects involved in the event look like. However, some triggered abilities are exceptions to this rule; the game “looks back in time” to determine if those abilities trigger, using the existence of those abilities and the appearance of objects immediately prior to the event. Two creatures are on the battlefield along with an artifact that has the ability “Whenever a creature dies, you gain 1 life.” Someone casts a spell that destroys all artifacts, creatures, and enchantments. The artifact’s ability triggers twice, even though the artifact goes to its owner’s graveyard at the same time as the creatures.

Any listed characteristics are the copiable values of that object’s characteristics. (See rule 613, “Interaction of Continuous Effects,” and rule 707, “Copying Objects.”)

cited_text.509.1i: First, the defending player declares blockers. This turn-based action doesn’t use the stack. To declare blockers, the defending player follows the steps below, in order. If at any point during the declaration of blockers, the defending player is unable to comply with any of the steps listed below, the declaration is illegal; the game returns to the moment before the declaration (see rule 733, “Handling Illegal Actions”). Any abilities that trigger on blockers being declared trigger. See rule 509.2a for more information.
cited_text.509.3c: Triggered abilities that trigger on blockers being declared may have different trigger conditions. An ability that reads “Whenever [a creature] becomes blocked, . . .” generally triggers only once each combat for that creature, even if it’s blocked by multiple creatures. It will trigger if that creature becomes blocked by at least one creature declared as a blocker. It will also trigger if that creature becomes blocked by an effect or by a creature that’s put onto the battlefield as a blocker, but only if the attacking creature was an unblocked creature at that time. (See rule 509.1h.)
cited_text.509.3g: Triggered abilities that trigger on blockers being declared may have different trigger conditions. An ability that reads “Whenever [a creature] attacks and isn’t blocked, . . .” triggers if no creatures are declared as blockers for that creature. It will trigger even if the creature was never declared as an attacker (for example, if it entered the battlefield attacking). It won’t trigger if the attacking creature is blocked and then all its blockers are removed from combat.

answer_gold: No. By default, triggered abilities are checked immediately after the event in question to see if they should trigger. However, "leaves-the-battlefield" triggers check the game state immediately before the event instead. At that point, The Scarab God had no abilities.

question: Alaia casts [Biogenic Upgrade] targeting [Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11]. In total how many counters are be placed on Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11?
answer:
Nine +1/+1 counters total are placed on Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 (it ends up with nine counters, making it a 10/10), assuming Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 had no +1/+1 counters before the spell resolved.

Step by step:

1. Biogenic Upgrade distributes all three +1/+1 counters onto the single target, Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11. Michelangelo's own replacement effect ("If one or more +1/+1 counters would be put on a creature you control, that many plus one +1/+1 counters are put on it instead") applies to that event as a single batch, so 3 + 1 = 4 counters are actually placed. This assumes Alaia controls Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 — the replacement only applies to creatures its controller controls.
2. Biogenic Upgrade then doubles the number of +1/+1 counters on Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11. Doubling means giving the permanent as many counters of that kind as it already has [701.10e], so it would be given 4 more.
3. That is again one or more +1/+1 counters being put on a creature Alaia controls, so Michelangelo's replacement applies once more: 4 + 1 = 5 counters are placed.

Total placed: 4 + 5 = 9 counters. Each +1/+1 counter adds +1/+1 in layer 7c [122.1a, 613.4c], so the 1/1 Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 becomes 10/10.

If Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 already had +1/+1 counters on it when Biogenic Upgrade resolved, step 2 would double a larger number and the totals would rise accordingly. Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.614.1a: Some continuous effects are replacement effects. Like prevention effects (see rule 615), replacement effects apply continuously as events happen—they aren’t locked in ahead of time. Such effects watch for a particular event that would happen and completely or partially replace that event with a different event. They act like “shields” around whatever they’re affecting. Effects that use the word “instead” are replacement effects. Most replacement effects use the word “instead” to indicate what events will be replaced with other events.
gold_text.701.10e: Double To double the number of a kind of counters on a player or permanent, give that player or permanent as many of those counters as that player or permanent already has.

cited_text.701.10e: Double To double the number of a kind of counters on a player or permanent, give that player or permanent as many of those counters as that player or permanent already has.
cited_text.122.1a: A counter is a marker placed on an object or player that modifies its characteristics and/or interacts with a rule, ability, or effect. Counters are not objects and have no characteristics. Notably, a counter is not a token, and a token is not a counter. Counters with the same name or description are interchangeable. A +X/+Y counter on a creature or on a creature card in a zone other than the battlefield, where X and Y are numbers, adds X to that object’s power and Y to that object’s toughness. Similarly, -X/-Y counters subtract from power and toughness. See rule 613.4c.
cited_text.613.4c: Within layer 7, apply effects in a series of sublayers in the order described below. Within each sublayer, apply effects in timestamp order. (See rule 613.7.) Note that dependency may alter the order in which effects are applied within a sublayer. (See rule 613.8.) Layer 7c: Effects and counters that modify power and/or toughness (but don’t set power and/or toughness to a specific number or value) are applied.

answer_gold: Nine. Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11's ability is a replacement effect that applies whenever counters are being placed on it When Biogenic Upgrade begins resolving, that replacement effect will add a counter, resulting in Alaia placing four +1/+1 counters. Afterwards, Biogenic Upgrade will then double the amount of counters on Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11. This results in an additional four counters being placed on it, which will then be modified by Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11's replacement effect again, resulting in nine +1/+1 counters in total.

question: Addison casts [Ferocious Zheng]. After it resolves, they cast [Elemental Eruption] and reveal [Everdream] from their hand, splicing it onto Elemental Eruption. When Elemental Eruption's Storm trigger resolves, will the copies of Elemental Eruption also have Everdream spliced onto them?
answer:
Yes. Each Storm copy of Elemental Eruption will have Everdream's text too, so each copy creates a 4/4 red Dragon Elemental token with flying and prowess and draws Addison a card.

Why: splice is a text-changing effect that adds the spliced card's rules text to the spell on the stack "the spell has the characteristics of the main spell, plus the rules text of each of the spliced cards" [702.47c], and it doesn't replace any of Elemental Eruption's own text [612.10]. So while Elemental Eruption is on the stack, "Draw a card" is part of Elemental Eruption's characteristics. Storm says "When you cast this spell, copy it for each other spell that was cast before it this turn" [702.40a], and a copy of a spell copies both the characteristics of the spell and all decisions made for it [707.10]. Since the added Everdream text is part of Elemental Eruption's characteristics at the time it's copied, the copies have it as well. Nothing extra is paid for the copies.

Count: Ferocious Zheng was cast earlier this turn, so Storm makes 1 copy (plus the original Elemental Eruption) — assuming those are the only two spells cast that turn. Note Everdream itself is not cast, so it doesn't add to the Storm count. Also note that the copies gain only Everdream's rules text, not its name, mana cost, or color [702.47c]; the copies remain red sorcery spells.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players — Storm and splice work identically at a two-player or multiplayer table (Storm counts spells cast by all players that turn).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.601.2b: To cast a spell is to take it from where it is (usually the hand), put it on the stack, and pay its costs, so that it will eventually resolve and have its effect. Casting a spell includes proposal of the spell (rules 601.2a–d) and determination and payment of costs (rules 601.2f–h). To cast a spell, a player follows the steps listed below, in order. A player must be legally allowed to cast the spell to begin this process (see rule 601.3). If a player is unable to comply with the requirements of a step listed below while performing that step, the casting of the spell is illegal; the game returns to the moment before the casting of that spell was proposed (see rule 733, “Handling Illegal Actions”). If the spell is modal, the player announces the mode choice (see rule 700.2). If the player wishes to splice any cards onto the spell (see rule 702.47), they reveal those cards in their hand. If the spell has alternative or additional costs that will be paid as it’s being cast such as buyback or kicker costs (see rules 118.8 and 118.9), the player announces their intentions to pay any or all of those costs (see rule 601.2f). A player can’t apply two alternative methods of casting or two alternative costs to a single spell. If the spell has a variable cost that will be paid as it’s being cast (such as an {X} in its mana cost; see rule 107.3), the player announces the value of that variable. If the value of that variable is defined in the text of the spell by a choice that player would make later in the announcement or resolution of the spell, that player makes that choice at this time instead of that later time. If a cost that will be paid as the spell is being cast includes hybrid mana symbols, the player announces the nonhybrid equivalent cost they intend to pay. If a cost that will be paid as the spell is being cast includes Phyrexian mana symbols, the player announces whether they intend to pay 2 life or a corresponding colored mana cost for each of those symbols. Previously made choices (such as choosing to cast a spell with flashback from a graveyard or choosing to cast a creature with morph face down) may restrict the player’s options when making these choices.
gold_text.702.47a: Splice Splice is a static ability that functions while a card is in your hand. “Splice onto [quality] [cost]” means “You may reveal this card from your hand as you cast a [quality] spell. If you do, that spell gains the text of this card’s rules text and you pay [cost] as an additional cost to cast that spell.” Paying a card’s splice cost follows the rules for paying additional costs in rules 601.2b and 601.2f–h. Since the card with splice remains in the player’s hand, it can later be cast normally or spliced onto another spell. It can even be discarded to pay a “discard a card” cost of the spell it’s spliced onto.
gold_text.707.2: When copying an object, the copy acquires the copiable values of the original object’s characteristics and, for an object on the stack, choices made when casting or activating it (mode, targets, the value of X, whether it was kicked, how it will affect multiple targets, and so on). The copiable values are the values derived from the text printed on the object (that text being name, mana cost, color indicator, card type, subtype, supertype, rules text, power, toughness, and/or loyalty), as modified by other copy effects, by its face-down status, and by “as . . . enters” and “as . . . is turned face up” abilities that set power and toughness (and may also set additional characteristics). Other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects), status, counters, and stickers are not copied. Chimeric Staff is an artifact that reads, “{X}: This artifact becomes an X/X Construct artifact creature until end of turn.” Clone is a creature that reads, “You may have this creature enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield.” After a Staff has become a 5/5 Construct artifact creature, a Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of it. The Clone is an artifact, not a 5/5 Construct artifact creature. (The copy has the Staff’s ability, however, and will become a creature if that ability is activated.) Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of a face-down Grinning Demon (a creature with morph {2}{B}{B}). The Clone is a colorless 2/2 creature with no name, no types, no abilities, and no mana cost. It will still be face up. Its controller can’t pay {2}{B}{B} to turn it face up.

cited_text.702.47c: Splice The spell has the characteristics of the main spell, plus the rules text of each of the spliced cards. This is a text-changing effect (see rule 612, “Text-Changing Effects”). The spell doesn’t gain any other characteristics (name, mana cost, color, supertypes, card types, subtypes, etc.) of the spliced cards. Text gained by the spell that refers to a card by name refers to the spell on the stack, not the card from which the text was copied. Glacial Ray is a red card with splice onto Arcane that reads, “Glacial Ray deals 2 damage to any target.” Suppose Glacial Ray is spliced onto Reach Through Mists, a blue spell. The spell is still blue, and Reach Through Mists deals the damage. This means that the ability can target a creature with protection from red and deal 2 damage to that creature.
cited_text.612.10: A splice ability changes a spell’s text by adding the rules text of the card with splice to the spell, following that spell’s own rules text. It doesn’t modify or replace any of that spell’s own text. (See rule 702.47, “Splice.”)
cited_text.702.40a: Storm Storm is a triggered ability that functions on the stack. “Storm” means “When you cast this spell, copy it for each other spell that was cast before it this turn. If the spell has any targets, you may choose new targets for any of the copies.”
cited_text.707.10: To copy a spell, activated ability, or triggered ability means to put a copy of it onto the stack; a copy of a spell isn’t cast and a copy of an activated ability isn’t activated. A copy of a spell or ability copies both the characteristics of the spell or ability and all decisions made for it, including modes, targets, the value of X, and additional or alternative costs. (See rule 601, “Casting Spells.”) Choices that are normally made on resolution are not copied. If an effect of the copy refers to objects used to pay its costs, it uses the objects used to pay the costs of the original spell or ability. A copy of a spell is owned by the player under whose control it was put on the stack. A copy of a spell or ability is controlled by the player under whose control it was put on the stack. A copy of a spell is itself a spell, even though it has no spell card associated with it. A copy of an ability is itself an ability. A player casts Fork, targeting an Emerald Charm. Fork reads, “Copy target instant or sorcery spell, except that the copy is red. You may choose new targets for the copy.” Emerald Charm is a modal green instant. When the Fork resolves, it puts a copy of the Emerald Charm on the stack except the copy is red, not green. The copy has the same mode that was chosen for the original Emerald Charm. It does not necessarily have the same target, but only because Fork allows choosing of new targets. Fling is an instant that reads, “As an additional cost to cast this spell, sacrifice a creature” and “Fling deals damage equal to the sacrificed creature’s power to any target.” When determining how much damage a copy of Fling deals, it checks the power of the creature sacrificed to pay for the original Fling. Dawnglow Infusion is a sorcery that reads, “You gain X life if {G} was spent to cast this spell and X life if {W} was spent to cast it.” Because mana isn’t an object, a copy of Dawnglow Infusion won’t cause you to gain any life, no matter what mana was spent to cast the original spell.

answer_gold: Yes. As Addison is casting Elemental Eruption they choose whether they want to splice as part of the casting process. When the storm trigger resolves it copies all the choices made when casting the original spell, including the choice to splice.

question: Nova controls a [Torsten Von Ursus] enchanted by their [Felidar Umbra]. Allen activates the last ability of [Sorin, Lord of Innistrad], targeting the Torsten Von Ursus. What happens?
answer:
Torsten Von Ursus is not destroyed and Allen gains nothing. Felidar Umbra grants umbra armor, which reads "If enchanted permanent would be destroyed, instead remove all damage marked on it and destroy this Aura" [702.89a]. So when Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's −6 ability resolves and tries to destroy Torsten Von Ursus, that destruction event is replaced: all damage marked on Torsten Von Ursus is removed, and Felidar Umbra is destroyed instead, going to Nova's graveyard. Torsten Von Ursus stays on the battlefield under Nova's control.

Because Torsten Von Ursus was never actually destroyed, no card was put into a graveyard "this way" for it, so Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's reanimation clause doesn't return Torsten Von Ursus to the battlefield under Allen's control. Felidar Umbra was destroyed by its own umbra armor replacement effect rather than by Sorin, Lord of Innistrad destroying a target, so Allen doesn't get Felidar Umbra either — and Felidar Umbra wasn't a legal target of that ability anyway (it targets creatures and/or other planeswalkers).

Note also that Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's ability may target up to three creatures and/or other planeswalkers; any other legal targets are destroyed normally and those cards do return to the battlefield under Allen's control. If Torsten Von Ursus had somehow become an illegal target (e.g., left the battlefield) before resolution, that part of the effect simply wouldn't affect it, and the ability would still resolve for its remaining legal targets [608.2b].

This analysis is the same regardless of the number of players at the table; nothing here depends on player count. Also, "totem armor" on older printings is the same ability, now called umbra armor [702.89b].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.303.4f: Some enchantments have the subtype “Aura.” An Aura enters the battlefield attached to an object or player. What an Aura can be attached to is defined by its enchant keyword ability (see rule 702.5, “Enchant”). Other effects can limit what a permanent can be enchanted by. If an Aura is entering the battlefield under a player’s control by any means other than by resolving as an Aura spell, and the effect putting it onto the battlefield doesn’t specify the object or player the Aura will enchant, that player chooses what it will enchant as the Aura enters the battlefield. The player must choose a legal object or player according to the Aura’s enchant ability and any other applicable effects.
gold_text.702.89a: Umbra Armor Umbra armor is a static ability that appears on some Auras. “Umbra armor” means “If enchanted permanent would be destroyed, instead remove all damage marked on it and destroy this Aura.”

cited_text.702.89a: Umbra Armor Umbra armor is a static ability that appears on some Auras. “Umbra armor” means “If enchanted permanent would be destroyed, instead remove all damage marked on it and destroy this Aura.”
cited_text.702.89b: Umbra Armor Some older cards were printed with the ability “totem armor” or referenced that ability. The text of these cards has been updated in the Oracle card reference to refer to umbra armor instead.
cited_text.608.2b: If the object that’s resolving is an instant spell, a sorcery spell, or an ability, its resolution may involve several steps. The steps described in rules 608.2a and 608.2b are followed first. The steps described in rules 608.2c–m are then followed as appropriate, in no specific order. The steps described in rule 608.2n and 608.2p are followed last. If the spell or ability specifies targets, it checks whether the targets are still legal. A target that’s no longer in the zone it was in when it was targeted is illegal. Other changes to the game state may cause a target to no longer be legal; for example, its characteristics may have changed or an effect may have changed the text of the spell. If the source of an ability has left the zone it was in, its last known information is used during this process. If all its targets, for every instance of the word “target,” are now illegal, the spell or ability doesn’t resolve. It’s removed from the stack and, if it’s a spell, put into its owner’s graveyard. Otherwise, the spell or ability will resolve normally. Illegal targets, if any, won’t be affected by parts of a resolving spell’s effect for which they’re illegal. Other parts of the effect for which those targets are not illegal may still affect them. If the spell or ability creates any continuous effects that affect game rules (see rule 613.11), those effects don’t apply to illegal targets. If part of the effect requires information about an illegal target, it fails to determine any such information. Any part of the effect that requires that information won’t happen. Sorin’s Thirst is a black instant that reads, “Sorin’s Thirst deals 2 damage to target creature and you gain 2 life.” If the creature isn’t a legal target during the resolution of Sorin’s Thirst (say, if the creature has gained protection from black or left the battlefield), then Sorin’s Thirst doesn’t resolve. Its controller doesn’t gain any life. Plague Spores reads, “Destroy target nonblack creature and target land. They can’t be regenerated.” Suppose the same creature land is chosen both as the nonblack creature and as the land, and the color of the creature land is changed to black before Plague Spores resolves. Plague Spores still resolves because the black creature land is still a legal target for the “target land” part of the spell. The “destroy target nonblack creature” part of the spell won’t affect that permanent, but the “destroy target land” part of the spell will still destroy it. It can’t be regenerated.

answer_gold: The Felidar Umbra is destroyed instead of the Torsten Von Ursus. It is then returned to the battlefield by the rest of Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's ability. The only creature on the battlefield is the Torsten Von Ursus, so the Felidar Umbra must enter the battlefield enchanting the Torsten Von Ursus. Felidar Umbra is now controlled by Allen.

question: Nico controls [Containment Priest]. Alma attempts to play [Dryad Arbor], which is exiled. Can Alma now play [Sequestered Stash] as their land for turn?
answer:
No. Alma has already used their land play for the turn by playing Dryad Arbor, so they can't also play Sequestered Stash this turn.

Why: Dryad Arbor is both a land and a creature, and an object that's both a land and another card type can only be played as a land — it can't be cast as a spell (rules 305.9, 300.2a). Playing a land is a special action that doesn't use the stack; the player simply puts the land onto the battlefield (rules 305.1, 701.18a). That special action is complete and counts as a land played this turn.

Containment Priest reads "If a nontoken creature would enter and it wasn't cast, exile it instead." Dryad Arbor is a nontoken creature that entered without being cast (it was played as a land), so Containment Priest's replacement effect exiles it. But a replacement effect changing where Dryad Arbor ends up doesn't undo or refund the land play — Alma still played a land.

To check legality, compare the number of lands Alma may play this turn with the number already played, including lands played as special actions (rule 305.2a). Normally that's one, and Alma has played one, so Alma can't play Sequestered Stash (rule 305.2b). If Alma has an effect granting an additional land play (e.g., "you may play an additional land this turn"), then playing Sequestered Stash is legal, provided it's Alma's main phase, the stack is empty, and Alma has priority (rules 305.1, 505.6b).

Note also that had Alma somehow tried to "put" Dryad Arbor onto the battlefield via a spell or ability instead of playing it, that would not have used a land drop (rules 305.4, 701.18a) — but that's not what happened here.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count; it works the same at a two-player or multiplayer table, since only Alma's own land plays and Alma's own turn matter (rule 305.3).

question: Norah controls [Blood Sun]. Ari plays [Dark Depths] and then destroys the Blood Sun with [Sultai Charm]. What happens?
answer:
Ari gets Marit Lage. Step by step:

While Norah's Blood Sun is on the battlefield, its static ability "All lands lose all abilities except mana abilities" strips Dark Depths of everything except mana abilities. Dark Depths has no mana ability at all, so it loses (a) the replacement ability "Dark Depths enters with ten ice counters on it," (b) the "{3}: Remove an ice counter" activated ability, and (c) the state-triggered ability "When Dark Depths has no ice counters on it, sacrifice it. If you do, create Marit Lage..."

Because the counter-placing ability is a replacement effect that must apply as Dark Depths enters, and it's already been removed by Blood Sun at that moment, Dark Depths enters the battlefield with zero ice counters. Its sacrifice trigger is also turned off, so nothing happens yet.

Ari then casts Sultai Charm choosing "Destroy target artifact or enchantment" targeting Blood Sun (Blood Sun is an enchantment, so it's a legal target). When Blood Sun leaves the battlefield, its ability-stripping effect ends and Dark Depths immediately gets all of its abilities back — including the state trigger. Dark Depths currently has no ice counters on it, so that state-triggered condition is already true and the ability triggers the next time a player would receive priority (state-based actions and triggers are handled before priority). It goes on the stack, and on resolution Ari sacrifices Dark Depths and creates Marit Lage, a legendary 20/20 black Avatar creature token with flying and indestructible — without ever paying {3} to remove a counter.

Assumption on timing: I'm reading the question as Dark Depths entering while Blood Sun was already on the battlefield, then Blood Sun being destroyed afterward. If instead Blood Sun were destroyed first and Dark Depths played after, Dark Depths would enter with ten ice counters and Ari would have to pay {3} ten times.

This works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

Voice of All says “As this creature enters, choose a color” and “This creature has protection from the chosen color.” An effect creates a token that’s a copy of Voice of All. As that token is created, the token’s controller chooses a color for it. answer_gold: Dark Depths entered the battlefield with no ice counters, since it didn't have the ability that would cause it to enter with them. When Blood Sun is destroyed, Dark Depths triggers since it has no ice counters on it and creates a Marit Lage token.

question: Alec controls [Elspeth Conquers Death] and puts the third lore counter it. With the triggered ability, they target [Eternal Witness] in their graveyard. When Eternal Witness returns to the battlefield, can it target Elspeth Conquers Death with its trigger?
answer:
Short answer: Yes — Eternal Witness can target Elspeth Conquers Death with its enters trigger, because by the time that trigger is put on the stack Elspeth Conquers Death is itself a card in Alec's graveyard, and Eternal Witness says "return target card from your graveyard to your hand" (any card type qualifies).

Why the timing works: Eternal Witness returns to the battlefield during the resolution of the chapter III triggered ability of Elspeth Conquers Death. Its "When this creature enters" ability triggers at that moment, but a triggered ability's targets are declared as part of putting the ability on the stack, not at the moment it triggers [115.1d]. That happens after the chapter III ability has finished resolving and Elspeth Conquers Death has been sacrificed (the Saga's own text: "Sacrifice after III"), so the Saga card is in the graveyard and is a legal target.

Assumption stated plainly: I'm assuming the sacrifice of Elspeth Conquers Death happens before Eternal Witness's trigger is put on the stack and targets are chosen. The rules excerpt provided here does not include the specific rule governing exactly when a Saga is sacrificed after its final chapter ability resolves, so that part rests on the card's own "Sacrifice after III" text rather than a numbered rule I can cite. If instead the Saga were somehow still on the battlefield when the trigger was put on the stack, Elspeth Conquers Death would not yet be a card in the graveyard and could not be chosen as the target — Alec would have to pick some other graveyard card (or, since the trigger says "you may," decline on resolution).

Player count doesn't matter here: nothing in this interaction depends on how many opponents Alec has, so the answer is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

See rule 714, “Saga Cards.”

Yes.

After this, triggers are placed onto the stack, and Elspeth Conquers Death is in the graveyard able to be the target of Eternal Witness's triggered ability.

question: Autumn attacks with [Robber of the Rich], exiling [Light Up the Stage] from Nehemiah's library. Can Autumn pay Light Up the Stage's Spectacle cost with only {C}?
answer:
Yes — assuming an opponent has actually lost life this turn, Autumn can pay Light Up the Stage's spectacle cost of {R} using a single {C}.

Why: Spectacle is a static ability that works on the stack, meaning "You may pay [cost] rather than pay this spell's mana cost if an opponent lost life this turn" [702.137a]. Light Up the Stage's spectacle cost is {R}, a single red mana — not generic, so ordinarily colorless mana could not pay it. However, Robber of the Rich's own text says that during any turn you attacked with a Rogue, you may cast that exiled card "and you may spend mana as though it were mana of any color to cast that spell." That card text lets Autumn spend {C} as though it were {R}. Per 609.4b, an effect that lets you spend mana "as though it were mana of any color" affects only how you may pay a cost — it doesn't change the cost itself, and the mana actually spent is still colorless. So the cost paid is still {R} (satisfied by one {C}), not {1}.

Two conditions to check first:
- Spectacle requires that an opponent lost life this turn [702.137a]. Robber of the Rich's attack trigger only exiles a card; it causes no life loss. If Autumn's attack has connected for combat damage to Nehemiah (or some other life loss happened), spectacle is available. Timing note: I'm assuming Autumn tries to cast Light Up the Stage after combat damage is dealt. If Autumn instead tries to cast it earlier in combat, before any opponent has lost life this turn, spectacle simply isn't an available alternative cost yet and Autumn would have to pay {2}{R} instead (again able to use colorless mana for the {R} thanks to Robber of the Rich).
- Robber of the Rich's permission applies during any turn Autumn attacked with a Rogue, and Robber of the Rich is a Rogue, so that's satisfied.

Paying an alternative cost like spectacle follows the normal cost-payment rules [601.2h], and Autumn must have the resources in full — one mana here [118.3].

Multiplayer note: Robber of the Rich's trigger checks the defending player (Nehemiah) specifically, while spectacle checks whether any opponent lost life. At a table with more than two players, life lost by a different opponent also turns spectacle on, even if Nehemiah took no damage. In a two-player game the only opponent is Nehemiah.

question: Aiden controls [Volrath's Shapeshifter] and [Yixlid Jailer]. The top card of their graveyard is [Mistform Skyreaver]. Does Volrath's Shapeshifter have flying?
answer:
Yes — Volrath's Shapeshifter has flying (and is a 6/6 Illusion named Mistform Skyreaver with the mana cost {5}{U}{U}, plus "{2}: Discard a card").

Why: Volrath's Shapeshifter says that while the top card of your graveyard is a creature card, it has the full text of that card. Rule [612.6] explains that "full text" means Volrath's Shapeshifter takes on the other object's name, mana cost, color indicator, types, abilities, power, and toughness — here, everything printed on Mistform Skyreaver, including Flying, which is the evasion ability described in [702.9a] and [702.9b] (a creature with flying can only be blocked by creatures with flying and/or reach, per [702.9b] and [702.17b]).

Yixlid Jailer says "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities." That effect applies to the card Mistform Skyreaver while it sits in Aiden's graveyard — it does not apply to Volrath's Shapeshifter, which is a permanent on the battlefield, not a card in a graveyard. Yixlid Jailer therefore stops Mistform Skyreaver from doing anything from the graveyard, but Volrath's Shapeshifter's own ability (which is still functioning, since Volrath's Shapeshifter is on the battlefield) is what grants the text, so Volrath's Shapeshifter ends up with Flying and the "{1}: This creature becomes the creature type of your choice until end of turn" ability.

A note on the ability Volrath's Shapeshifter grants: because Volrath's Shapeshifter never entered the battlefield as Mistform Skyreaver, any "as this enters" choices from a copied card would be undefined ([607.5a]) — but Mistform Skyreaver has no such choice, so that's not an issue here.

Player count doesn't matter: nothing in this interaction depends on the number of opponents, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game.

question: Autumn controls [Bridge from Below] and [Silvercoat Lion]. They cast [Hour of Revelation]. Do they create a Zombie token?
answer:
No — Autumn does not create a Zombie token.

Bridge from Below's first ability only functions while Bridge from Below itself is in the graveyard ("if this card is in your graveyard"). In this situation Bridge from Below is on the battlefield when Hour of Revelation resolves, and Hour of Revelation destroys all nonland permanents, so Bridge from Below and Silvercoat Lion are put into the graveyard simultaneously.

The trigger condition "whenever a nontoken creature is put into your graveyard from the battlefield" is a leaves-the-battlefield trigger, and rule [603.10a] tells the game to "look back in time": it uses the objects and abilities as they existed immediately before the event. Immediately before Silvercoat Lion died, Bridge from Below was on the battlefield, not in the graveyard, so its graveyard-only ability wasn't there to trigger. Compare the [603.10a] example, where an artifact on the battlefield with "whenever a creature dies" still triggers — that works because the ability functioned from the battlefield, which is exactly what Bridge from Below's ability does not do.

So Silvercoat Lion's death yields nothing, and Bridge from Below simply sits in the graveyard afterward, ready to trigger on future nontoken creature deaths.

Timing note: I'm assuming Bridge from Below was on the battlefield when Hour of Revelation resolved. If instead Bridge from Below had already been in Autumn's graveyard beforehand and only Silvercoat Lion was destroyed, the ability would trigger and Autumn would create one 2/2 black Zombie creature token.

Cost aside: Hour of Revelation costs {3}{W}{W}{W}, reduced to {W}{W}{W} if ten or more nonland permanents are on the battlefield — the reduction only touches the generic {3}, never the {W}{W}{W}.

This answer is the same whether the game has two players or more; nothing here depends on the number of opponents (Bridge from Below's second ability, about a creature dying under an opponent's control, would similarly key off any opponent).

question: Axl activates [Ring of Ma'rûf]'s ability in their upkeep. What happens in Axl's draw step if they don't own any cards outside the game?
answer:
Nothing happens: Axl's draw-step draw is replaced and Axl ends up with no card. The turn-based draw at the beginning of the draw step (rule 504.1) is the "next time you would draw a card this turn," so Ring of Ma'r\u00fbf's replacement effect applies to it. Instead of drawing, Axl is instructed to put a card they own from outside the game into their hand \u2014 and since they own no such cards, they simply put nothing into their hand.

Key points:

1. Ring of Ma'r\u00fbf's ability sets up a replacement effect on a card draw. Effects that replace card draws are applied even when the draw couldn't have happened normally (rules 121.6a and 614.11), so the replacement absolutely applies here \u2014 it isn't skipped for being partly impossible.

2. "Outside the game" isn't a zone at all; it's simply cards not in any of the game's zones, such as sideboard cards in sanctioned play or your collection in casual play (rule 400.11c). If Axl owns nothing there that they can legally bring in, the instruction does as much as possible, which is nothing.

3. Because the draw was replaced, Axl never actually attempts to draw a card. That matters if Axl's library is empty: there's no attempted draw from an empty library, so the state-based action that would make Axl lose the game (rules 121.4 and 704.5b) doesn't trigger. Axl just gets no card and the draw step continues normally.

Timing note: I'm assuming the Ring of Ma'r\u00fbf activation resolved during the upkeep and that no other draw occurred between resolution and the draw step. If Axl had drawn a card for any other reason first (a triggered draw in upkeep, for instance), that earlier draw would have been the one replaced, and the draw step draw would be a normal draw.

This answer is the same whether the game has two players or more \u2014 nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

question: Athena control [Krark, the Thumbless] and [Spark Double] copying it. They cast [Song of Totentanz], which triggers both Krark, the Thumbless. When the first trigger resolves they lose the flip and return Song of Totentanz to hand. What happens when the second trigger resolves?
answer:
Short answer: the provided rules don't contain what's needed to settle this, so I won't guess at the outcome.

What's at issue: the second Krark, the Thumbless trigger (from the Spark Double that entered as a copy of Krark, the Thumbless — note Spark Double's copy isn't legendary, so both can coexist) refers to "that spell," meaning Song of Totentanz. To state authoritatively whether the coin flip is still performed and whether the trigger simply does as much as it can (or is removed from the stack), I would need the rules on resolving a spell or ability whose referenced object no longer exists / doing as much as possible (rule 608.2 and related), the rules on coin flips (701.x), and the copy rules for copying a spell on the stack (707.10). None of those are in the context I was given. The context's copy-related rule about linked copy effects and the state-based-action, melded-permanent, and end-the-turn rules provided don't address this situation.

question: Alden cast [Ixidron]. Natalie controls a very cute [Tangled Florahedron]. What happens to it?
answer:
Short answer: the provided materials don't settle this one, because the key rule about modal double-faced cards and face-down status isn't in the context.

What the context does support: Ixidron's text "As this creature enters, turn all other nontoken creatures face down" is a replacement effect that modifies how Ixidron enters the battlefield, applied as it enters rather than after (rule 614.12, and see 616.1f for how multiple such effects are ordered). Natalie's Tangled Florahedron, on its front face, is a nontoken creature she controls, so it is within the set of objects Ixidron's ability describes. If it were turned face down it would be a 2/2 with no name, no types beyond creature, and no abilities (so no "{T}: Add {G}"), and Ixidron's power and toughness — each equal to the number of face-down creatures on the battlefield — would count it.

Why I'm not asserting that outcome: Tangled Florahedron // Tangled Vale is a modal double-faced card. The Comprehensive Rules contain a specific restriction on turning double-faced cards face down, and that rule was not provided here, so I can't confirm from this context whether Tangled Florahedron is actually turned face down or simply unaffected. Rule 712.5f, the only 712 rule given, is about meld pairs and doesn't help.

Timing note: I'm assuming Tangled Florahedron was already on the battlefield as a creature when Ixidron resolved and entered. If Natalie instead had it on the battlefield as Tangled Vale (a land), it wouldn't be a creature at all and Ixidron's ability would simply ignore it; if it entered after Ixidron, Ixidron's as-enters ability has already finished and wouldn't touch it.

Player count doesn't change any of this: Ixidron's ability says "all other nontoken creatures," not just an opponent's, so in a multiplayer game every player's nontoken creatures (including Alden's) are affected the same way.

question: Amani controls [Leyline of the Void] and casts [Hypnotic Cloud] to have Nicolas discard a card. Nicolas discards [Loxodon Smiter]. Does it end up on the battlefield or in exile?
answer:
Nicolas chooses, so in practice Loxodon Smiter ends up on the battlefield (under Nicolas's control) if Nicolas wants it there; only if Nicolas chose the other effect would it be exiled.

Why: discarding means moving the card from its owner's hand to that player's graveyard [Discard], and two replacement effects are both trying to change that same event:
- Loxodon Smiter's own text: "If a spell or ability an opponent controls causes you to discard this card, put it onto the battlefield instead of putting it into your graveyard." Hypnotic Cloud is a spell controlled by Amani, an opponent of Nicolas, so this applies. Note that Loxodon Smiter's printed text is what creates this exception to the normal discard-to-graveyard rule.
- Leyline of the Void: "If a card would be put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere, exile it instead." Nicolas is an opponent of Amani, its controller, so this also applies.

When multiple replacement effects would apply to the same event, the affected object's controller — or, for a card not on the battlefield, its owner — chooses one to apply first; the analogous choice is shown in the example at [712.21d], where the affected player chooses one of Leyline of the Void's or Wheel of Sun and Moon's effects. Here the affected card is Loxodon Smiter in Nicolas's hand, so Nicolas makes the choice. If Nicolas applies Loxodon Smiter's own effect, the card is put onto the battlefield instead, the card never heads to a graveyard, and Leyline of the Void's effect no longer has an event to replace. Loxodon Smiter enters under Nicolas's control, since he's the player the effect instructs to put it onto the battlefield [110.2a]. If Nicolas instead applies Leyline of the Void, Loxodon Smiter is exiled and never reaches the battlefield.

Timing assumption: this is all one discard event during Hypnotic Cloud's resolution, with both Leyline of the Void and Loxodon Smiter's ability applicable at that moment; nothing changes if Hypnotic Cloud was kicked (each of the three discarded cards is handled the same way).

Multiplayer: the answer is the same at any table size. Leyline of the Void checks "an opponent's graveyard," so it applies to every opponent of Amani, and Loxodon Smiter's clause applies as long as the discard was caused by a spell or ability an opponent of Nicolas controls — true here regardless of how many players are in the game.

question: In a Commander game with 4 players, Ari casts [Kardur, Doomscourge]. Bode controls [Oxidda Finisher], and [Parhelion II], which is not a creature at the time Kardur, Doomscourge's enter the battlefield ability resolves. During Bode's next turn, can they attack Ari with Parhelion II? Can they have the Angel tokens created by Parhelion II attack Ari?
answer:
Short answer: with Parhelion II, no — assuming Bode has another opponent to attack, Parhelion II must attack someone other than Ari. But the two Angel tokens created by Parhelion II's attack trigger can be put onto the battlefield attacking Ari.

Parhelion II: Kardur, Doomscourge's ability says "until your next turn, creatures your opponents control attack each combat if able and attack a player other than you if able." That's a continuous effect that looks at what is a creature at the time attackers are declared, not only at the moment the ability resolved. So even though Parhelion II wasn't a creature when the trigger resolved, once Bode crews it (Crew 4) during their turn it is an artifact creature Bode controls, and the requirement/restriction applies: Parhelion II must attack, and it must attack a player other than Ari if able. In this four-player Commander game Bode has two other opponents besides Ari, and Commander uses no attack-left/attack-right restriction, so all of Bode's opponents (and their planeswalkers/battles) are legal targets of attack (rule 801.3; the seating restrictions in 803.1a, 803.1b, 811.4 and 809.3c apply only to those specific variants, which Commander is not). Because attacking a non-Ari player is possible, Parhelion II can't be declared as attacking Ari (508.1b). If Ari were somehow Bode's only remaining opponent, Parhelion II would have to attack Ari. Note also that Oxidda Finisher is likewise subject to Kardur, Doomscourge's effect and must attack a player other than Ari if able.

The Angel tokens: Parhelion II's trigger creates two 4/4 Angels "that are attacking." Under rule 508.4a/508.4b, a creature put onto the battlefield attacking has its controller choose which defending player, planeswalker, or battle it's attacking as it enters (the effect here doesn't specify), and such creatures are "attacking" but never "attacked" — they were never declared as attackers. Kardur, Doomscourge's requirement/restriction constrains the declaration of attackers, so it doesn't govern this choice; Bode may choose Ari for both Angel tokens. Bode could also choose a planeswalker Ari controls or a battle Ari protects (506.3, 506.3c).

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Parhelion II is crewed and attacks during Bode's turn while Kardur, Doomscourge's effect is still active (i.e., before Ari's next turn). If Bode's combat happens after Ari's next turn begins, the effect has expired and Parhelion II could freely attack Ari.

In a two-player game the analysis would differ: with Ari as the only opponent, Parhelion II would have to attack Ari, since "attack a player other than you if able" couldn't be satisfied.

answer_gold:
Bode cannot attack Ari with Parhelion II, but they can choose for the Angel tokens to attack Ari.

Kardur, Doomscourge's enters-the-battlefield ability sets up a rules change that causes any creatures Ari's opponents control to have to attack if able and to have to attack another player if able. The Angel tokens are created attacking, but are never declared as attackers. Because of this, Bode can choose Ari to be the defending player for the tokens.

question: Aislinn controls two [Bramblewood Paragon]s and casts [Thunder-Thrash Elder]. What is the maximum amount of counters Thunder-Thrash Elder can enter the battlefield with?
answer:
With only the two Bramblewood Paragons available to sacrifice, Thunder-Thrash Elder can enter with a maximum of 8 +1/+1 counters.

How that breaks down:

- Devour 3 on Thunder-Thrash Elder lets Aislinn sacrifice any number of creatures as it enters; it enters with three times that many +1/+1 counters. Sacrificing both Bramblewood Paragons gives 2 × 3 = 6 counters.
- Each Bramblewood Paragon says "Each other Warrior creature you control enters with an additional +1/+1 counter on it." Thunder-Thrash Elder is a Lizard Warrior, so each of the two Bramblewood Paragons adds one more counter: +2. Both still apply, because all of these are replacement effects that modify how Thunder-Thrash Elder enters the battlefield and are applied together as it enters; the sacrifice for devour happens as part of that same event (614.13b), so the Bramblewood Paragons' abilities are still in effect when the counters are determined.
- 6 + 2 = 8 counters, and Aislinn (Thunder-Thrash Elder's controller) puts them on it (122.6a).

Assumption stated plainly: I'm assuming the only creatures Aislinn could sacrifice are the two Bramblewood Paragons. Devour has no cap on how many creatures you sacrifice, so if Aislinn controlled additional creatures the maximum would be 3 counters per sacrificed creature plus 2 from the two Bramblewood Paragons. Note also that if Aislinn sacrificed no creatures, Thunder-Thrash Elder would still enter with just the 2 counters from the Bramblewood Paragons (614.13b's example confirms devour can be used for zero).

Nothing here depends on player count: this works identically in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

Such effects watch for a particular event that would happen and completely or partially replace that event with a different event. They act like “shields” around whatever they’re affecting. Effects that read “[This permanent] enters with . . . ,” “As [this permanent] enters . . . ,” or “[This permanent] enters as . . . “ are replacement effects.

The same object can’t be chosen to change zones more than once when applying replacement effects that modify how one or more permanents enter the battlefield. Jund (a plane card) says, “Whenever a player casts a black, red, or green creature spell, it gains devour 5.” A player controls Runeclaw Bear and casts Thunder-Thrash Elder, a red creature spell with devour 3. As Thunder-Thrash Elder enters the battlefield, its controller can choose to sacrifice Runeclaw Bear when applying the devour 3 effect or when applying the devour 5 effect, but not both. Thunder-Thrash Elder will enter the battlefield with zero, three, or five +1/+1 counters, depending on this choice.

If the effect doesn’t specify a player, the object’s controller puts those counters on it.

While Thunder-Thrash Elder is entering the battlefield the game checks which replacement effects to apply, and sees that there are two Bramblewood Paragons that want to place an additional +1/+1 counter on Thunder-Thrash Elder as well as a Devour ability. If Aislinn chooses to devour the Bramblewood Paragons, they will place an additional six +1/+1 counters on Thunder-Thrash Elder.

question: Nico controls [Urza's Saga] with two lore counters on it. Alexzander uses [Jinx] to change its land type. What happens?
answer:
Short answer: Jinx makes Urza's Saga a basic land type of Alexzander's choice until end of turn, which strips Urza's Saga of the abilities generated by its own rules text — including its three chapter abilities. While that's true, Urza's Saga is no longer a Saga permanent "with one or more chapter abilities," so the sacrifice state-based action can't apply to it, and no chapter ability can trigger from lore counters. When Jinx's effect ends at end of turn, Urza's Saga gets its chapter abilities back, keeping whatever lore counters are on it.

Details:

1. Type change: Jinx says "Target land becomes the basic land type of your choice until end of turn." Setting a land's subtype to a basic land type means the land loses its old land types, loses all abilities generated from its rules text, its old land types, and copiable effects affecting it, and gains the mana ability for the new basic type [305.7]. Card types and supertypes are unchanged [305.7], [205.4b], so Urza's Saga is still an enchantment land.

2. Lost abilities: a chapter symbol is a keyword ability printed in Urza's Saga's text box representing a triggered ability [107.15a], [714.2b]. Since those come from its rules text, chapters I, II, and III are gone for the turn. Abilities that were *granted* to the land by other effects are not removed [305.7] — so if chapter I and/or chapter II had already resolved and granted Urza's Saga "{T}: Add {C}" and the "{2}, {T}: Create a 0/0 Construct token…" ability, those granted abilities remain usable this turn (note that {C} is colorless mana specifically, not generic).

3. No sacrifice, no chapter III: the sacrifice happens only if the number of lore counters on a Saga permanent *with one or more chapter abilities* is at least its final chapter number [704.5s], [714.4]. With two counters and no chapter abilities, nothing happens. Even if a third counter were somehow added while Jinx's effect is active, no chapter ability exists to trigger [714.2b], and no sacrifice occurs.

4. After end of turn: Jinx wears off, Urza's Saga is again an Urza's Saga land with its chapter abilities. It still has two lore counters (the type change doesn't remove counters), so it is not yet sacrificed. On Nico's next turn a lore counter is added — Urza's Saga's own text says "after your draw step," which overrides the general precombat-main-phase turn-based action in [703.4f]/[505.4]/[714.3c] — reaching three counters, chapter III triggers, and after that ability leaves the stack Nico sacrifices Urza's Saga [704.5s].

Timing assumption: I assumed Jinx resolves while Urza's Saga has exactly two counters and that Jinx's effect expires before the next lore counter is added. If instead Jinx resolved during the same turn *after* a third counter went on but while chapter III's trigger was still on the stack, chapter III would still resolve (an ability on the stack exists independently of its source), and the sacrifice would then occur once the type change ends and Urza's Saga again has chapter abilities.

Player count doesn't matter here: this works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table, since Jinx targets a single land and the lore-counter turn-based action is per-controller [505.4].

question: Is [Umori, the Collector] a legal companion for a deck containing only [Grist, the Hunger Tide], creatures, and lands?
answer:
Yes. Umori, the Collector is a legal companion for that deck. Umori, the Collector's companion condition is "Each nonland card in your starting deck shares a card type," and Grist, the Hunger Tide has the ability "As long as Grist isn't on the battlefield, it's a 1/1 Insect creature in addition to its other types." While Grist, the Hunger Tide is in your deck (and while it's outside the game), it is not on the battlefield, so it is a creature card in addition to being a planeswalker card. Every nonland card therefore shares the card type creature, satisfying Umori, the Collector's condition.

Details and caveats:
- The check is made on your starting deck, which is your deck after sideboard cards are set aside; in a Commander game it's also before you set aside your commander [702.139b]. So if you're playing Commander, your commander card also has to share the creature type for Umori, the Collector to be legal.
- You reveal the companion from outside the game before the game begins, as part of the pregame procedure, and it stays outside the game [103.2b], [702.139a]. Once during the game, when you have priority with an empty stack during a main phase of your turn, you may pay {3} (three generic mana) as a special action to put Umori, the Collector into your hand [702.139a], [Companion].
- If this is a Commander deck, the color identity rule also applies: Umori, the Collector's color identity is black and green (from its {B/G} hybrid symbols), so every color in it must be within your commander's color identity for it to enter the game from outside [903.11a], [903.4], [903.5c].
- These rules are the same regardless of the number of players; nothing here depends on a two-player game.

question: Abel crews their [Adrestia]. Nathalie activates their [Mobilized District] causing it to become a creature. After that resolves, Nathalie casts [Mirrorweave] targeting their Mobilized District. What are Adrestia's characteristics after Mirrorweave resolves?
answer:
Adrestia becomes a copy of Mobilized District's copiable values: a nonlegendary land named Mobilized District with no mana cost, no power/toughness, and the abilities "{T}: Add {C}" and "{4}: This land becomes a 3/3 Citizen creature with vigilance until end of turn. It's still a land. This ability costs {1} less to activate for each legendary creature and planeswalker you control." It is no longer an artifact, a Vehicle, legendary, 4/3, or a creature, and it loses islandwalk and its attack trigger and Crew 1.

Why: a copy effect copies only the copiable values — the values derived from the printed text (name, mana cost, color indicator, card types, subtypes, supertypes, rules text, power, toughness, loyalty), as modified by other copy effects, face-down status, and "as … enters" abilities that set power and toughness. Other continuous effects, including type-changing effects, counters, and status, are NOT copied [707.2] [707.2a]. So the resolved activated ability that turned Mobilized District into a 3/3 Citizen creature with vigilance is not part of what Adrestia copies — Adrestia copies the plain land. Copy effects are applied in layer 1 (sublayer 1a) before other layers [613.1a] [613.2a] [613.2c].

Consequences: because Adrestia is now a noncreature land, having been crewed earlier is irrelevant; if it was attacking, it's removed from combat as it's no longer a creature (Mirrorweave's own copy effect does the work; nothing in the copy makes it a creature). Adrestia could later be animated by activating the copied {4} ability (reduced by {1} for each legendary creature and planeswalker its controller controls) to become a 3/3 Citizen with vigilance until end of turn. Mirrorweave's effect ends at end of turn, after which Adrestia returns to being the legendary 4/3 artifact Vehicle.

Timing note: I'm assuming Mobilized District's animation ability had fully resolved before Mirrorweave was cast, as stated. That ordering doesn't change the result — even if the animation resolved after Mirrorweave, Adrestia's copied values would still be the plain land, since type-changing effects apply in a later layer and only to the permanent they affect.

Multiplayer note: nothing here depends on the number of players; Mirrorweave affects each other creature on the battlefield regardless of controller, so in a game with more than two players every other creature (not just Abel's) becomes a copy of Mobilized District too.

question: Ari controls a [Lunarch Inquisitors] that exiled a [Jasmine Boreal] when it transformed. Nyla casts [Moonmist]. Does the Jasmine Boreal return to the battlefield?
answer:
No. Jasmine Boreal stays in exile.

Lunarch Inquisitors' exile effect lasts "until this creature leaves the battlefield." Moonmist reads "Transform all Humans," and Lunarch Inquisitors is a Human Cleric represented by a double-faced card, so it does transform back to its front face, Avacynian Missionaries (see rule 712.9 — only permanents represented by double-faced tokens/cards, other than meld cards, can transform). But transforming does not move the permanent between zones; it stays on the battlefield as the same permanent, so the specified event ("leaves the battlefield") never occurs and the second one-shot effect that would return Jasmine Boreal is never created (rule 610.3c). Jasmine Boreal remains exiled indefinitely until Avacynian Missionaries // Lunarch Inquisitors actually leaves the battlefield.

Also note Jasmine Boreal is itself a Human, but it is in the exile zone, not on the battlefield, so Moonmist's transform instruction doesn't bring it back or otherwise affect it (and it isn't a double-faced card anyway, so nothing would happen to it — rule 712.9).

One wrinkle: if Avacynian Missionaries later transforms again into Lunarch Inquisitors, that triggers a fresh "you may exile another target creature" ability with a new duration; it does not return the previously exiled Jasmine Boreal.

This answer is the same whether the game is two-player or multiplayer, with one multiplayer caveat: if Ari leaves the game, rule 800.4d governs — objects and triggered abilities tied to a departed player can fail to be created or put on the stack, which can leave Jasmine Boreal stranded in exile.

question: Addison controls [Carth the Lion] and [Bioessence Hydra]. Addison activates the [+1] ability of [Dovin, Architect of Law]. How many times does Bioessence Hydra trigger?
answer:
Bioessence Hydra triggers exactly once, and that single trigger puts two +1/+1 counters on Bioessence Hydra.

Why: Carth the Lion says "Planeswalkers' loyalty abilities you activate cost an additional [+1] to activate." So activating the [+1] ability of Dovin, Architect of Law has a total cost of [+1] plus an additional [+1]. Rule 606.5 says that when the total cost of a loyalty ability contains multiple costs to add or remove loyalty counters, those costs are combined into a single cost to add or remove loyalty counters. So Addison pays by putting two loyalty counters on Dovin, Architect of Law in one action, not two separate one-counter events.

Bioessence Hydra's ability reads "Whenever one or more loyalty counters are put on planeswalkers you control, put that many +1/+1 counters on this creature." Because it triggers on "one or more" counters being put on at once, the single event of adding two loyalty counters to Dovin, Architect of Law causes one trigger, and "that many" is two — so Bioessence Hydra grows by two +1/+1 counters (to 6/6 from a base 4/4, ignoring any counters it already had).

Multiplayer note: nothing here depends on the number of players — Carth the Lion, Bioessence Hydra, and Dovin, Architect of Law are all Addison's own permanents, so the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Nico casts [Assert Authority] targeting Ainsley's [Blightsteel Colossus]. What happens as Assert Authority resolves?
answer:
Assert Authority counters Blightsteel Colossus, and then Ainsley — as the controller of the countered spell — chooses which replacement effect applies to it leaving the stack. Ainsley will almost certainly choose Blightsteel Colossus's own ability, so Blightsteel Colossus is revealed and shuffled into Ainsley's library instead of being exiled.

Why: the counter itself is unaffected — Blightsteel Colossus is countered no matter what. The only contested part is where the countered spell goes. Two replacement effects are trying to modify the same event (the card being put into its owner's graveyard from the stack): Assert Authority's "exile it instead of putting it into its owner's graveyard" and Blightsteel Colossus's "If Blightsteel Colossus would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, reveal Blightsteel Colossus and shuffle it into its owner's library instead." Under [616.1f], when two or more replacement effects would modify how an event affects an object, the affected object's controller (or owner if it has none) picks the order; the affected object here is the Blightsteel Colossus card on the stack, which Ainsley controls. Once one is applied, the event is no longer "put into a graveyard," so the other does nothing.

So if Ainsley applies Blightsteel Colossus's ability first, Blightsteel Colossus is shuffled into Ainsley's library and Assert Authority's exile clause never applies. Ainsley could instead choose Assert Authority's effect first, exiling Blightsteel Colossus, but there's no reason to. Note also that Blightsteel Colossus's printed text overrides the default graveyard destination for a countered spell ([608.2c] — read the whole text of Assert Authority together, its exile clause only replaces the graveyard event).

On cost, for completeness: Assert Authority's affinity for artifacts reduces only the generic portion {5}; the {U}{U} must always be paid.

This analysis doesn't change with more than two players — the choice always belongs to the countered spell's controller, Ainsley, regardless of table size.

question: Amani has 3 life. Briar casts [Chain of Plasma], targeting Amani. As it resolves, Amani pays the cost to copy it, and chooses to have the copy target Campbell. What happens?
answer:
Direct answer: Chain of Plasma deals 3 damage to Amani, dropping Amani to 0 life; Amani may still discard a card and make the copy at that moment, because the resolution of Chain of Plasma continues to completion before anyone gets priority and the game checks who has lost. The copy is put onto the stack targeting Campbell, and that copy is owned and controlled by Amani, not Briar (707.10). It isn't "cast" — it's just put on the stack as a copy of Chain of Plasma, with the same characteristics and choices except for the new target Amani chose (707.10, 707.10c).

Details and assumptions:
- Timing: I'm assuming the normal sequence printed on Chain of Plasma — damage first, then the discard-and-copy option — all as part of the single resolution of Chain of Plasma. Since state-based checks for a player at 0 or less life happen only after the spell finishes resolving (not mid-resolution), Amani is still a player in the game when the discard and the copy choice are made. If instead you rule that Amani has already left the game before the copy option, no copy would be made at all.
- Because Chain of Plasma's own text says the damaged player "may copy this spell and may choose a new target for that copy," the copy legally targets Campbell; only the final set of targets matters for legality (115.7e), and Campbell must be a legal target for the copy (707.10c). Card text controls here over any general expectation that the original controller keeps control of copies.
- Gap I can't fill from the provided rules: what happens to Amani's copy of Chain of Plasma on the stack once Amani loses the game at 0 life is not covered by any rule given to me. The provided material only tells me that if damage would be redirected to or from a player who has left the game, that effect does nothing (614.9), which is not this situation. So I can't state from these rules whether the copy still resolves and damages Campbell or ceases to exist along with its controller leaving the game.
- Player count: nothing here depends on there being exactly two players; with three or more (as your example with Amani, Briar, and Campbell suggests), the copy simply targets whoever Amani chose. If a limited range of influence variant is in use, Amani could only choose a target within their range of influence (801.5a).

question: In a multiplayer game, Achilles uses [Jon Irenicus, Shattered One] to give [Vastwood Gorger] to Brynn. If Brynn dies, what happens to Vastwood Gorger?
answer:
Vastwood Gorger goes back to Achilles. When Brynn leaves the game, all objects Brynn owned leave with them, and any effect giving Brynn control of an object ends [800.4a]. Vastwood Gorger is owned by Achilles, so it doesn't leave the game; Jon Irenicus, Shattered One's control-change effect simply ends and Vastwood Gorger reverts to its owner/default controller, Achilles, still on the battlefield. This is the same result as the Act of Treason example in [800.4a].

Exile only happens if the default controller of the object had also left the game and no other effect grants control [800.4c] — not the case here, since Achilles is still in the game.

Details that carry over: the two +1/+1 counters Jon Irenicus, Shattered One put on Vastwood Gorger stay (counters aren't tied to the control effect), and the granted ability "This creature can't be sacrificed" and the goad effect were given "for the rest of the game" by Jon Irenicus, Shattered One, so they persist even under Achilles' control. Goad means it attacks each combat if able and must attack a player other than the goader if able — with Brynn gone, Vastwood Gorger must still attack, and must attack some player other than the player who goaded it if able. Vastwood Gorger also remains tapped/untapped as it was; leaving the game doesn't untap it.

Note this whole scenario is multiplayer-specific: rule [800.4a] exists because multiplayer games continue after a player leaves. In a two-player game, one player leaving simply ends the game.

One assumption: I read "Brynn dies" as Brynn losing and leaving the game, not a creature dying — [700.4] defines "dies" only for permanents put into a graveyard from the battlefield, so a player never technically "dies." If instead you meant Vastwood Gorger died while Brynn controlled it, it would go to its owner Achilles' graveyard [400.3].

question: Aspen attacks with [Hammers of Moradin]. During the combat damage step, they use [Time Stop] to end the turn. What happens to the tokens created by myriad?
answer:
The token copies created by Hammers of Moradin's myriad ability stay on the battlefield — they are not exiled.

Why: Myriad is a triggered ability that, when tokens are created, sets up a delayed triggered ability reading "exile the tokens at end of combat" [702.116a]. That delayed ability only triggers as the end of combat step begins [511.2]. When Time Stop ends the turn, the current phase or step ends immediately, all creatures and planeswalkers are removed from combat, and the game skips straight to the cleanup step, skipping every phase and step in between [724.1d] — including the end of combat step. Since that step never begins, the "at end of combat" delayed trigger never triggers (the same reasoning the rules spell out for skipped end-step triggers [724.1e]), so nothing ever exiles the Hammers of Moradin tokens.

Also note that any abilities that had already triggered during the combat damage step but hadn't yet been put on the stack simply cease to exist when Time Stop resolves [724.1a], and no player gets priority during the end-the-turn process [724.1f]. During the cleanup step, damage is removed and "until end of turn" effects end [514.2], but that does nothing to the tokens.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Time Stop resolved during the combat damage step, after the myriad tokens were already on the battlefield and before the end of combat step began. If instead the end of combat step had already begun and the exile delayed trigger had gone on the stack and resolved, the tokens would already be exiled and Time Stop would change nothing; if that trigger had triggered but not yet been put on the stack, it would cease to exist under [724.1a] and the tokens would survive.

Multiplayer note: Myriad only creates tokens when there are opponents other than the defending player, so this scenario inherently involves three or more players. The end-the-turn rules work identically regardless of player count; each opponent's token that was created simply remains on the battlefield.
