question: If Avery is going first, they'd like to reveal [Umori, the Collector] as their companion. If they're going second, they don't want to have a companion. Can they do this?
answer:
Yes. Revealing a companion happens as an additional step *after* the starting player has been determined, so Avery legally knows whether they're going first before deciding whether to reveal Umori, the Collector at all [103.2b][702.139a].

Details:
- Companion is a keyword ability that works from outside the game: "Companion—[Condition]"; before the game begins you may reveal one card you own from outside the game whose condition is met by your starting deck. Umori, the Collector's condition is that each nonland card in your starting deck shares a card type. The revealed card stays outside the game until you pay {3} (a special action, any time you have priority with an empty stack during a main phase of your turn, once per game) to put it into your hand [702.139a][116.2g][702.139c][Companion].
- "Starting deck" means your deck after setting aside sideboard cards, and in a Commander game before setting aside your commander — so Avery must be able to fulfill Umori, the Collector's condition either way; they're simply choosing whether to reveal [702.139b].
- Revealing is optional and no player may reveal more than one card, so declining when going second is fine [103.2b].

Multiplayer: the same works with more than two players. If multiple players are making these start-of-game choices at the same time, they're made in APNAP order — the player taking the first turn chooses first, then the others in turn order, and each knows the earlier choices [101.4b]. So going first, Avery reveals Umori, the Collector before opponents make their reveals; going second (or later), Avery decides after seeing the earlier player's choice. One caveat: in an Archenemy game the archenemy takes the first turn rather than a randomly determined player, which changes who "goes first" but not Avery's ability to decide afterward [904.6].

question: Aspen casts [Greater Good] sacrificing their [Bane Alley Blackguard] which is enchanted with [Mystic Subdual]. How many cards do they draw?
answer:
Aspen draws zero cards, then still discards three cards.

First, a correction on wording: Greater Good is an enchantment already on the battlefield; sacrificing Bane Alley Blackguard is the cost of activating Greater Good's ability "Sacrifice a creature: Draw cards equal to the sacrificed creature's power, then discard three cards."

Bane Alley Blackguard is a 1/3. Mystic Subdual, the Aura enchanting it, says "Enchanted creature gets -2/-0 and loses all abilities," so Bane Alley Blackguard's power as it last existed on the battlefield was 1 - 2 = -1. Greater Good tells Aspen to draw cards equal to that power. Magic only uses integers and you cannot draw a negative number of cards, so the draw instruction does as much as possible \ which is nothing (see [107.1c], [609.3]). Draws also happen one card at a time when there are any ([121.2a]), and here there simply are none.

The "then discard three cards" part of Greater Good is not conditional on drawing anything, so Aspen discards three cards from hand (or as many as possible if holding fewer, per [609.3]).

Timing note: I'm assuming Mystic Subdual was already attached when Bane Alley Blackguard was sacrificed, so the -2/-0 applies to the last-known-information power used by Greater Good. If instead Mystic Subdual had left the battlefield (or was cast only after the sacrifice), Bane Alley Blackguard's power would be 1 and Aspen would draw one card, then discard three.

This result is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

If a 3/4 creature gets -5/-0, it’s a -2/4 creature. It doesn’t assign damage in combat. Its total power and toughness is 2. Giving it +3/+0 would raise its power to 1. question: Ari controls [Mana Reflection] and [Looming Spires]. Nicole controls [Damping Sphere]. If Ari taps the Looming Spires for mana, how much mana is produced, and of what type(s)?
answer:
Short answer: it depends on the order the two replacement effects are applied, and Ari — the player affected by the mana-production event — is the one who picks that order, so in practice Ari taps Looming Spires for {R}{R} (two red mana).

Why both effects are in play. "Tapping a permanent for mana" means activating a mana ability of that permanent whose activation cost includes {T} — here Looming Spires' "{T}: Add {R}" — and a replacement effect that applies when a permanent "is tapped for mana" modifies the mana-production event while that ability is resolving [106.12b]. Both Mana Reflection ("If you tap a permanent for mana, it produces twice as much of that mana instead") and Damping Sphere ("If a land is tapped for two or more mana, it produces {C} instead of any other type and amount") are such replacement effects, and Looming Spires is a land, so both are candidates.

The two possible orders:
- Damping Sphere considered first: Looming Spires is being tapped for only one mana ({R}), so Damping Sphere's condition isn't met and it does nothing. Mana Reflection then doubles the production, giving {R}{R}. Damping Sphere doesn't get a second look — a replacement effect applies only once to a given event.
- Mana Reflection first: production becomes {R}{R}, which is "two or more mana," so Damping Sphere then replaces it with a single {C} (one colorless mana, not generic).

So the outcome is either {R}{R} or a single {C}. Note {C} is colorless mana specifically, not generic {1}, and it can't pay colored costs.

Assumption and caveat: I'm assuming Ari chooses the order, which is the normal handling for replacement effects modifying an event affecting an object or player under that player's control — Ari would obviously choose to get {R}{R}. The specific ordering rule (rule 616) wasn't included in the context I was given, so if your group applies a different ordering convention, the result would instead be one {C}. Rule 106.7 does at least acknowledge that multiple replacement effects can be taken "in any possible order" when determining what mana a permanent could produce.

Multiplayer: nothing here changes with more than two players — Mana Reflection cares only about permanents Ari taps, and Damping Sphere applies to any land tapped for two or more mana regardless of who controls it or how many players are at the table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

A player controls two permanents, each with an ability that reads “If a creature you control would deal damage to a permanent or player, it deals double that damage to that permanent or player instead.” A creature that normally deals 2 damage will deal 8 damage—not just 4, and not an infinite amount.

cited_text.106.12b: To “tap [a permanent] for mana” is to activate a mana ability of that permanent that includes the {T} symbol in its activation cost. See rule 605, “Mana Abilities.” A replacement effect that applies if a permanent “is tapped for mana” or tapped for mana of a specific type and/or amount modifies the mana production event while such an ability is resolving and producing mana or the specified type and/or amount of mana.

Ignore whether any costs of the ability could or could not be paid. If that permanent wouldn’t produce any mana under these conditions, or no type of mana can be defined this way, there’s no type of mana it could produce. The same is true if you and your opponent each control no lands other than Exotic Orchards. However, if you control a Forest and an Exotic Orchard, and your opponent controls an Exotic Orchard, then each Exotic Orchard could produce {G}.

question: Ada controls [Ethersworn Canonist]. They want to suspend [Shade of Trokair] and then cast [Divination]. Can they?
answer:
Yes — assuming Ada hasn't already cast a nonartifact spell this turn, they can suspend Shade of Trokair and then still cast Divination.

Why: Suspending is a special action, not casting a spell. A player with a suspend card in hand may exile it with time counters any time they have priority, but only if they could begin to cast that card from hand at that moment [116.2f], [702.62a], [702.62b]. Because Shade of Trokair is a creature card, that means during Ada's main phase with an empty stack and priority [117.1a].

The suspend check does take prohibition effects into account [702.62c], [601.3]. Ethersworn Canonist reads "Each player who has cast a nonartifact spell this turn can't cast additional nonartifact spells." If Ada has cast nothing (or only artifact spells) this turn, Ethersworn Canonist isn't prohibiting anything yet, so Ada "could begin to cast" Shade of Trokair and the special action is legal.

Taking that special action does not cast a spell — Shade of Trokair goes from hand straight to exile with three time counters, never using the stack. So Ethersworn Canonist's condition is still unmet afterward, and Ada may then cast Divination as their (first) nonartifact spell of the turn. After Divination, Ethersworn Canonist shuts off any further nonartifact spells that turn.

Order matters: if Ada casts Divination first, they then cannot suspend Shade of Trokair, because Ethersworn Canonist would prohibit them from beginning to cast it, failing the suspend legality check [702.62c].

Later, when the last time counter is removed, the suspend trigger lets Ada cast Shade of Trokair without paying its mana cost [702.62a] — but only if Ethersworn Canonist doesn't prohibit casting at that time (i.e., Ada hasn't cast a nonartifact spell that turn yet).

Multiplayer note: Ethersworn Canonist applies per player, so nothing here changes with more than two players; each opponent independently gets one nonartifact spell per turn.

This action doesn’t use the stack,” and “At the beginning of your upkeep, if this card is suspended, remove a time counter from it,” and “When the last time counter is removed from this card, if it’s exiled, you may play it without paying its mana cost if able. If you don’t, it remains exiled. If you cast a creature spell this way, it gains haste until you lose control of the spell or the permanent it becomes.”

question: Natasha and Nico are playing Two-Headed Giant, and each controls their own copy of [Bloodbond Vampire]. Ariel controls [Wall of Shards], and on their next upkeep they put the third age counter on it. Can Ariel have Natasha gain one life and Nico gain two? If so, how many triggered abilities of Bloodbond Vampire will be put on the stack?
answer:
Yes — Ariel can have Natasha gain 1 life and Nico gain 2 life, and three Bloodbond Vampire triggers go on the stack (one from Natasha's Bloodbond Vampire, two from Nico's Bloodbond Vampire).

Why the split is legal: Wall of Shards' cumulative upkeep cost is "An opponent gains 1 life," and with three age counters on Wall of Shards, Ariel must pay that cost once for each age counter — three separate payments of "an opponent gains 1 life." Nothing in Wall of Shards' text requires the same opponent each time, so Ariel may choose Natasha for one payment and Nico for the other two. In Two-Headed Giant, life gain still happens to each player individually and the result is then applied to the team's shared life total (rule 810.9), so Natasha and Nico are each genuinely gaining life as individuals even though their team's shared total simply goes up by 3 (see also [Shared Life Total]).

Why three triggers: Bloodbond Vampire reads "Whenever you gain life, put a +1/+1 counter on this creature." "You" is that Bloodbond Vampire's own controller, so Natasha's Bloodbond Vampire only watches Natasha's life gain and Nico's Bloodbond Vampire only watches Nico's. Natasha gains life once, triggering her Bloodbond Vampire once. Nico gains life in two separate events (two separate payments of the cumulative upkeep cost), triggering Nico's Bloodbond Vampire twice — the same way two separate lifelink damage events cause two separate life gain events and two triggers of an "whenever you gain life" ability (rule 702.15e). Total: 3 triggers, each putting one +1/+1 counter on the appropriate Bloodbond Vampire.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Ariel pays all three instances of the cost as part of resolving the cumulative upkeep trigger, choosing recipients at that time; the three payments are made one at a time, hence three distinct life-gain events. If instead you treated all 3 life as a single simultaneous gain by Nico, Nico's Bloodbond Vampire would trigger only once — but the cost is paid once per age counter (rule 702.24b's example likewise counts each cumulative upkeep payment separately), so three events is the correct reading.

Team-size note: this is the standard 2-player-per-team Two-Headed Giant answer. The same reasoning holds in Three-Headed Giant or larger (rule 810.11) — Ariel could spread the three life gains among any opponents, and only opponents who personally gained life trigger their own Bloodbond Vampire.

Then you may pay [cost] for each age counter on it. If you don’t, sacrifice it.” If [cost] has choices associated with it, each choice is made separately for each age counter, then either the entire set of costs is paid, or none of them is paid. Partial payments aren’t allowed. A creature has “Cumulative upkeep {W} or {U}” and two age counters on it. When its ability next triggers and resolves, the creature’s controller puts an age counter on it and then may pay {W}{W}{W}, {W}{W}{U}, {W}{U}{U}, or {U}{U}{U} to keep the creature on the battlefield. A creature has “Cumulative upkeep—Sacrifice a creature” and one age counter on it. When its ability next triggers and resolves, its controller can’t choose the same creature to sacrifice twice. Either two different creatures must be sacrificed, or the creature with cumulative upkeep must be sacrificed.

This means Ariel can make the stated choice, and the result of this is Natasha gains one life and Nico gains two life. Because of this, each player's Bloodbond Vampire will trigger separately, causing two instances of the triggered ability to be put on the stack. question: Nataly controls [Urza's Saga] with 2 lore counters on it. Alex casts [Magus of the Moon]. What does Urza's Saga look like?
answer:
Short answer: Urza's Saga becomes a Mountain that taps for {R}, keeps its 2 lore counters, and is not sacrificed — but it also stops doing anything Saga-like while Magus of the Moon is on the battlefield.

What I can ground in the provided rules:
- Magus of the Moon's text is "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." Urza's Saga is a nonbasic land (Enchantment Land), so Magus of the Moon applies to it: it becomes a Mountain, which sets its land subtype and gives it "{T}: Add {R}," and it loses its own abilities — including the chapter abilities represented by the chapter symbols I, II, and III (a chapter symbol is a keyword ability representing a triggered ability, per [107.15]/[714.2b]).
- Because Urza's Saga no longer has any chapter abilities, the Saga state-based action does not apply to it: that action only sacrifices a Saga permanent "with one or more chapter abilities" whose lore counters equal or exceed its final chapter number ([704.5s], [714.4]). In this case it also has only 2 counters, below its final chapter number of III, so it wouldn't be sacrificed even without Magus of the Moon.
- Likewise, the precombat-main-phase turn-based action only puts a lore counter on each Saga its controller controls "with one or more chapter abilities" ([505.4], [703.4f], [714.3c]). While Magus of the Moon is out, Nataly's Urza's Saga gets no new lore counters and no chapter ability can trigger.
- The 2 lore counters already on it stay put — nothing removes counters.

Caveat on grounding: the layer/timestamp rules that govern exactly how a type-changing effect strips subtypes and abilities were not included in the context provided, so the "loses its abilities and becomes a Mountain" part rests on Magus of the Moon's own printed text rather than a cited numbered rule.

Timing note: Magus of the Moon only matters once it has resolved and is on the battlefield; while it is still a spell on the stack, Urza's Saga is unaffected. If Magus of the Moon later leaves the battlefield, Urza's Saga regains its chapter abilities and resumes gaining lore counters at Nataly's precombat main phase — and if it then has 3 or more lore counters, the state-based action in [704.5s]/[714.4] makes Nataly sacrifice it.

question: Niko controls [Metallurgeon] and [Ornithopter of Paradise]. Avery casts [Prismari Command], choosing the "deal 2 damage" and "destroy target artifact" modes, targeting Ornithopter of Paradise with both. In response, Niko activates Metallurgeon's ability targeting Ornithopter of Paradise. What happens?
answer:
Ornithopter of Paradise survives. Metallurgeon's activated ability resolves first and creates a regeneration shield on Ornithopter of Paradise. Then Prismari Command resolves and performs its chosen modes in the order printed on the card (rule 608.2c): the "deals 2 damage" mode comes before the "destroy target artifact" mode. So Ornithopter of Paradise (a 0/2) first has 2 damage marked on it, then the destroy mode tries to destroy it. Regeneration is a replacement effect that replaces a destruction event (rule 701.8c): the shield is used up, Ornithopter of Paradise is instead tapped, all damage marked on it is removed, and it's removed from combat if it was in combat. Because the marked damage is gone, when state-based actions are next checked Ornithopter of Paradise no longer has lethal damage, so it stays on the battlefield — tapped, and with its regeneration shield spent.

Timing note: this assumes the modes resolve in printed order (damage, then destroy), which is what rule 608.2c requires. If instead the destroy happened first and the 2 damage were marked afterward, the shield would be consumed by the destroy and the subsequently marked 2 lethal damage would destroy Ornithopter of Paradise as a state-based action with no shield left. Also note Niko had to activate Metallurgeon's ability before Prismari Command resolved for the shield to exist in time.

Metallurgeon's ability can legally target Ornithopter of Paradise because Ornithopter of Paradise is an artifact (an Artifact Creature). Nothing here depends on the number of players, so the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Asa controls an [Inventors' Fair], a [Krark-Clan Ironworks], and two [Piston Sledge]. They want to activate the last ability of Inventors' Fair and sacrifice a Piston Sledge to help pay the cost. Is this legal?
answer:
Yes, it's legal. Asa can activate the last ability of Inventors' Fair and, while paying its costs, activate Krark-Clan Ironworks' mana ability by sacrificing a Piston Sledge to add {C}{C}, then use that mana toward the {4}.

Why it works:

1. Legality of activating Inventors' Fair: its ability says "Activate only if you control three or more artifacts." At the moment of activation Asa controls Krark-Clan Ironworks and two Piston Sledge — three artifacts (Inventors' Fair itself is a land, not an artifact), so the restriction is satisfied. This is checked as the ability is activated, before any costs are paid.

2. Sacrificing during payment: a player may activate a mana ability whenever they are casting a spell or activating an ability that requires a mana payment, even in the middle of paying costs [605.3a]. So Asa can sacrifice a Piston Sledge to Krark-Clan Ironworks partway through paying for Inventors' Fair. Losing an artifact at that point doesn't retroactively invalidate the activation restriction.

3. Mana type: Krark-Clan Ironworks produces {C}{C} (colorless specifically). Inventors' Fair asks for {4}, which is generic mana and can be paid with any mana, including {C}. So {C}{C} covers 2 of the {4}; Asa still needs 2 more mana from somewhere (sacrificing the second Piston Sledge to Krark-Clan Ironworks for another {C}{C} would finish it). Note the {T} and "Sacrifice Inventors' Fair" parts of the cost are separate and still must be paid, and partial payment isn't allowed — Asa must be able to produce the full {4} [601.2h][118.3].

4. One payment, one cost: the sacrifice of a Piston Sledge pays only Krark-Clan Ironworks' activation cost; it can't simultaneously pay any other cost such as a Piston Sledge equip cost [118.10].

Timing caveat: I'm assuming Asa activates Inventors' Fair first and sacrifices a Piston Sledge during cost payment. If instead Asa sacrificed a Piston Sledge to Krark-Clan Ironworks *before* activating Inventors' Fair, they'd only control two artifacts (Krark-Clan Ironworks and one Piston Sledge) at that time and could not legally activate the ability at all — so order matters.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; it's the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Ahmed controls [Bronze Sable]. They cast [Genesis Wave], putting [Phylactery Lich] and [Solemnity] onto the battlefield. Does Bronze Sable get a phylactery counter?
answer:
No — Bronze Sable does not get a phylactery counter, and Phylactery Lich is then sacrificed.

Genesis Wave puts Phylactery Lich and Solemnity onto the battlefield simultaneously, so Solemnity is already on the battlefield (where its abilities function) at the moment Phylactery Lich's replacement effect "As this creature enters, put a phylactery counter on an artifact you control" would apply. Solemnity says "Counters can't be put on artifacts, creatures, enchantments, or lands," so no phylactery counter can be placed on Bronze Sable (an artifact creature). A prohibition like this applies both to counters placed on permanents already on the battlefield and to counters given as an object enters ([122.6a]), and it also applies when the counter placement comes from another replacement effect rather than a resolving spell ([614.16]). Card text like Solemnity's overrides the general expectation that Phylactery Lich's counter gets placed.

Because no permanent ends up with a phylactery counter, Phylactery Lich's second ability, "When you control no permanents with phylactery counters on them, sacrifice this creature," has its condition true immediately and triggers; on resolution Ahmed sacrifices Phylactery Lich (its indestructibility doesn't stop a sacrifice).

Timing note: I'm assuming the standard reading, that both permanents enter at the same time from the one Genesis Wave resolution. If instead Solemnity somehow arrived later (e.g., it was already going to enter after Phylactery Lich), Bronze Sable would get the phylactery counter and Phylactery Lich would stay; the counter already on Bronze Sable wouldn't be removed by Solemnity arriving afterward.

This answer doesn't depend on player count — it works the same in a two-player or multiplayer game, since everything involved is Ahmed's own permanents.

question: Ashley controls [Tatterkite]. Ashley casts [Genesis Wave], putting [Phylactery Lich] and [Humility] onto the battlefield. Can they put a phylactery counter on Tatterkite?
answer:
Direct answer: Yes — nothing stops a phylactery counter from going on Tatterkite, because Humility strips Tatterkite of the very ability that would forbid it. The bigger question is whether Phylactery Lich's counter-placing ability works at all.

Why Tatterkite can receive counters: Tatterkite's printed ability "This creature can't have counters put on it" is an ability that functions both as Tatterkite enters and while Tatterkite is on the battlefield [113.6i]. Humility says "All creatures lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1," and ability-removing effects are applied in layer 6 [613.1f]. Once Humility is on the battlefield, Tatterkite has no abilities at all, so it has no "can't have counters put on it" restriction left to invoke; the "can't beats can" principle of [101.2a] expressly does not cover adding or removing abilities. Note this is a removal effect, not a "can't have that ability" effect of the [113.11] type, so it's simply gone. (Humility does not remove Tatterkite from the battlefield or change that it's a creature; it becomes a 1/1 with no abilities, and counters that modify power/toughness would still apply in layer 7c [613.4c].)

The catch with Phylactery Lich: Genesis Wave puts Phylactery Lich and Humility onto the battlefield simultaneously, so Humility is already on the battlefield and applying to Phylactery Lich at the moment Phylactery Lich is there. Phylactery Lich therefore has lost "As this creature enters, put a phylactery counter on an artifact you control" (and "Indestructible," and its sacrifice trigger) under the same layer-6 application [613.1f]. The rules provided here don't fully spell out how an "as this creature enters" replacement effect interacts with an ability-removing static effect that begins applying in the same event, so I can't settle that half definitively from this context — but if that ability does apply, Tatterkite is a legal recipient (it's an artifact you control, and it no longer refuses counters).

Timing assumption: I'm assuming both permanents hit the battlefield in the same Genesis Wave resolution, simultaneously. If instead Phylactery Lich were already on the battlefield and Humility arrived later, the counter would have been placed at the earlier time — and back then Tatterkite still had its ability, so Tatterkite could not have been chosen.

Player count: this interaction is entirely between Ashley's own permanents, so it plays out the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

Direct answer: at the start of Avery's next turn, both copies of The One Ring phase back in / are present, and then the "legend rule" makes Avery choose one The One Ring to keep and put the other into their graveyard. Teferi's Protection's protection-from-everything and life-total lock also expire at that point.

Step by step, with my timing assumption stated: I'm assuming Avery cast Teferi's Protection and the second The One Ring during a single turn, and that "the start of the next turn" you mean is the beginning of Avery's own next turn (that's when Teferi's Protection's effects end and phased-out permanents return). 

1. Teferi's Protection phases out all permanents Avery controls, including the first The One Ring. Phasing means a permanent is treated as though it doesn't exist while phased out, and Teferi's Protection's own reminder text says those permanents "phase in before you untap during your untap step." Because the first The One Ring doesn't exist while phased out, it doesn't conflict with the newly cast second The One Ring, which enters normally and (since it was cast) gives Avery protection from everything until Avery's next turn.
2. During Avery's untap step, the first The One Ring phases in. Now Avery controls two legendary permanents with the same name, and the legend rule applies as a state-based action, so Avery keeps one and puts the other into the graveyard. Note that both are indestructible, but the legend rule doesn't destroy — it puts the permanent into the graveyard, which indestructible does not stop (compare the note that umbra armor doesn't help "if the 'legend rule' applies to it" — [Spider Umbra ruling #8]).
3. Also at that time, Teferi's Protection's "until your next turn" effects (life total can't change, protection from everything) have ended, and so has the protection from the second The One Ring's enters trigger. So in that turn's upkeep, The One Ring's "lose 1 life for each burden counter" trigger will actually cost Avery life. (While Avery's life total couldn't change, such loss did nothing.)

Caveat on grounding: the provided rules context does not include the numbered legend-rule rule itself; the analogous state-based actions given are the "world rule" [704.5k] and the Role rule [704.5y]/[303.7a], plus [702.26p] on phasing being redundant. My statement of the legend rule rests on Teferi's Protection's and The One Ring's card text plus [Spider Umbra ruling #8]'s reference to it. Also note [514.2]: damage marked on phased-out permanents is still removed at cleanup, which doesn't matter for artifacts here.

If instead you meant the start of the very next turn and that turn belongs to an opponent, nothing happens yet: Avery's permanents stay phased out and keep not existing, so no legend-rule choice occurs until Avery's own untap step. In a two-player game the next turn is the opponent's; at a multiplayer table there may be several turns before Avery's untap step, and during all of them Avery has protection from everything and an unchangeable life total, with only the second The One Ring visible on the battlefield.

question: Amaya controls [Dralnu, Lich Lord], [Furnace of Rath] and six [Snow-Covered Forest]s. Nico casts [Incinerate] targeting Dralnu, Lich Lord. If Amaya chooses to sacrifice Furnace of Rath, how many other permanents will they need to sacrifice?
answer:
Direct answer: if the damage is doubled first, Amaya sacrifices six permanents total, so five permanents besides Furnace of Rath. Note that sacrificing Furnace of Rath doesn't shrink the number — the doubling was already locked in when the replacement applied.

Why: Incinerate would deal 3 damage to Dralnu, Lich Lord. Furnace of Rath changes that to 6 damage, and Dralnu, Lich Lord's own text ("If damage would be dealt to Dralnu, sacrifice that many permanents instead") converts 6 damage into sacrificing 6 permanents. Sacrificing means moving a permanent you control from the battlefield directly to its owner's graveyard ([701.21a], [Sacrifice]); Furnace of Rath counts as one of those six, so five more permanents (e.g. five of the six Snow-Covered Forests) must go. Sacrificing is not destruction, so regeneration-type effects can't save them ([701.21a]).

Important timing/ordering caveat: both Furnace of Rath and Dralnu, Lich Lord are damage-replacement effects applying to the same damage event, and the provided rules context does not include the rule governing who orders multiple applicable replacement effects. If instead Dralnu, Lich Lord's replacement is applied first, the 3 damage is replaced by sacrificing 3 permanents and there is no damage left for Furnace of Rath to double — that would be 2 other permanents besides Furnace of Rath. I've answered the reading your question implies (doubling applied, 6 sacrifices).

This analysis doesn't depend on player count: Amaya is the one sacrificing her own permanents either way, so the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Two or five, Amaya's choice.

Both Dralnu, Lich Lord and Furnace of Rath have replacement effects that modify how the game handles damage that is being dealt to Dralnu, Lich Lord. As Amaya is the controller of the affected object, Amaya will choose which order to apply the replacement effects in. If Amaya chooses to apply Dralnu, Lich Lord's effect first, the 3 damage will be converted into sacrificing three permanents, and Furnace of Rath will no longer apply to that event since there's no longer any damage being dealt. If they chooses to apply Furnace of Rath first, then the three damage will be doubled to six damage, and then will be replaced by sacrificing six permanents.

Whether Amaya chooses to sacrifice Furnace of Rath or not is irrelevant, as all replacement effects are applied to the event before anything is actually sacrificed.

question: Aubrey and Arely are playing 2HG. Aubrey attacks with [Coral Commando] and Arely casts [Flash Conscription] to gain control of Coral Commando after it's been declared as an attacker in the declare attackers step. Is it still attacking?
answer:
No — Coral Commando stops being an attacking creature the moment Flash Conscription resolves and Arely gains control of it.

A permanent is removed from combat if its controller changes, and a creature removed from combat stops being an attacking, blocking, blocked, and/or unblocked creature [506.4a]. Flash Conscription's control-change effect therefore takes Coral Commando out of combat entirely; it also untaps Coral Commando and gives it haste, but that doesn't put it back into combat. No combat damage will be dealt by Coral Commando this combat unless some other effect states it's attacking again.

A couple of related points:
- Coral Commando is still considered to have been declared as an attacker for the purposes of anything that already triggered on attackers being declared [508.3]; removal from combat doesn't undo that historical fact, but ongoing 'is attacking' checks fail.
- Nothing here is a 'reselect what it's attacking' effect [508.7], nor an effect that states a creature is attacking [508.4], so Coral Commando is simply out of combat.

Two-Headed Giant note: 2HG uses shared team turns, where the active team declares attackers as one combined attack [805.10b]. That doesn't change the outcome. If Arely is Aubrey's teammate on the attacking team, the controller of Coral Commando still changed, so 506.4a still removes it from combat. If Arely is an opposing player, the same rule applies. Either way Coral Commando is no longer attacking.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Flash Conscription resolves during the declare attackers step, after attackers were declared and before combat damage. If instead it somehow resolved before attackers were declared, Coral Commando would simply never have been declared as an attacker by Aubrey [508.1c].

question: Nicolas controls [Razorfield Thresher], [Lake of the Dead], and [Veinfire Borderpost]. Aubrey controls [Omniscience] and casts [Casualties of War], choosing Razorfield Thresher as the artifact target and the creature target. Then they cast [Radiate], targeting Casualties of War. What will be destroyed after all spells and abilities have resolved?
answer:
Only Razorfield Thresher is destroyed. Nothing else on the battlefield dies.

Why: Casualties of War is modal, and Aubrey chose two modes ("Destroy target artifact" and "Destroy target creature") both pointing at Razorfield Thresher, an artifact creature. Because both instances of "target" are on the same permanent, the spell targets only a single permanent, so it is a legal choice for Radiate. Razorfield Thresher is simply destroyed once when Casualties of War resolves — the two modes both apply to the same object, exactly as in the Plague Spores example in rule [608.2b], where one permanent chosen for two target instances is affected by the parts of the spell it's legal for.

Radiate then copies Casualties of War "for each other permanent or player the spell could target," with each copy targeting a different one. A copy of this Casualties of War keeps the same two chosen modes, so it needs a permanent that is legal for both "target artifact" and "target creature" — that is, another artifact creature. Lake of the Dead is a land, Veinfire Borderpost is a noncreature artifact, and Omniscience is an enchantment, so none of them qualifies (and players can't be targeted by these modes at all). With no other legal object, Radiate produces no copies and nothing additional is destroyed.

Timing note: I'm assuming Radiate resolves while Casualties of War is still on the stack (as it must be, since Radiate targets a spell). If Razorfield Thresher somehow left the battlefield before Casualties of War resolved, all of its targets would be illegal and Casualties of War would not resolve at all ([608.2b]).

Multiplayer: the answer is the same at any player count with only these permanents, but at a larger table Radiate would make one copy for each other artifact creature on the battlefield, destroying each of those too.

question: Amare controls [Psychogenic Probe] and casts [Pain], targeting Nico. They discard a [Progenitus]. Does Psychogenic Probe trigger?
answer:
Yes — Psychogenic Probe triggers and deals 2 damage to Nico.

Pain makes Nico discard a card. Progenitus's own replacement ability reads "If Progenitus would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, reveal Progenitus and shuffle it into its owner's library instead." That card text overrides the general result of a discard (going to the graveyard), so instead Progenitus is revealed and shuffled into Nico's library. Because the shuffle actually happens, and it happens as a result of a spell (Pain) and an ability (Progenitus's replacement ability), Psychogenic Probe's trigger condition — "Whenever a spell or ability causes a player to shuffle their library" — is met, and it deals 2 damage to Nico, the player who shuffled.

Note that the trigger only exists because the shuffle genuinely occurs; a trigger condition that is prevented or replaced away never triggers ([603.2g]). Here nothing prevents the shuffle, so Psychogenic Probe triggers once for that one shuffle. This works the same regardless of whether it's a two-player or multiplayer game: the damage goes to Nico, the player who shuffled, not to Amare.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

An ability triggers only if its trigger event actually occurs. An event that’s prevented or replaced won’t trigger anything. An ability that triggers on damage being dealt won’t trigger if all the damage is prevented.

answer_gold: Yes. Progenitus's replacement effect changes the effect of Pain from "Nico discards a card, putting it into their graveyard" to "Nico reveals a card and shuffles it into their library". Pain still caused the shuffle, so Psychogenic Probe triggers.

question: Alonso controls [Spark Double] and casts [Clone]. Alonso would like to have Clone copy Spark Double, then they would like to apply the replacement effect Clone inherited from Spark Double and have it copy Spark Double again. If Alonso has Clone copy Spark Double a total of four times, how many +1/+1 counters will Clone enter the battlefield with?
answer:
Clone enters the battlefield with exactly one +1/+1 counter, no matter how many times it copies Spark Double.

Why: Spark Double's copy effect is written as "You may have this creature enter as a copy of a creature or planeswalker you control, except it enters with an additional +1/+1 counter on it if it's a creature..." That "except it enters with an additional +1/+1 counter" clause is an additional effect, not a modification of the copiable characteristics. Rule 707.9e says that when a replacement effect generating a copy effect has such an exception, and another copy effect is later applied to that object, the earlier exception's effect simply doesn't happen.

So the chain works like this: Clone's own replacement effect (which has no counter clause) makes Clone a copy of Spark Double. Now Clone has Spark Double's replacement effect, which Alonso applies to copy Spark Double again — that application would grant a counter, but because Alonso then applies yet another copy effect (the newly inherited Spark Double effect) afterward, the earlier one's counter never materializes. Only the very last copy effect applied still has a live exception, and it grants exactly one +1/+1 counter. Repeating this four times, or forty, still yields one counter, since each prior exception is wiped out by the next copy effect.

Note that after the last iteration Clone is a copy of Spark Double, so its printed power/toughness is 0/0 (copiable values, applied in layer 1a per 613.2a and 613.1a); with one +1/+1 counter it will be a 1/1 unless something else copied changes that. Nothing here depends on the number of players — the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game, since only Alonso's own permanents are involved.

If you then choose a creature to copy as you apply the replacement effect Altered Ego gains by copying Clone, Altered Ego’s replacement effect won’t cause it to enter the battlefield with any +1/+1 counters on it.

question: Nickolas controls a [Nyx Herald] enchanted by [Drake Umbra]. Ainsley casts [Fracturing Gust]. How much life do they gain?
answer:
Ainsley gains 2 life from this pair of permanents (plus 2 more for each other artifact or enchantment Fracturing Gust destroys anywhere on the battlefield).

Why: Fracturing Gust says "Destroy all artifacts and enchantments. You gain 2 life for each permanent destroyed this way." Both Nyx Herald (an enchantment creature) and Drake Umbra (an enchantment Aura) are hit. But Drake Umbra grants umbra armor: "If enchanted creature would be destroyed, instead remove all damage from it and destroy this Aura." That replacement effect applies to Nyx Herald's destruction, so Nyx Herald is not destroyed at all \u2014 instead damage is removed from it and Drake Umbra is destroyed. Card text like umbra armor overrides the general expectation that everything named by Fracturing Gust dies.

So the only permanent of Nickolas's that Fracturing Gust actually destroys is Drake Umbra, which is one permanent \u2192 2 life. Nyx Herald survives (now unenchanted, so it loses the +3/+3 and flying).

Timing note: Drake Umbra is itself already being destroyed by Fracturing Gust at the same time; the umbra armor replacement doesn't add a second, separately-counted destruction of Drake Umbra, so you don't get 4 life. Either way Nyx Herald is never "destroyed this way" and never contributes life.

This works the same in a two-player or multiplayer game \u2014 Fracturing Gust destroys artifacts and enchantments controlled by every player, and Ainsley gains 2 life for each one, so at a larger table the total is usually much higher.

question: Avery controls [Corpsejack Menace] and casts [Rescuer Sphinx], choosing to return Corpsejack Menace to their hand. How many +1/+1 counters will Rescuer Sphinx enter the battlefield with?
answer:
Rescuer Sphinx enters the battlefield with just one +1/+1 counter, not two.

Why: Rescuer Sphinx's ability is a replacement effect that modifies how it enters — "As this creature enters, you may return a nonland permanent you control to its owner's hand. If you do, this creature enters with a +1/+1 counter on it." An effect that modifies how a permanent enters the battlefield may cause other objects to change zones as part of applying it [614.13b]. So Corpsejack Menace is returned to Avery's hand before Rescuer Sphinx actually enters and before the counter is placed.

Corpsejack Menace's doubling effect ("If one or more +1/+1 counters would be put on a creature you control, twice that many +1/+1 counters are put on it instead") only functions while Corpsejack Menace is on the battlefield. Since Avery chose to bounce Corpsejack Menace itself, it is no longer on the battlefield to apply its replacement effect to the single counter Rescuer Sphinx would enter with. Result: one +1/+1 counter, making Rescuer Sphinx a 4/3 flyer.

If Avery had instead returned some other nonland permanent and left Corpsejack Menace on the battlefield, the one counter would be doubled to two, and Rescuer Sphinx would enter as a 5/4.

Player count doesn't matter here — this works identically in a two-player game or a multiplayer game, since only Avery's own permanents and Avery's own choice are involved.

question: Arabella casts [Mind's Desire]. In response, Neil casts [Lim-Dûl's Vault]. How many copies of Mind's Desire are created when the storm trigger resolves?
answer:
Zero copies — assuming Mind's Desire was the first spell cast this turn.

Storm means "When you cast this spell, copy it for each other spell that was cast before it this turn" [702.40a]. The key word is *before*: only spells cast earlier in the turn than Mind's Desire count. Neil's Lim-Dûl's Vault was cast in response, i.e. after Mind's Desire was already on the stack, so it does not add a copy no matter when the storm trigger actually resolves.

So the count is simply however many spells (by any player) were cast earlier in that turn before Mind's Desire. If Mind's Desire was the turn's first spell, the storm trigger resolves and makes zero copies; Arabella still resolves the original Mind's Desire (shuffle, exile top card, may play it without paying its mana cost this turn). If, say, two spells had already been cast that turn before Mind's Desire, you'd get two copies, and Lim-Dûl's Vault still wouldn't make it three.

Each copy would be a spell on the stack that wasn't cast, and it copies all decisions made for the original [707.10b]. Mind's Desire has no targets, so the "you may choose new targets" clause of storm is irrelevant here [702.40a].

This works the same in two-player and multiplayer games: storm counts spells cast before it that turn by *any* player, not just its controller, so opponents' earlier spells in the turn do increase the count — but a spell cast in response afterward never does.

question: Aubrey casts [Bitter Ordeal], targeting Natasha. At their first opportunity, Aubrey sacrifices their [Westvale Abbey]. How many cards will Aubrey be able to exile from Natasha's library?
answer:
Short answer: the provided rules don't contain the gravestorm rules needed to settle this cleanly, so I can't fully ground a number.

What I can say from the given material: Bitter Ordeal's own text is "Search target player's library for a card and exile it," so each resolution of Bitter Ordeal (and of each gravestorm copy) exiles exactly one card from Natasha's library, and if Natasha's library is empty or has fewer cards than the total number of resolutions, Aubrey simply finds as many as possible [701.23d], since an effect that attempts the impossible does only as much as possible [609.3].

So the total number of cards exiled equals 1 (for Bitter Ordeal itself) plus the number of gravestorm copies. Determining whether Aubrey's Westvale Abbey, sacrificed after Bitter Ordeal was cast but (presumably) before the gravestorm triggered ability resolves, is counted for gravestorm requires the gravestorm rules and the rules for when a triggered ability's count is determined — neither is in the context I was given. Note also that Westvale Abbey's printed abilities don't themselves sacrifice Westvale Abbey (its third ability sacrifices five creatures to transform it), so the question presupposes some other effect sacrificing it; and the exact timing (before or after the gravestorm trigger resolves) is the crux. If the sacrifice happens in time to be counted, Aubrey exiles 2 cards; if the count was already locked in, Aubrey exiles 1.

This analysis is the same whether the game has two players or more, since Bitter Ordeal targets a single player, Natasha.

question: Albert controls [Doubling Season] and [Pir, Imaginative Rascal] and activates the +1 ability of [Ajani, Mentor of Heroes]. How many loyalty counters does it gain?
answer:
Albert chooses the order, so Ajani, Mentor of Heroes gains either 3 or 4 loyalty counters — 4 if he applies Pir, Imaginative Rascal first, 3 if he applies Doubling Season first. He'll almost certainly choose 4.

Why: the +1 puts one loyalty counter on Ajani, Mentor of Heroes. Both Doubling Season ("If an effect would put one or more counters on a permanent you control, it puts twice that many...") and Pir, Imaginative Rascal ("If one or more counters would be put on a permanent your team controls, that many plus one...") are replacement effects that want to modify that same event. When two or more replacement effects would apply to one event, the affected object's controller picks the order one at a time (rule 616.1g), and each effect only gets one chance to apply — it doesn't re-trigger off its own modification (rule 614.5).

- Pir, Imaginative Rascal first: 1 + 1 = 2, then Doubling Season: 2 × 2 = 4.
- Doubling Season first: 1 × 2 = 2, then Pir, Imaginative Rascal: 2 + 1 = 3.

So Albert should apply Pir, Imaginative Rascal before Doubling Season for 4 loyalty counters. (The same math applies to the three +1/+1 counters that ability distributes when it resolves: each targeted creature's counters get the same replacement treatment, chosen per event.)

I'm assuming Albert controls both permanents when the ability is activated, and that both were already on the battlefield at that time. This works identically in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table — only Albert, as the controller of the affected permanent, makes the ordering choice.

question: Ainsley activates [Priest of Forgotten Gods]'s ability, but doesn't choose a target for the first part. Can Nickolas respond to the ability?
answer:
Yes. Nickolas can respond normally. Choosing zero targets doesn't stop Priest of Forgotten Gods's activated ability from going on the stack; it sits there like any other activated ability, and players receive priority and may cast spells or activate abilities in response before it resolves.

Why: Priest of Forgotten Gods's ability reads "Any number of target players each lose 2 life and sacrifice a creature of their choice. You add {B}{B} and draw a card." "Any number of target players" permits zero targets. Rule 115.6 says such an ability is still said to require targets, but it is only actually "targeted" if one or more targets were chosen — so with zero players chosen, the ability simply isn't a targeted ability. That affects things like effects that say "counter target spell or ability that targets you," but it does not remove the ability from the stack or deny anyone priority.

Because Priest of Forgotten Gods's ability targets, it is not a mana ability, even though it adds {B}{B}. Only mana abilities skip the stack and resolve immediately without being respondable (rule 605.3b); this ability does use the stack, so Nickolas gets a window to respond. Note Nickolas can respond by, for example, removing Priest of Forgotten Gods — but the ability still resolves, since the cost ({T}, sacrificing two other creatures) was already paid.

On resolution with zero target players, no one loses 2 life or sacrifices a creature, and Ainsley still adds {B}{B} and draws a card.

Multiplayer: the answer is the same regardless of player count; with more than two players Ainsley could have chosen several target players ("any number"), and each chosen player would lose 2 life and sacrifice a creature of their choice.

question: Analia controls [Volrath's Shapeshifter] and [Muldrotha, the Gravetide], and the top card of their graveyard is [Grid Monitor]. Can Analia cast the Grid Monitor?
answer:
No. Analia can't cast Grid Monitor.

Why: Volrath's Shapeshifter says that as long as the top card of your graveyard is a creature card, it has the full text of that card. Grid Monitor is an artifact creature card on top of Analia's graveyard, so Volrath's Shapeshifter — a permanent on the battlefield — has Grid Monitor's text, including the static ability "You can't cast creature spells." That effect applies to Analia.

Muldrotha, the Gravetide grants a permission: during each of Analia's turns they may cast a permanent spell of each permanent type from their graveyard. But permission alone isn't enough — a player may begin to cast a spell only if a rule or effect allows it AND no rule or effect prohibits it [601.3]. The Volrath's Shapeshifter-copied "You can't cast creature spells" is exactly such a prohibition, so it overrides Muldrotha, the Gravetide's permission.

Can Analia dodge this by using Muldrotha, the Gravetide's "choose one permanent type as you play it" clause to cast Grid Monitor as an artifact spell? No. That choice only picks which of Muldrotha, the Gravetide's per-type permissions is being used; it doesn't change the card's types. Grid Monitor is still a creature card, so the resulting spell is still a creature spell and remains prohibited. (Compare bestow [702.103d] and "cast transformed" [712.11d], where the rules explicitly say modified characteristics are what get evaluated — there is no such text for Muldrotha, the Gravetide's type choice, and 601.3e limits alternative-characteristics evaluation to effects that state it.)

Note the self-defeating loop: this holds as long as Grid Monitor is the top card of the graveyard, because that's exactly the condition that makes Volrath's Shapeshifter copy the anti-creature-casting text. If Grid Monitor stops being on top (or Volrath's Shapeshifter leaves the battlefield or loses the copied text), the prohibition goes away and Muldrotha, the Gravetide's permission can be used.

Nothing here depends on player count — the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since both cards affect only Analia.

question: Antoine owns an [Eternal Scourge] that was exiled by Nico's [Ixalan's Binding]. Can Antoine cast it?
answer:
No. Antoine can't cast Eternal Scourge while it's exiled by Nico's Ixalan's Binding.

Eternal Scourge's own text, "You may cast this card from exile," does grant permission to cast it from the exile zone, and Ixalan's Binding exiles it face up, so it's a known, examinable card. But Ixalan's Binding also says "Your opponents can't cast spells with the same name as the exiled card" — a prohibition affecting each of Nico's opponents. Under rule 601.3, a player can begin to cast a spell only if a rule or effect allows it AND no rule or effect prohibits it; a prohibition always beats a permission. Since Antoine is Nico's opponent, and Eternal Scourge obviously has the same name as the exiled card (it is that card), Antoine is prohibited (601.3, 601.3f).

The same reasoning blocks Antoine from casting any other copy of Eternal Scourge from hand, graveyard, or elsewhere for as long as Ixalan's Binding remains on the battlefield.

Multiplayer note: the restriction applies to every opponent of Nico, not just Antoine, so at a table of three or more no opponent of Nico can cast an Eternal Scourge. Nico is not restricted by his own Ixalan's Binding, but Eternal Scourge's permission is granted to its owner (Antoine), so Nico has no effect letting him cast it either. If Ixalan's Binding leaves the battlefield, the card returns to the battlefield under Antoine's control per Ixalan's Binding's first ability rather than staying castable in exile.

question: Avery manifests the top card of their library with [Soul Summons]. Then, they mutate [Trumpeting Gnarr] targeting the manifested creature. What are the characteristics of the resulting creature if Avery chooses to put the manifested creature on top?
answer:
The resulting mutated permanent is a face-down 2/2 colorless creature with no name, no card types beyond creature, no subtypes, and no mana cost — the characteristics of the manifested card on top — but it has the abilities of both components, so it has Trumpeting Gnarr's "Whenever this creature mutates, create a 3/3 green Beast creature token" and Trumpeting Gnarr's mutate ability.

Details:

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming the manifest from Soul Summons fully resolved before Trumpeting Gnarr was cast (as stated). question: Nayeli controls a [Yixlid Jailer]. Ariel has a [Golgari Brownscale] in their graveyard and returns it to their hand with [Disturbing Plot]. Does Ariel gain 2 life?
answer:
No — Ariel does not gain 2 life.

Why: Yixlid Jailer says "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities." Golgari Brownscale's ability, "When this card is put into your hand from your graveyard, you gain 2 life," is a triggered ability that must exist and trigger at the moment Golgari Brownscale is still in the graveyard (the event is it leaving the graveyard for the hand). While Golgari Brownscale is in Ariel's graveyard, Yixlid Jailer has stripped that ability, so there is nothing there to trigger when Disturbing Plot returns it. Once Golgari Brownscale is in Ariel's hand it has its abilities again, but the triggering event has already passed. Yixlid Jailer's printed text controls here, overriding how the ability would otherwise work.

Since no life gain event happens at all, nothing that cares about life gain applies either: effects and triggers worded "if/whenever [a player] gains life" only function when an actual life gain event occurs ([119.9], [119.10]), and a player's life total is only adjusted when an effect actually causes them to gain life ([119.3]).

Same answer regardless of table size — Yixlid Jailer affects cards in all graveyards, so it doesn't matter whether Nayeli and Ariel are the only two players or part of a larger multiplayer game. (In a Two-Headed Giant game, life gain would apply to the team's shared total per [810.9g], but here there is no life gain to apply.)

Also note the same reasoning kills Golgari Brownscale's dredge while Yixlid Jailer is on the battlefield: dredge is a graveyard ability, so Ariel can't use it either.

question: Aryana has taken control of an [Ahn-Crop Crasher] from Noe with [Tibalt, the Fiend-Blooded], which Aryana exerts. After Aryana ends their turn, will it untap during Noe's untap step?
answer:
Yes — Ahn-Crop Crasher untaps during Noe's untap step.

Why: exerting means "you choose to have it not untap during your next untap step" [701.43a]. "Your" refers to the player who exerted it — Aryana. So the effect only stops Ahn-Crop Crasher from untapping in Aryana's next untap step, not in Noe's.

Meanwhile, Tibalt, the Fiend-Blooded's −6 grants control of Ahn-Crop Crasher only until end of turn, so once Aryana's turn ends Ahn-Crop Crasher is back under Noe's control. During Noe's untap step, Noe (the active player) determines which permanents they control untap and untaps them all simultaneously as a turn-based action [502.3][703.4c]; nothing is stopping Ahn-Crop Crasher from untapping for Noe, so it untaps.

Note also that the exert effect will still be waiting for Aryana's next untap step; if Ahn-Crop Crasher happened to be under Aryana's control again by then and tapped, it wouldn't untap then, and such effects expire during that untap step [701.43b].

Multiplayer difference: none in substance. With more than two players, other players' untap steps may occur in between, but Ahn-Crop Crasher still untaps normally at Noe's untap step, since only Aryana's untap step is affected by the exert.

question: Andres controls [Strionic Resonator] and plays [Clive's Hideaway]. They activate Strionic Resonator targeting the hideaway trigger, exiling 2 cards. On their next turn, they activate Clive's Hideaway's ability to cast the exiled card. What happens as it resolves?
answer:
Direct answer: When the {2}, {T} ability of Clive's Hideaway resolves, Andres checks whether he controls four or more legendary creatures. If he does, he may play one of the two face-down exiled cards without paying its mana cost, right then as the ability resolves. If he controls fewer than four legendary creatures, the ability does nothing and both cards stay in exile.

Why two cards are in exile and both are eligible: Hideaway 4 is a triggered ability that exiles one card face down and gives it a permission for its controller to look at it in exile [702.75a]. Copying that triggered ability with Strionic Resonator makes a second instance of the same ability that resolves independently, so a second card was exiled face down by the same (copied) hideaway ability. Because the hideaway ability that exiled the cards and the {2}, {T} ability that plays "the exiled card" are linked abilities printed on Clive's Hideaway, that second ability can refer to any card in exile that got there as a result of that first ability's instruction [607.2a] — which includes the card exiled by the copy. It cannot reach cards exiled by anything else.

How to handle the singular wording: Clive's Hideaway says "the exiled card," but two cards now qualify. The rules provided don't spell out a tiebreaker for that wording, so treat it as Andres choosing one of the qualifying exiled cards as the ability resolves; the other remains exiled face down, still viewable by Andres [702.75a], and a later activation of the {2}, {T} ability could play it (again subject to the four-legendary-creatures check at that time). If your group instead reads the singular strictly, the practical outcome is the same for this resolution: only one card gets played now.

Other notes: the ability says "play," so if the chosen card is a land, playing it uses Andres's land play for the turn and can only happen when he could normally play a land; if it's a nonland card, it's cast (and the effect can still find it after it moves to the stack) [400.7h]. "Without paying its mana cost" means he pays no mana cost, though he'd still pay any additional costs.

This interaction involves only Andres's own permanents, so the answer is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

question: Aminah has no cards in their library and activate [Words of Wind] in their upkeep. Do they lose the game?
answer:
No — as long as the replacement is still in place when Aminah's draw step draw would happen, Aminah does not lose the game to the empty library at that point.

Why: Words of Wind's activated ability ({1}) sets up a replacement effect: "The next time you would draw a card this turn, each player returns a permanent they control to its owner's hand instead." An effect that replaces a card draw is applied even if no cards could be drawn because the affected player's library is empty [121.6a]. So when Aminah would draw in their draw step, that draw event is replaced by each player returning a permanent they control to its owner's hand. Aminah never actually attempts to draw from the empty library, so the state-based action that makes a player lose for having attempted to draw from an empty library never applies [704.5b], and neither does the priority-based loss described in [121.4] and [104.3c].

Important caveats:
- The replacement is one-shot and only lasts this turn. Any *second* draw Aminah would be required to make this turn (or any draw on a later turn) with an empty library means they attempted to draw from an empty library and they lose the game the next time a player would receive priority [121.4] [704.5b] [104.3c]. Activating Words of Wind multiple times stacks up multiple one-shot replacements, one per draw.
- Timing assumption: I'm assuming Aminah activates it during their own upkeep, before their draw step, so the pending replacement is what eats the draw-step draw. If instead the ability were activated after the draw had already been attempted, the loss is already locked in and Words of Wind can't undo it.
- Note also that effects that move cards from a library to hand without the word "draw" are not draws at all [121.5], and an effect that tries to do the impossible does only as much as possible [609.3] — but neither of those is what saves Aminah here; the replacement in [121.6a] is.

Multiplayer: this works the same with two players or more. Words of Wind's replacement makes *each* player (including every opponent) return a permanent they control to its owner's hand, so at a larger table more permanents bounce, but Aminah's survival is unaffected by player count.

question: Allan controls [Living Inferno]. They activate it, targeting Nathaly's [Runeclaw Bear]. In response, Nathaly casts [Chemister's Trick], targeting the Living Inferno. How much damage will be dealt to Runeclaw Bear when the Living Inferno's ability resolves?
answer:
Runeclaw Bear is still dealt 8 damage.

Why: Living Inferno's ability reads "{T}: This creature deals damage equal to its power divided as you choose among any number of target creatures." The division of that damage is chosen as Allan activates the ability, using Living Inferno's power at that time (8), and Allan assigned all 8 to Runeclaw Bear. Chemister's Trick giving Living Inferno -2/-0 (a layer 7 power-changing continuous effect, [613.1g]) lowers Living Inferno's power to 6, but it does not go back and re-divide or reduce the already-locked-in assignment, so 8 damage is dealt to Runeclaw Bear when the ability resolves. That damage is then dealt and processed normally ([120.4b], [120.4c], [120.4d]) — 8 damage marked on the 2/2 Runeclaw Bear, which is lethal.

The second half of the ability still happens too: Runeclaw Bear deals damage equal to its power (2) to Living Inferno. Living Inferno's toughness is unchanged by Chemister's Trick (-2/-0 only reduces power), so it survives with 2 damage marked on its 5 toughness.

Note on grounding: the provided rules context does not include the specific rule that locks in a damage division at activation; that step comes from Living Inferno's own wording ("divided as you choose" at activation) plus the fact that nothing re-divides it on resolution. If your group instead recalculated power on resolution, Living Inferno would deal only 6 — but that is not how the divided-damage wording works.

Chemister's Trick's "attacks this turn if able" clause is irrelevant here since the ability resolves before any combat requirement matters. Nothing in this interaction depends on player count, so the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: After both players finish taking mulligans, Adrian is going second and has both [Gemstone Caverns] and [Chancellor of the Annex] in their hand. Can they reveal Chancellor of the Annex for its ability and also exile it to begin the game with Gemstone Caverns on the battlefield?
answer:
Short answer: Adrian can legally do both actions in sequence, but the provided rules only support the Chancellor of the Annex reveal if that card stays revealed — and exiling it to Gemstone Caverns takes it out of the revealed state, so on the text given here you should not count on getting both effects from the same copy of Chancellor of the Annex.

Details:

1. Both are opening-hand actions. Once mulligans are done, the starting player takes any such actions in any order, then each other player in turn order does the same [103.6], [103.6a], [103.6b]. Adrian, going second, takes their actions after the starting player.

2. Gemstone Caverns' own text is satisfied: "If this card is in your opening hand and you're not the starting player, you may begin the game with Gemstone Caverns on the battlefield with a luck counter on it. If you do, exile a card from your hand." Adrian is not the starting player, so Gemstone Caverns can be put onto the battlefield from the opening hand [103.6a], and Adrian must then exile a card from hand.

3. Chancellor of the Annex says "You may reveal this card from your opening hand. If you do, when each opponent casts their first spell of the game, counter that spell unless that player pays {1}." Revealing doesn't move the card — it stays in hand [701.20b] — but rule [103.6b] specifies that a card revealed this way "remains revealed until the first turn begins." Exiling Chancellor of the Annex to Gemstone Caverns' cost ends that revealed state before the first turn begins, which is exactly what [103.6b] says should not happen. So the safe, rules-supported line is to reveal Chancellor of the Annex and exile some *other* card in hand to Gemstone Caverns; then both the luck-counter land and the Chancellor of the Annex tax on each opponent's first spell apply.

4. Timing assumption: I'm assuming Adrian would reveal Chancellor of the Annex first and then put Gemstone Caverns onto the battlefield. Reversing the order doesn't help — if Chancellor of the Annex is already exiled, it is no longer in Adrian's opening hand and can't be revealed from there at all.

Multiplayer note: the same works with more than two players; each non-starting player takes opening-hand actions in turn order [103.6], and Chancellor of the Annex's revealed ability applies to *each* opponent's first spell of the game, so at a bigger table it can tax several players (one {1} tax each). Gemstone Caverns only requires that Adrian isn't the starting player, which is true for every non-starting seat.

question: Aspen controls [Cosima, God of the Voyage] and mutates [Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt] onto it, putting it underneath Cosima, God of the Voyage. At the beginning of their next upkeep, Aspen exiles Cosima, God of the Voyage to its own triggered ability. What happens?
answer:
Direct answer: The mutated permanent is exiled as a single event, but both cards go to exile as separate objects — Cosima, God of the Voyage and Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt each end up in the exile zone as individual cards, and Aspen chooses their relative timestamp order at that time [730.3b]. Because Cosima, God of the Voyage was the top card, the merged permanent's name and other characteristics were Cosima, God of the Voyage's (while having all abilities of both cards) [702.140e], which is why the upkeep ability could exile it at all.

Why both cards leave: a merged permanent leaving the battlefield is one permanent leaving, with each individual component put into the appropriate zone [730.3b], and because Cosima, God of the Voyage's ability is an effect that can find the new object the merged permanent becomes, it finds all of those objects and applies the same action to each [730.3c]. So the exile applies to both cards, and likewise the later return-to-the-battlefield portion of the granted ability finds both cards and returns both — Cosima, God of the Voyage and Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt would each return as its own separate permanent (they are no longer merged), each getting X +1/+1 counters and Aspen drawing X cards once, where X is the number of voyage counters.

One caveat: the rules provided here don't spell out exactly how voyage counters are tracked once the merged object has become two separate exiled cards, so treat that bookkeeping detail (which card the counters sit on, and thus what X is) as unresolved by the provided context. Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt's mutate trigger already resolved earlier and is not re-triggered by this, since a mutate trigger only fires when a spell merges with a creature from a resolving mutating creature spell [702.140d].

This analysis doesn't depend on player count; it works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Aubrey controls [Whiskervale Forerunner] and casts [Growth Cycle] to give it +3/+3. Before it resolves, Aubrey casts [Cooperate] choosing to copy Growth Cycle and changes the target to another creature. Does Whiskervale Forerunner trigger again?
answer:
No. Whiskervale Forerunner does not trigger again.

Why: Whiskervale Forerunner's Valiant ability only triggers "the first time each turn" it becomes the target of a spell or ability you control. Growth Cycle targeting Whiskervale Forerunner was that first time this turn, so the ability has already triggered and any later targeting this turn does nothing.

On top of that, the copy of Growth Cycle created by Cooperate never targets Whiskervale Forerunner at all — you chose a new target, another creature. A copy of a spell is itself a spell put onto the stack (it isn't cast), and Cooperate lets you choose new targets for it, so the copy of Growth Cycle simply doesn't target Whiskervale Forerunner (707.10e). Cooperate itself targeted the Growth Cycle spell, not Whiskervale Forerunner, so casting Cooperate also didn't target Whiskervale Forerunner.

Even if you had left the copy of Growth Cycle targeting Whiskervale Forerunner, it still wouldn't trigger Valiant a second time this turn because of the once-per-turn restriction in the card's own text.

Timing note: I'm assuming Growth Cycle was still on the stack when Cooperate was cast (as stated), so the original Growth Cycle's trigger from Whiskervale Forerunner is already on the stack or has resolved; the order doesn't change the answer, since the trigger is limited to once per turn either way. This is independent of player count — nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

question: Nico has a [Pillarfield Ox] and a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 3 +1/+1 counters in their graveyard. Arjun casts [Ghastly Conscription], targeting Nico. What happens to the counters on the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave? Will Nico know which manifested card is which?
answer:
The three +1/+1 counters stay on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave the whole way, so the manifested Skullbriar, the Walking Grave enters the battlefield face down as a 2/2 with three +1/+1 counters on it — a 5/5 — and yes, that makes it obvious to Nico (and everyone) which face-down card is Skullbriar, the Walking Grave and which is Pillarfield Ox.

Why: normally counters on an object simply cease to exist when it changes zones (rule [122.2]). But Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's own text says "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." Card text beats the general rule, so the counters survive the graveyard-to-exile move and the exile-to-battlefield move made by Ghastly Conscription. Exile and the battlefield are neither hand nor library, so nothing strips them.

The face-down "pile" step doesn't matter here: while cards are grouped into a pile they haven't left whatever zone they're in ([700.3a], [700.3c]) — Ghastly Conscription's exile effect is what moves them, and each exiled creature card must go into that one pile.

So Pillarfield Ox is manifested as a vanilla face-down 2/2 with no counters, while the other face-down permanent is a 2/2 with three +1/+1 counters. The shuffle was meant to hide identities, but the visible counters give Skullbriar, the Walking Grave away. Note the manifested creatures are under Nico's control only if Ghastly Conscription said so — as written Arjun manifests them, so they enter under Arjun's control; either way the counters are public information and identify the card. Face down, it isn't legendary and has no name, and its controller could turn it face up later for {B}{G}.

This works the same at a two-player table and in multiplayer; Ghastly Conscription just targets one player either way.

question: Avery activates [Ascendant Spirit]'s first ability. Before it resolves Avery casts [Slip Out the Back] targeting Ascendant Spirit. When it phases back in, what will it look like?
answer:
When Ascendant Spirit phases back in, it will still be just a 1/1 Snow Creature — Spirit with one +1/+1 counter on it (so a 2/2). It will not be a Spirit Warrior with base power and toughness 2/3 — the first ability's effect never applied to it.

Why: Slip Out the Back was cast after the ability was activated, so it resolves first. It puts a +1/+1 counter on Ascendant Spirit and phases it out — "phased out" means the game treats the permanent (and anything attached) as though it doesn't exist until its controller's next turn ([702.26c], [610.4]). When the {S}{S} ability then tries to resolve, Ascendant Spirit doesn't exist as far as the game is concerned, so the type-changing/base-P/T effect has nothing to apply to and does nothing.

When it phases in, it's the same permanent, not a new object: its status simply changes back to "phased in" and the game treats it as existing again ([702.26c], [110.5c] — a permanent keeps its status and other characteristics/counters until something changes them). The +1/+1 counter Slip Out the Back put on it is still there, so it's a 2/2.

Timing of the return: because Slip Out the Back phases it out "until its controller's next turn," a second one-shot effect phases it in at that point ([610.4], [610.4a]) rather than via the normal untap-step phasing turn-based action ([502.1], [703.4a]).

Assumed order: the activation happened first and Slip Out the Back was cast while that ability was still on the stack (as stated). If instead the {S}{S} ability had fully resolved before Slip Out the Back resolved, Ascendant Spirit would already be a Spirit Warrior with base 2/3 and would phase back in that way, as a 3/4 with the counter — those changes last indefinitely and phasing doesn't undo them.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game, since only Avery's own permanent and untap step are involved.

question: Aspen controls [Parallel Lives] and a [Caldera Hellion]. They cast [Rite of Replication] targeting the Caldera Hellion. Can Aspen apply the devour replacement effect before the Parallel Lives replacement effect, sacrificing 1 creature to have each token enter with a +1/+1 counter?
answer:
No. Parallel Lives' replacement effect must be applied first, and even then a single sacrificed creature can only be counted once.

Why Parallel Lives goes first: when one replacement effect applies to an event and another applies to an event contained within it, the outer effect must be chosen first [616.1g]. Creating a token is the outer event, and the token entering the battlefield is contained within it, so Parallel Lives ("If an effect would create one or more tokens under your control, it creates twice that many of those tokens instead") applies before any devour effect on the tokens as they enter. Devour is a replacement effect that modifies how the permanent enters the battlefield [702.82c], so it can't be chosen ahead of Parallel Lives.

So Rite of Replication (uncast without its {5} kicker) creates one token copy of Caldera Hellion, doubled by Parallel Lives to two tokens; kicked, five becomes ten. Each token is a copy of Caldera Hellion and thus has Devour 1, and each token's devour choice is made before it enters [614.12a], in either order [616.1g].

The key limit: the same object can't be chosen to change zones more than once when applying replacement effects that modify how one or more permanents enter the battlefield [614.13b]. So sacrificing one creature satisfies devour for only one of the tokens — that token enters with one +1/+1 counter, and the other token(s) enter with zero unless you sacrifice additional, different creatures. Also, you can't sacrifice any of the Caldera Hellion tokens themselves, since objects entering the battlefield at the same time can't be chosen [614.13a].

Note too that the original Caldera Hellion on the battlefield is a legal sacrifice for devour (it isn't entering), and each token's "When this creature enters, it deals 3 damage to each creature" triggers will go on the stack after all tokens have entered.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — it's the same in a two-player or multiplayer game, since all the choices here belong to Aspen (APNAP ordering under [616.1] only matters when multiple players choose simultaneously).

question: Aubrey controls [Exotic Orchard]. Nikolas controls [Crumbling Vestige]. If Aubrey taps Exotic Orchard, what type(s) of mana can it produce?
answer:
Exotic Orchard produces no mana at all.

Exotic Orchard's ability is "{T}: Add one mana of any color that a land an opponent controls could produce." The only land Nikolas controls is Crumbling Vestige, whose activated mana ability is "{T}: Add {C}." {C} is colorless mana specifically — colorless is not a color, so Crumbling Vestige could produce no *color* of mana. Crumbling Vestige's other mana-producing ability ("When this land enters, add one mana of any color") is a triggered ability tied to it entering the battlefield; it isn't an ability that would resolve at the time Aubrey taps Exotic Orchard, so it doesn't define a color for the "could produce" check either (106.7 asks what an ability of that permanent would produce if it were to resolve at that time).

With no color definable, the type of mana Exotic Orchard would produce is undefined, and an ability that would produce mana of an undefined type produces no mana instead (106.5, and the Exotic Orchard example in 106.7). Aubrey still taps Exotic Orchard and gets nothing.

Multiplayer note: Exotic Orchard checks lands controlled by any opponent, not just one. In a two-player game Nikolas's Crumbling Vestige is the whole picture; at a table with more opponents, any color that any other opponent's land could produce would also be available to Exotic Orchard.
