question: Azariah, Beckham, and Caelan are playing a multiplayer game. Beckham controls [Stalking Leonin]. Azariah casts [Worst Fears] to take control of Beckham's next turn. After Beckham begins their turn, can Azariah see which player was chosen for the Stalking Leonin?
answer:
Yes. Once Azariah's Worst Fears effect begins and Azariah controls Beckham for Beckham's turn, Azariah can see which opponent Beckham secretly chose for Stalking Leonin.

Why: Worst Fears reads "You control target player during that player's next turn... (You see all cards that player could see and make all decisions for them.)" Rule 723.4 says that if information about an object in the game would be visible to the player being controlled, it's visible to both that player and the controller of the player. The secret choice recorded for Stalking Leonin is information about an object in the game (Stalking Leonin, a permanent Beckham controls) that Beckham can see, so Azariah sees it too. (By contrast, 723.4 keeps information about cards *outside* the game private to the controlled player — that exception doesn't apply here.)

Practical consequences during that turn: under 723.5b Azariah makes all choices and decisions Beckham is allowed to make, including whether to activate Stalking Leonin's "Reveal the player you chose" ability — though note that ability only exiles an attacking creature if it's controlled by the chosen player, and on Beckham's own turn Beckham is unlikely to be attacked. Control of objects doesn't change: Stalking Leonin is still Beckham's permanent (723.3), and Beckham remains the active player. Beckham also still makes their own non-game decisions and personal choices (723.5b, 723.8).

Multiplayer note: this is already a three-player game, and nothing changes with more players — the chosen opponent could be Azariah or Caelan, and either way Azariah sees it. If your table uses the limited range of influence option, the secret choice of an opponent must be a player within Beckham's range (801.5a); with a normal unlimited range that's no restriction here.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Stalking Leonin already entered and the secret choice was made before Beckham's controlled turn began. If instead Stalking Leonin enters during the turn Azariah controls Beckham, Azariah makes that secret choice themselves (723.5b) and obviously knows it.

If information about cards outside the game would be visible to the player being controlled, it’s visible only to that player, not the controller of the player. The controller of a player can see that player’s hand and the face of any face-down creatures they control.

The controller of another player can’t make choices or decisions for that player that aren’t called for by the rules or by any objects. The controller also can’t make any choices or decisions for the player that would be called for by the tournament rules. The player who’s being controlled still decides if they will leave to visit the restroom, trade a card to someone else, agree to an intentional draw, or call a judge about an error or infraction.

Rob must choose a target that’s in both his range of influence and in the range of influence of the controller of Cuombajj Witches. He must therefore choose himself, Alex, or a creature controlled by either himself or Alex.

answer_gold: No. The choice was made as Stalking Leonin entered the battlefield, which already happened- it's no longer visible to Beckham. Azariah can choose to activate the ability (at which point all players will know who was chosen), but otherwise the choice is not visible to any player.

question: Angela controls [Mirror Gallery] and two [Sakashima the Impostor]s. One is a copy of their [Master of the Hunt]; the other is copying a wolf token created by Master of the Hunt. They attack with all four creatures. What are the possible bands that Angela may declare?
answer:
Angela can't declare any bands at all — all four creatures attack as individual, unbanded attackers.

Why: Rule 702.22c gives exactly two ways to form an attacking band.

1) The plain-banding way: one or more attacking creatures with the banding keyword, plus up to one attacking creature without banding (even one that has "bands with other"). None of Angela's four attackers has plain banding. Master of the Hunt has no banding — it only creates tokens; the Sakashima the Impostor that copied Master of the Hunt likewise has no banding (copying doesn't grant one, and Master of the Hunt's granted ability lives on the tokens it makes). So this route is unavailable.

2) The "bands with other [quality]" way: one or more attacking [quality] creatures that have "bands with other [quality]" plus any number of other attacking [quality] creatures. Here the quality is "creatures named Wolves of the Hunt." The Wolves of the Hunt token qualifies — it is named Wolves of the Hunt and has "bands with other creatures named Wolves of the Hunt." But it is the only creature on Angela's side with that name, and a band needs at least two creatures, so it has nothing to band with. The Sakashima the Impostor copying the Wolves of the Hunt token does have the ability "bands with other creatures named Wolves of the Hunt," but Sakashima the Impostor's copy effect keeps its name as Sakashima the Impostor, so it is not itself a creature named Wolves of the Hunt. It therefore fails both halves of 702.22c: it isn't a [quality] creature with the "bands with other" ability, and it isn't another [quality] creature that could be swept into a band.

Mirror Gallery matters only in that its text ("The 'legend rule' doesn't apply") lets Angela keep two legendary Sakashima the Impostors plus a legendary-copied Master of the Hunt on the battlefield at once; it has no effect on banding.

Also note that banding doesn't share abilities between attackers (702.22g), so the Sakashima the Impostor copying Master of the Hunt can't lend anything here either. Had a band been legal, every member would have had to attack the same player, planeswalker, or battle (702.22d, 802.3b) — that restriction is the same in a two-player game and in multiplayer, where the attacking player chooses a defending player per attacker (802.3b). Attackers and any bands are declared as part of the declare attackers turn-based action (508.1e).

If Angela made a second Wolves of the Hunt token before attacking, then the two real Wolves of the Hunt tokens could band together (the Sakashima the Impostor copy still couldn't join).

A player may declare as many attacking bands as they want, but each creature may be a member of only one of them. (Defending players can’t declare bands but may use banding in a different way; see rule 702.22j.)

The Sakashima the Impostor with "bands with other creatures named Wolves of the Hunt" is not itself named "Wolves of the Hunt", so it cannot declare itself as in a band with the token.

question: Avery controls a Germ token that's equipped with [Barbed Bloodletter]. Nadia controls two [Teferi's Curse]s, one on the Germ, the other on the Barbed Bloodletter. During Avery's untap step, which permanents will phase out? Which of these will phase back in?
answer:
All four permanents phase out during Avery's untap step, and none of them phase back in during that same untap step — they all phase in during Avery's *next* untap step.

Detail:

1. **Phasing out (this untap step).** Phasing is a static ability that modifies the untap step: before the active player untaps, every phased-in permanent with phasing that player controls phases out, and every phased-out permanent that player controlled when it phased out phases in — all simultaneously [702.26a] [502.1] [703.4a].
 - The Germ token has phasing (granted by Nadia's Teferi's Curse attached to it) and is controlled by Avery, so it phases out directly.
 - Barbed Bloodletter also has phasing (granted by the second Teferi's Curse attached to Barbed Bloodletter) and is controlled by Avery, so it too phases out directly.
 - Both copies of Teferi's Curse phase out "indirectly" — Auras attached to a permanent that phases out phase out at the same time, even though Nadia controls them [702.26g].

2. **Nothing phases in this untap step**, since nothing of Avery's was already phased out.

3. **Phasing back in.** On Avery's next untap step, every permanent that phased out under Avery's control phases in: the Germ token and Barbed Bloodletter [702.26a] [502.1]. The two Teferi's Curses phased out indirectly, so they don't phase in on their own (and won't phase in on Nadia's untap step) — each phases in along with the permanent it's attached to [702.26g], which is the same moment. Barbed Bloodletter, having phased out directly, phases in attached to the Germ token if that token is still on the battlefield [702.26i].

Notes: phasing out isn't a zone change or change of control, so no leaves-the-battlefield or unattach triggers occur, the token keeps existing while phased out, and counters stay on it [702.26d] [702.26j]. If some effect makes Avery skip their untap step, the phasing event simply doesn't happen that turn [702.26m].

This works identically in a two-player or multiplayer game, with one multiplayer caveat: if the controller of a phased-out permanent leaves the game, that permanent may leave the game or be exiled, and a permanent that phased out under a departed player's control phases in during the next untap step after that player's next turn would have begun [702.26n].

Effects that check a phased-in permanent’s history won’t treat the phasing event as having caused the permanent to leave or enter the battlefield or its controller’s control.

question: Alessandra controls [Sheoldred, the Apocalypse]. During their main phase, they cast [Day's Undoing]. How much life does each player gain/lose?
answer:
Short answer: nobody gains or loses any life (assuming Alessandra casts Day's Undoing on their own turn, as stated).

Why: Day's Undoing has each player shuffle hand and graveyard into their library and draw seven cards. Sheoldred, the Apocalypse's abilities do trigger on those draws \,, you gain 2 life" for each of Alessandra's seven draws, and "whenever an opponent draws a card, they lose 2 life" for each opponent's seven draws \, so 14 life would be gained by Alessandra and 14 lost by each opponent. However, those are triggered abilities: they wait to be put on the stack, and Day's Undoing is still resolving. Because it's Alessandra's turn, Day's Undoing then says "end the turn," whose reminder text reads "Exile all spells and abilities from the stack, including this card." The Sheoldred, the Apocalypse triggers are exiled along with everything else and never resolve, so no life is gained or lost.

Timing caveat: if instead Day's Undoing were somehow cast during an opponent's turn (it's a sorcery, so this would require an effect allowing it), the "end the turn" clause would not apply, the Sheoldred, the Apocalypse triggers would resolve normally, and Alessandra would gain 14 life while each opponent lost 14 life.

Multiplayer: with more than two players, every opponent draws seven, so in the "turn doesn't end" case each opponent separately loses 14 life; in the actual case (Alessandra's own turn) it's still zero for everyone. In a Two-Headed Giant game, life gained or lost happens to each player individually but is applied to that team's shared life total [810.9], and if an effect says a player can't gain or lose life, no one on that team can [810.9g][810.9h].

One limitation: the numbered rule governing exactly how "end the turn" handles abilities that triggered during resolution was not included in the context; the conclusion above rests on Day's Undoing's own printed text, which overrides the general expectation that triggers go on the stack.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.723.1a: Some cards allow a player to control another player during that player’s next turn. This effect applies to the next turn that the affected player actually takes. The affected player is controlled during the entire turn; the effect doesn’t end until the beginning of the next turn. Multiple player-controlling effects that affect the same player overwrite each other. The last one to be created is the one that works.

cited_text.810.9: Damage, loss of life, and gaining life happen to each player individually. The result is applied to the team’s shared life total. In a Two-Headed Giant game, a player casts Flame Rift, which reads, “Flame Rift deals 4 damage to each player.” Each team is dealt a total of 8 damage.
cited_text.810.9g: Damage, loss of life, and gaining life happen to each player individually. The result is applied to the team’s shared life total. If an effect says that a player can’t gain life, no player on that player’s team can gain life.
cited_text.810.9h: Damage, loss of life, and gaining life happen to each player individually. The result is applied to the team’s shared life total. If an effect says that a player can’t lose life, no player on that player’s team can lose life or pay any amount of life other than 0.

answer_gold: None. The players first draw seven cards each, triggering Sheoldred, the Apocalypse fourteen times. Then Alessandra ends the turn, which nullifies those triggers before they're even put onto the stack.

question: It is currently day and Adonis controls [Lazotep Convert] (the back face of [Invasion of Amonkhet]), which is a copy of [Kessig Naturalist]. What happens if it becomes night?
answer:
Nothing happens — Adonis's Lazotep Convert does not transform when it becomes night.

Why: Lazotep Convert is the back face of the double-faced card Invasion of Amonkhet, so the permanent is physically back face up. Copying Kessig Naturalist gives it Kessig Naturalist's copiable text, including daybound, but daybound only says "As it becomes night, if this permanent is front face up, transform it" [702.145b], and the ongoing check in [702.145c] likewise only applies to a permanent that is front face up with daybound while it's night. Lazotep Convert is back face up, so neither the "as it becomes night" trigger-like static ability nor the continuous check does anything. It also doesn't have nightbound (Kessig Naturalist's front face has daybound, not nightbound), so [702.145e]/[702.145f] don't apply either. Daybound additionally says the permanent can't transform except due to its daybound ability [702.145b], so no other effect will flip it.

Day/night itself still behaves normally: the game changes designation during the untap step based on the previous turn's active player's spellcasting [502.2], [731.2], [731.2a], [731.2b]. Note also that because Adonis controls a permanent with daybound, if the game had no designation it would become day [702.145d]; here it is already day, and once the game has a designation it always has exactly one [731.1].

Multiplayer: the rules given for the day/night check are worded around "the previous turn's active player," so they work the same with more than two players (with a modification only for shared team turns) [731.2a], [731.2b]; Lazotep Convert's non-transformation is unaffected by player count.

Timing note: I'm assuming Lazotep Convert is already on the battlefield as a copy of Kessig Naturalist when night arrives. If instead it were entering the battlefield while it's night, the "enters transformed" part of daybound applies only to a permanent represented by a double-faced card and would try to put it onto the battlefield with its other face — Invasion of Amonkhet, a Siege battle, not an instant or sorcery — so unlike the sorcery-back case described in [712.13a] it would not be put into the graveyard.

question: Adelina's [Fireblade Charger] dies, and Nasir responds with [Thwart the Enemy]. Is the damage prevented?
answer:
No — Thwart the Enemy does not prevent that damage. Once Fireblade Charger has died, it's a card in Adelina's graveyard, not a creature Adelina controls on the battlefield, so its death-trigger damage isn't "damage dealt by creatures your opponents control."

Why: Thwart the Enemy's effect is a prevention shield from a resolved spell that applies to damage from sources with a certain property (a creature controlled by one of Nasir's opponents). When the source would actually deal the damage, the shield rechecks the source's properties; if they no longer match, the damage isn't prevented and the shield isn't used up [609.7b, 615.9, 615.2]. At the time Fireblade Charger's triggered ability resolves and deals damage equal to its power, the source is Fireblade Charger as it last existed on the battlefield — but it is no longer a creature on the battlefield that Adelina controls, so the property check fails.

Timing note: I'm assuming Nasir cast Thwart the Enemy after Fireblade Charger died (in response to the death trigger), which is the reading in the question. Prevention effects must exist before the damage event, so casting it then is legal timing-wise [615.4] — the problem is the source check, not the timing. If Nasir had instead cast Thwart the Enemy earlier in the turn while Fireblade Charger was still on the battlefield, the answer would be the same, because the shield still rechecks the source's properties at the moment damage would be dealt [609.7b].

Terminology: "prevent" means the damage simply never happens; if all of it is prevented, abilities that trigger on damage being dealt don't trigger [615.1a, 615.6, 603.2g]. Here nothing is prevented, so Fireblade Charger's damage is dealt in full to the chosen target.

Multiplayer: no difference. "Creatures your opponents control" covers every opponent's creatures, so whether it's just Nasir and Adelina or a larger table, Fireblade Charger's post-death damage still isn't prevented.

question: Aminah casts a [Show and Tell]. As it resolves, Aminah chooses to put a [Haru-Onna] onto the battlefield and Nico chooses to put a [Domestication] onto the battlefield enchanting Haru-Onna. Who controls the enters-the-battlefield ability of Haru-Onna?
answer:
Nico controls Haru-Onna's enters-the-battlefield trigger, so Nico draws the card.

Why: Show and Tell puts both cards onto the battlefield simultaneously as it resolves. Haru-Onna would enter under Aminah's control by default (110.2a), and Domestication enters under Nico's control attached to Haru-Onna. But Domestication's "You control enchanted creature" is a continuous control-changing effect, applied in layer 2 (613.1b), and it applies immediately as both permanents exist on the battlefield. So at the moment Haru-Onna is on the battlefield, its controller is Nico.

Haru-Onna's ability ("When this creature enters, draw a card") triggers on that event, and a triggered ability is controlled by the player who controlled its source at the time it triggered (113.8, 603.3a, 109.4b). Since Nico controls Haru-Onna at that time, Nico puts the trigger on the stack and Nico draws the card. Note that an Aura's controller and the enchanted creature's controller are separate matters (303.4e); here Nico happens to be both.

Timing note: I'm assuming Domestication was put onto the battlefield attached to Haru-Onna simultaneously with Haru-Onna, as Show and Tell resolves. If instead Domestication somehow arrived later (e.g., a separately cast Aura after Haru-Onna was already on the battlefield), Haru-Onna's enters trigger would have already triggered under Aminah's control, and Aminah would draw the card; later gaining control of Haru-Onna would not change the controller of that already-triggered ability.

This works the same at a two-player or multiplayer table \-- control of the trigger simply follows whoever controls Haru-Onna the instant it enters.

question:
Amani controls a [Founding the Third Path], and its third ability is resolving. Amani chooses to cast a [Fatal Push] from their graveyard. Amani currently does not have Revolt.
Can Amani choose to target [Skyhunter Patrol] with Fatal Push? Will Skyhunter Patrol be destroyed by Fatal Push?
answer:
Yes, Amani can legally target Skyhunter Patrol with Fatal Push — but Skyhunter Patrol will not be destroyed.

Why targeting is legal: Fatal Push says "Destroy target creature if it has mana value 2 or less." The only targeting restriction is "target creature" — the mana value clause is a condition on the destruction effect, not part of the target requirement. Skyhunter Patrol is a creature permanent on the battlefield, so it is a legal target (115.2). Nothing about its mana value of 4 makes it an illegal choice.

Why nothing happens: when the copy of Fatal Push resolves, it checks that Skyhunter Patrol is still a legal target; it is, so Fatal Push resolves (608.2b). It then applies its effect, which only destroys the creature if Skyhunter Patrol's mana value is 2 or less. Skyhunter Patrol's mana cost is {2}{W}{W}, so its mana value is 4. Without Revolt (no permanent left the battlefield under Amani's control this turn), the alternative "4 or less" threshold doesn't apply, so Fatal Push resolves and does nothing. Skyhunter Patrol survives.

A note on the Founding the Third Path chapter III: it exiles the Fatal Push card from Amani's graveyard, creates a copy, and Amani may cast that copy — targets for the copy of Fatal Push are chosen as it's cast, at which point Skyhunter Patrol is a valid choice. Also, targeting Skyhunter Patrol counts as committing a crime if Skyhunter Patrol is controlled by an opponent (700.13); this is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

If Amani did somehow enable Revolt before the copy of Fatal Push resolved, the 4-or-less threshold would apply and Skyhunter Patrol would be destroyed.

This state-based action doesn’t use the stack.

Sorin’s Thirst is a black instant that reads, “Sorin’s Thirst deals 2 damage to target creature and you gain 2 life.” If the creature isn’t a legal target during the resolution of Sorin’s Thirst (say, if the creature has gained protection from black or left the battlefield), then Sorin’s Thirst doesn’t resolve. The “destroy target nonblack creature” part of the spell won’t affect that permanent, but the “destroy target land” part of the spell will still destroy it. It can’t be regenerated.

answer_gold:
Yes Amani can target Skyhunter Patrol, and it will be destroyed by Fatal Push.

Fatal Push does not check for the target's mana value when put on the stack, so Amani is allowed to target Skyhunter Patrol.

Amani will put Fatal Push on the stack as part of the resolution of Founding the Third Path's third chapter. Once the ability is done resolving, SBAs are checked and the saga is sacrificed. In particular this means that Amani will have Revolt when Fatal Push resolves, thus Skyhunter Patrol will get destroyed.

question: Nico controls Analia's [Bane Alley Blackguard] enchanted with their [Corrupted Conscience]. Analia casts their own [Lay Claim], targeting Nico's Corrupted Conscience. After it resolves, who controls the Bane Alley Blackguard? Who controls the Corrupted Conscience?
answer:
Analia ends up controlling both.

Corrupted Conscience: Analia. Lay Claim reads "You control enchanted permanent," and it's enchanting Nico's Corrupted Conscience, so Analia (Lay Claim's controller) gains control of Corrupted Conscience. Control-changing effects like this are applied in layer 2 [613.1b].

Bane Alley Blackguard: Analia. Corrupted Conscience reads "You control enchanted creature," and "you" means Corrupted Conscience's controller. Once Analia controls Corrupted Conscience, its control-changing effect now grants Bane Alley Blackguard to Analia instead of Nico. An Aura's controller is tracked separately from the enchanted object's controller, and changing control of one doesn't automatically change control of the other [303.4e] — but here the change flows because Corrupted Conscience's own text points at whoever currently controls it, and both effects are applied together in layer 2 [613.1b]. Note also that Bane Alley Blackguard is Analia's card, but that's incidental: ownership doesn't determine control [110.2b]. Even if Analia weren't the owner, she'd control it via Corrupted Conscience.

One side note: Nico losing control of Bane Alley Blackguard is the kind of event that "leaves the battlefield"-style or "loses control" triggers look back in time for [603.10d], so any such triggered abilities would still see Nico as its controller at that moment.

This works identically in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; nothing here depends on the number of players. (If Analia later leaves a multiplayer game, Lay Claim leaves with her and Corrupted Conscience would revert to Nico's control, which would in turn hand Bane Alley Blackguard back to Nico [800.4a].)

question: Autumn controls [Traveling Chocobo] and casts [Phyrexian Ingester]. Autumn exiles [Scarwood Goblins] and then [Tor Giant] with the triggers. What are Phyrexian Ingester's power and toughness?
answer:
Phyrexian Ingester only gets one imprint trigger here, so only one creature is exiled — and Phyrexian Ingester ends up 5/5 if Scarwood Goblins is the exiled card, or 6/6 if Tor Giant is.

Why there's only one trigger: Traveling Chocobo's text reads "If a land or Bird you control entering the battlefield causes a triggered ability of a permanent you control to trigger, that ability triggers an additional time." Phyrexian Ingester is a Phyrexian Beast, not a land and not a Bird, so its own enter-the-battlefield Imprint trigger is not doubled by Traveling Chocobo. This is card text controlling the outcome, and it overrides the premise of the question that there were two triggers.

The math: Phyrexian Ingester is printed 3/3 (rule 302.4c: start with the printed numbers, then apply continuous effects). - Exiling Scarwood Goblins (2/2): 3+2 / 3+2 = 5/5.

question: Beverly controls [Pandemonium]. Adalynn casts [Knight Errant] and targets Beverly's [Forest Bear] with the Pandemonium trigger. In response Channing casts [Ral's Outburst] targeting Adalynn causing them to lose the game. Will Beverly's creature die?
answer:
I can't fully settle this with the rules provided. Direct answer: the key question is what happens to Adalynn's Pandemonium trigger when Adalynn leaves the game while that trigger is still on the stack, and the rule that governs objects controlled by a player who leaves the game (the "leaves the game" cleanup rule, 800.4 in the Comprehensive Rules) was not included in the context, so I can't ground an answer on it.

What the provided material does establish:
- Pandemonium reads "Whenever a creature enters, that creature's controller may have it deal damage equal to its power to any target of their choice," so even though Beverly controls Pandemonium, the trigger from Knight Errant entering is controlled by Adalynn, the controller of Knight Errant, and Adalynn chose Beverly's Forest Bear as the target.
- Knight Errant is a 2/2 and Forest Bear is a 2/2, so if the Pandemonium trigger were to resolve with Adalynn choosing to have Knight Errant deal damage, Forest Bear would be dealt 2 damage and would be destroyed by state-based actions.
- An effect can state a player loses the game [104.3e], and abilities that trigger on a player losing the game "look back in time" [603.10f], triggering regardless of the reason for the loss [603.9] — but neither Pandemonium nor Ral's Outburst has such an ability, so those rules don't change this case.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Ral's Outburst is cast in response and resolves while the Pandemonium trigger is still on the stack, and that the 3 damage reduces Adalynn to 0 or less life so Adalynn loses the game before that trigger resolves. If instead the Pandemonium trigger resolved first, Adalynn would already have had the chance to have Knight Errant deal 2 damage to Forest Bear, and Forest Bear would die from that damage as a state-based action.

What's missing: a rule stating whether a spell or ability controlled by a player who has left the game ceases to exist (and whether Knight Errant, owned by Adalynn, also leaves). Player count also matters here — this is clearly a multiplayer game with at least Beverly, Adalynn, and Channing, and the departure rules for multiplayer weren't provided; the only multiplayer rules in context concern range of influence [801.7a] and win-replacement [801.14], neither of which applies.

question: Asher casts [Show and Tell]. As it resolves, Asher wants to put [Hall of Triumph] onto the battlefield. Do they know what Noa is putting onto the battlefield while making the choice for Hall of Triumph's replacement effect?
answer:
Yes — by the time Asher chooses a color for Hall of Triumph, Noa's card is already known.

Why, step by step:

1. Show and Tell has each player put a card onto the battlefield at the same time. Because multiple players make choices simultaneously, rule 101.4b (APNAP order) applies: the active player chooses first, then each other player in turn order, and each player knows the earlier players' choices. So if Asher is the active player, Asher must decide *which card* (Hall of Triumph) without knowing what Noa will pick; Noa then chooses knowing Asher picked Hall of Triumph. Then the actions — the cards actually being put onto the battlefield — happen simultaneously.

2. Hall of Triumph reads "As Hall of Triumph enters, choose a color." That's a replacement effect modifying how the permanent enters the battlefield, and the choice it requires is made before the permanent enters (614.12a). That choice happens during the zone-change event itself, after the "which card" choices are locked in.

3. When objects move to the battlefield, each player who will be able to look at them does so, and then replacement effects are applied (400.6). Since Noa's card is entering the battlefield simultaneously and is a public object, it's visible at that point. So Asher makes the color choice for Hall of Triumph with Noa's permanent known.

4. If both players' entering permanents had "as it enters" choices at the same time, those choices are likewise made in APNAP order (616.1f, 101.4).

Assumption on timing: I'm reading the question as asking about the color choice for Hall of Triumph, not the choice of which card to reveal. If you meant the latter, the answer flips — as active player Asher picks the card first, blind to Noa's pick.

Multiplayer: with more than two players the same structure holds; the active player chooses a card first, then each other player in turn order, and all cards enter simultaneously, so the color choice for Hall of Triumph is made with every other player's entering permanent visible.

question: Adriel controls [Wandering Ones] equipped with [Fleetfeather Sandals]. On Nico's turn, they enchant it with [Tightening Coils]. On Adriel's next turn, they activate Fleetfeather Sandals's equip ability, targeting Wandering Ones. After that resolves, does it have flying?
answer:
Yes — after the equip ability resolves, Wandering Ones has flying (and haste).

Why: both Fleetfeather Sandals ("Equipped creature has flying and haste") and Tightening Coils ("Enchanted creature gets -6/-0 and loses flying") are continuous effects from static abilities. The flying-granting and flying-removing effects are both applied in layer 6 (ability-adding and ability-removing effects) [613.1f], and neither depends on the other, so they're applied in timestamp order — the later one wins [613.9].

Originally Fleetfeather Sandals was attached first, so Tightening Coils had the later timestamp and Wandering Ones lost flying. When Adriel activates Fleetfeather Sandals's equip ability targeting Wandering Ones and it resolves, the Equipment becomes attached (re-attached) to that creature, and its static ability's continuous effect receives a new timestamp at that moment [613.7a]. That new timestamp is later than Tightening Coils's, so "Equipped creature has flying and haste" is applied after "loses flying," and Wandering Ones ends up with flying.

Note that Tightening Coils still applies its other effect: Wandering Ones is a 1/1 getting -6/-0, so it's a -5/1 flier (power is treated as 0 for damage purposes; its toughness is still 1, so it doesn't die). The static abilities aren't "locked in" — they apply based on current attachments at all times [611.3a], [604.4].

Assumption on timing: I'm reading it as the equip ability resolving successfully with Wandering Ones still on the battlefield and still enchanted by Tightening Coils. If instead Tightening Coils had been attached after this equip resolved, its later timestamp would win and Wandering Ones would not have flying.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players — the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Ari controls [Bludgeon Brawl] and [Soldevi Digger]. They cast [Titania's Song]. Once it resolves, what are the characteristics of Soldevi Digger?
answer:
Soldevi Digger becomes a colorless 2/2 Artifact Creature — Equipment named Soldevi Digger with mana cost {2} and no abilities at all.

How it gets there (characteristics are computed by applying continuous effects in layers, rule 613.1a; a single effect's parts each apply in their own layer, rule 613.6):

- Copiable/printed base: name Soldevi Digger, mana cost {2} (two generic mana), colorless, card type Artifact, mana value 2, ability "{2}: Put the top card of your graveyard on the bottom of your library."
- Layer 4 (types/subtypes): Bludgeon Brawl (earlier timestamp) makes Soldevi Digger an Equipment, since at the time it applies Soldevi Digger is a noncreature, non-Equipment artifact. Titania's Song then makes Soldevi Digger an artifact creature. Once an effect starts applying to an object it keeps applying to it in later layers even if the object no longer fits the original description (rule 613.6), so both effects stay on.
- Layer 6 (abilities): Bludgeon Brawl grants equip {2} and "Equipped creature gets +2/+0" (X = Soldevi Digger's mana value, 2). Titania's Song has the later timestamp and says the artifact loses all abilities, so it strips Soldevi Digger's own {2} activated ability AND the equip and +2/+0 abilities Bludgeon Brawl granted. Net: no abilities. Note it keeps the Equipment subtype but has no equip ability, and it isn't attached to anything.
- Layer 7b (power/toughness setting): Titania's Song sets power and toughness each equal to mana value, which is 2, so 2/2.

Mana cost, color, and name are unchanged: cost {2}, colorless (nothing here adds a colored mana symbol or color). Whether a permanent is tapped, who controls it, etc., aren't characteristics (rule 109.3).

Also note Titania's Song's own text: if Titania's Song later leaves the battlefield, the effect continues until end of turn, so Soldevi Digger stays an ability-less 2/2 for the rest of that turn (card text governs). If Bludgeon Brawl leaves instead, Soldevi Digger stops being an Equipment but remains a 2/2 artifact creature with no abilities.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Addilynn activates the Unearth ability of their [Extractor Demon], returning it to the battlefield. Before their end step, Addilynn casts [Reality Ripple] targeting Extractor Demon. What happens to it?
answer:
Extractor Demon phases out and stays on the battlefield; because phasing out is not leaving the battlefield, the unearth replacement effect ("If it would leave the battlefield, exile it instead of putting it anywhere else") never applies. Per Reality Ripple's own reminder text, while Extractor Demon is phased out it's treated as though it doesn't exist, and it phases in before Addilynn's untap step on their next turn.

Key terms: unearth ([702.84a]) means "{2}{B}: Return this card from your graveyard to the battlefield. It gains haste. Exile it at the beginning of the next end step. If it would leave the battlefield, exile it instead of putting it anywhere else. Activate only as a sorcery." Phasing out means the permanent remains on the battlefield but is treated as though it doesn't exist until it phases in.

The practical result players rely on: since a phased-out permanent is treated as nonexistent, the delayed triggered ability from unearth that would exile Extractor Demon at the beginning of the next end step doesn't find it, so Extractor Demon isn't exiled and returns (phases in) untapped-step of Addilynn's next turn, now free of the unearth exile clause because that delayed trigger has already had its one chance. Compare [603.7c]: a delayed triggered ability that refers to a particular object won't affect it if it isn't in the zone the ability expects it in at resolution.

Honest caveat: the rules excerpts provided here do not include the full phasing rules (the section that spells out that a phased-out permanent is treated as though it doesn't exist for abilities and that it phases in before its controller's untap step) beyond Reality Ripple's reminder text, so the exile-at-end-step step above rests on that reminder text plus [603.7c] rather than on a quoted phasing rule.

Timing note: I'm assuming Reality Ripple resolves before the beginning of the end step, as stated. If instead the end-step delayed trigger had already resolved first, Extractor Demon would have been exiled and Reality Ripple would have had no legal target. Nothing here depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Avery controls [Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher] and Natalie controls [Verity Circle] and [Koskun Falls]. Avery attacks Natalie with Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher, and then taps it to pay for the cost required by Koskun Falls. Will Natalie's Verity Circle trigger?
answer:
Yes — Natalie's Verity Circle triggers.

Why: Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher has vigilance, so declaring it as an attacker doesn't tap it (attacking normally taps a creature, but that's not a cost — see [508.1f]). The tap that actually happens is Avery activating Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher's own mana ability ({T}: add {C} equal to its toughness) to produce mana for Koskun Falls' "pays {2} for each creature they control that's attacking you" attack cost. Because Koskun Falls' cost requires mana, Avery gets a chance to activate mana abilities during the declare attackers step, after the total cost is locked in ([508.1h], [508.1i]).

Verity Circle reads "Whenever a creature an opponent controls becomes tapped, if it isn't being declared as an attacker, you may draw a card." Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher becomes tapped here by paying an activation cost of its own mana ability, not by being declared as an attacker, so the exception doesn't apply and the trigger condition is met.

Details worth noting:
- Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher's toughness is 3, so it adds {C}{C}{C}; Koskun Falls asks for {2} generic per attacking creature, and colorless mana can pay generic costs, so one attacking creature costs {2} and is covered. Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher's restriction is only that this mana can't be spent to cast spells from your hand — paying an attack cost isn't casting a spell, so the payment is legal.
- If Avery can't pay the {2}, the attack declaration is illegal and the game rewinds to before the declaration ([508.1i], [118.3]).
- Two players vs. multiplayer: Koskun Falls only taxes creatures attacking its controller, and Verity Circle only cares about creatures an opponent controls becoming tapped. With more than two players, the answer is the same as long as Avery is attacking Natalie; Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher attacking a different player wouldn't incur Koskun Falls' cost at all, but any tap of it would still trigger Verity Circle if it wasn't the tap from being declared an attacker.
- Timing assumption: I'm assuming the tap happens as part of paying Koskun Falls' cost during declaration of attackers ([508.1i]). If instead Avery had tapped Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher for mana before combat (e.g., in the precombat main phase), Verity Circle would still trigger for the same reason.

question: Nico controls [Platinum Emperion]. Alexandra attacks with [Hopeful Eidolon], which Nico doesn't block. Does Alexandra gain life?
answer:
Yes — Alexandra gains 1 life. Platinum Emperion only locks Nico's own life total; it does nothing to Alexandra's.

Why: Hopeful Eidolon is a 1/1 with lifelink, and it's unblocked, so it deals 1 combat damage to Nico. Damage dealt by a source with lifelink causes that source's controller to gain that much life, in addition to whatever else the damage does [702.15b, 120.3f]. The two results are separate parts of the same damage event: the damage to Nico would make Nico lose 1 life [120.3a], and separately Alexandra gains 1 life [120.4d]. Platinum Emperion's text "Your life total can't change" applies only to its controller, Nico, so Nico's life total stays where it is, but that has no bearing on Alexandra's life gain [119.3].

Note that the life gain depends on damage actually being dealt — if the combat damage to Nico were prevented entirely, no damage would be dealt and Alexandra would gain nothing. Platinum Emperion doesn't prevent damage; it just stops Nico's life total from changing, so the damage is still dealt and lifelink still applies.

This reasoning is the same at a multiplayer table: Platinum Emperion restricts only its controller's life total, and Hopeful Eidolon's lifelink credits life to Alexandra regardless of which opponent is the defending player. (In Two-Headed Giant, damage and life gain happen to each player individually and then apply to the team's shared total [810.9g].)

question: Ari casts a [Hero of Oxid Ridge]. In response, Nixon casts [Hallow], targeting the Hero of Oxid Ridge. When Ari attacks with the Hero of Oxid Ridge that turn, will the damage be prevented?
answer:
No — Hero of Oxid Ridge's combat damage will not be prevented. Hallow says "Prevent all damage target spell would deal this turn," and it created a prevention shield tied to the Hero of Oxid Ridge *spell* on the stack. A creature spell doesn't deal damage; when it resolves it becomes a permanent on the battlefield, which is a different object from the spell Hallow targeted. When Hero of Oxid Ridge later deals combat damage as a creature, the shield rechecks the source's properties, finds they no longer match the source it was set up for, so no damage is prevented and the shield isn't used up [609.7b, 615.9, 615.2]. Prevention effects aren't locked in ahead of time — they apply as damage events actually happen, acting as shields around what they affect [615.1a], and Hallow's shield is around damage from the spell, not from the resulting creature.

A target detail worth noting: Hallow can legally target the Hero of Oxid Ridge spell, and it will simply resolve and prevent nothing, so Nixon gains no life either (there's no damage prevented to match).

Assumption on timing: I'm reading this as Hallow resolving while Hero of Oxid Ridge is still on the stack, then Hero of Oxid Ridge resolving and attacking later in the same turn. If instead Nixon had cast a prevention spell targeting the creature *permanent* after it resolved (a different card, since Hallow only targets spells), that shield could prevent its combat damage, and if all the damage were prevented, abilities that trigger on damage being dealt wouldn't trigger [603.2g].

This analysis is the same whether the game is two-player or multiplayer, with one multiplayer caveat: a prevention effect can only affect sources, permanents, and players within its controller's range of influence [801.13b]. In a normal multiplayer game with no range-of-influence restriction, that's no different from the two-player case.

question: Ariel wants to participate in a sanctioned Magic tournament, but doesn't know where to find one. To which section of the comprehensive rules should they refer?
answer:
Ariel should look at rule 100.6, specifically rule 100.6b, in section 1 ("Game Concepts") of the Comprehensive Rules. That rule states that players can use the Magic Store & Event Locator at Locator.Wizards.com to find tournaments in their area [100.6b].

The same rule also notes that most Magic tournaments (organized play activities where players compete against other players for prizes) have additional rules covered in the Magic: The Gathering Tournament Rules, found at WPN.Wizards.com/en/rules-documents, and that those rules may limit the use of some cards, including barring all cards from some older sets [100.6] [100.6b]. Related pointers to the Tournament Rules appear elsewhere too — for multiplayer tournament play and deck construction see rule 800.3, and for tournament shortcut/loop handling see rule 732.1c, where the Tournament Rules take precedence over the Comprehensive Rules when they conflict.

question: Ariel controls [Mycosynth Lattice]. Nora controls [Kaslem's Strider] enchanted with [Spirit Away]. Ariel casts [Opportunistic Dragon] and takes control of Spirit Away. What will happen after Opportunistic Dragon's ability resolves?
answer:
Ariel gains control of Spirit Away and Spirit Away loses all abilities; as a result Nora keeps Kaslem's Strider, which is now a plain 5/5 artifact creature with no flying and no +2/+2.

Why:

1. Legality of the target: Opportunistic Dragon's trigger says "choose target Human or artifact an opponent controls." Mycosynth Lattice makes all permanents artifacts in addition to their other types, so Nora's Spirit Away (normally just an Enchantment — Aura) is also an artifact and is a legal target.

2. When Opportunistic Dragon's ability resolves, Ariel gains control of Spirit Away, Spirit Away loses all abilities, and Spirit Away can't attack or block (irrelevant unless it somehow becomes a creature).

3. Losing all abilities strips Spirit Away of "Enchant creature," "You control enchanted creature," and "Enchanted creature gets +2/+2 and has flying." The control-changing effect from Spirit Away therefore no longer exists in layer 2 (control-changing effects), so Kaslem's Strider is controlled by Nora, who controlled it apart from that effect [613.1b]. The power/toughness boost and flying also go away, leaving Kaslem's Strider as a 5/5 artifact creature — Golem (it's an artifact both natively and via Mycosynth Lattice).

4. Spirit Away stays on the battlefield under Ariel's control and remains attached to Kaslem's Strider — losing "Enchant creature" doesn't detach it by itself; nothing in the provided rules unattaches it here. It simply does nothing.

5. Duration: the control-and-ability-stripping effect lasts "for as long as this creature remains on the battlefield." If Opportunistic Dragon leaves the battlefield, Spirit Away regains its abilities and reverts to its prior controller, and its "You control enchanted creature" effect would then hand Kaslem's Strider back to Spirit Away's controller.

Multiplayer note: nothing changes with more than two players — Opportunistic Dragon just needs the chosen permanent to be controlled by any one opponent. If the player who controlled Spirit Away by default were to leave the game while Ariel's control effect is still running, Spirit Away would be exiled when that effect ends [800.4c].

For a token or a copy of a spell or card, that means the values of the characteristics defined by the effect that created it. question: Atlas attacks with [Pristine Angel], and Nico targets it with [Cephalid Snitch] before blockers. After combat, Atlas casts a spell, untapping Pristine Angel. Once untapped, can Nico target it with [Mob]?
answer:
Yes — Nico can target Pristine Angel with Mob, assuming all of this happens in the same turn.

Why: Pristine Angel's static ability says "As long as this creature is untapped, it has protection from artifacts and from each color." Attacking tapped Pristine Angel, so it had no protection at all when Cephalid Snitch was sacrificed. Cephalid Snitch's ability reads "Target creature loses protection from black until end of turn" — that's a continuous effect lasting for the rest of the turn, and it keeps applying even after Pristine Angel becomes untapped again. So when Atlas casts a spell and uses Pristine Angel's "Whenever you cast a spell, you may untap this creature" trigger, Pristine Angel regains protection from artifacts and from white, blue, red, and green, but not from black for the remainder of that turn.

Protection here means the creature can't be blocked by, targeted by, dealt damage by, enchanted or equipped by anything of that quality. Since Mob is a black instant, and Pristine Angel's protection from black is switched off until end of turn, Mob can legally target Pristine Angel and destroy it (Pristine Angel is a 4/4 with no other protective ability).

Timing caveat: if instead the untap happened on a later turn (i.e., "after combat" meant after that turn ended), Cephalid Snitch's until-end-of-turn effect would have expired, and an untapped Pristine Angel would once again have protection from black — Mob could not target it then. Also note that if Nico casts Mob using convoke and taps creatures, that has no bearing on Pristine Angel's protection.

This analysis rests entirely on the printed card text of Pristine Angel, Cephalid Snitch, and Mob; nothing in the general rules provided contradicts it. Nothing about this changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer table.

question: Ashley controls a [Gaea's Liege] and 1 [Bayou]. Naomi controls a [Reverence] and 3 Bayous. Can Ashley attack with the Gaea's Liege?
answer:
Yes — Ashley can declare Gaea's Liege as an attacker against Naomi.

Why: Reverence says "Creatures with power 2 or less can't attack you," which is an attack restriction checked during the declare attackers step (rule 508.1c). The active player first chooses which creatures will attack and whom they attack (rules 508.1a, 802.3a), and only then are restrictions checked. By that point Gaea's Liege is an attacking creature, so its own text — "As long as Gaea's Liege is attacking, its power and toughness are each equal to the number of Forests defending player controls" — applies. Naomi's 3 Bayous are Forests (Bayou is a Land — Swamp Forest), so Gaea's Liege is 3/3 as an attacker. Power 3 is not "2 or less," so Reverence doesn't stop it. Note that Gaea's Liege's own printed ability is what changes its power here, overriding the 1/1 it would be from Ashley's single Bayou while not attacking.

Gaea's Liege must still be untapped and either have haste or have been controlled by Ashley continuously since the turn began (rule 508.1a).

If instead Naomi controlled two or fewer Forests, Gaea's Liege would be power 2 or less while attacking and Reverence would make the declaration illegal, and the game would rewind to before the declaration (rules 508.1c).

Multiplayer: with more than two players, Ashley chooses a defending player per attacking creature and may only attack opponents in range (rules 801.3, 802.3a); Reverence only restricts attacks on Naomi, and Gaea's Liege's power would be set by whichever defending player it's attacking. If Ashley attacked a different opponent with few or no Forests, Gaea's Liege could be very small — but Reverence wouldn't apply to that attack at all.

question: Arjun's [Morality Shift] resolves, in what order do they put cards in their graveyard?
answer:
Arjun arranges them in any order he likes. When Morality Shift resolves, Arjun's library and graveyard swap: the cards that were in his library all become his graveyard at the same time, and because an effect is putting two or more cards into the same graveyard simultaneously, the owner of those cards (Arjun) may arrange them in any order he chooses (rule 404.3). That new graveyard is kept as a single face-up pile that normally can't be reordered afterward (rule 404.2), so the order chosen on resolution is the order it stays in.

The other half of the exchange doesn't matter for ordering: the cards that were in Arjun's graveyard become his library, and Morality Shift's own text then tells him to shuffle that library, randomizing it regardless of any arrangement.

Nothing here depends on the number of players — Arjun makes this choice himself for his own cards, so the answer is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

question: Ares controls [Gaea's Cradle] and no creatures. Nico controls a [Contamination]. If Ares taps the Gaea's Cradle, what mana is produced, if any?
answer:
Ares produces one black mana, {B}.

Why: "To tap a permanent for mana" is defined as activating a mana ability of that permanent that includes {T} in its activation cost — it does not require that the ability actually be capable of producing mana on its own [106.12b]. Gaea's Cradle's ability, "{T}: Add {G} for each creature you control," is still a mana ability even with zero creatures [605.2], and on its own it would produce nothing (zero green mana). Contamination is a replacement effect that reads "If a land is tapped for mana, it produces {B} instead of any other type and amount." Because Ares activated Gaea's Cradle's {T} mana ability, Gaea's Cradle was tapped for mana, and Contamination replaces both the type and the amount — including an amount of zero — so what Gaea's Cradle actually produces is {B}. Contamination's printed text explicitly overrides the amount Gaea's Cradle would otherwise make, so the "{G} for each creature" count is irrelevant.

Note that the mana is added to Ares's mana pool, not Nico's: Contamination only changes what the land produces, not who gets it. Note also that {B} is one black mana specifically, not generic mana, so Ares can spend it only where black or generic costs allow.

Alternate reading, stated plainly: rule 106.12b says the replacement "modifies the mana production event while such an ability is resolving and producing mana," and one could read that as requiring some mana to exist to be replaced, in which case Gaea's Cradle would produce nothing at all under rule 106.5 (an undefined/zero amount yields no mana). I'm going with the reading that Contamination's "instead of any other type and amount" covers an amount of zero, since the card's own text governs.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — Contamination affects any land tapped for mana by any player, so it works the same at a two-player table or a multiplayer one.

question: Audrey casts [Enlarge] targeting [Goblin Piker], and then attacks with the Goblin Piker. Nico blocks it with a [Baron Sengir], which has gained infect due to their [Grafted Exoskeleton] and indestructible due to their [Withstand Death]. What happens at the end of the turn?
answer:
At end of turn, Goblin Piker dies; Baron Sengir survives and gets a +2/+2 counter.

Setup: Enlarge makes Goblin Piker 9/8 with trample until end of turn. Baron Sengir is 7/7 (5/5 plus Grafted Exoskeleton's +2/+2) with infect and indestructible.

Combat damage: Goblin Piker deals 9 damage to Baron Sengir (assigning lethal to Baron Sengir and any excess trampling over to Nico, if Audrey chooses that assignment). Because Baron Sengir has infect from Grafted Exoskeleton, its 7 damage isn't marked on Goblin Piker — instead Audrey... rather, Nico puts seven -1/-1 counters on Goblin Piker (702.90c, 120.4c). Goblin Piker is then 2/1 and survives combat. Baron Sengir has damage marked on it but is indestructible from Withstand Death, so it isn't destroyed.

Cleanup step: all damage marked on permanents is removed and all "until end of turn" effects end simultaneously (514.2, 500.5a). Enlarge's +7/+7 ends, but the seven -1/-1 counters stay — counters aren't a duration effect. Both are applied in layer 7 (613.1g), so Goblin Piker is now 2/1 minus seven = -5/-6. As a state-based action, a creature with toughness 0 or less is put into its owner's graveyard, and regeneration can't save it (704.5f) — indestructible wouldn't have helped either, since 0-or-less toughness still kills.

Baron Sengir's triggered ability then triggers, because a creature Baron Sengir dealt damage to this turn died: Nico puts a +2/+2 counter on Baron Sengir. Since a triggered ability triggered during the cleanup step, players get priority and another cleanup step follows. Baron Sengir itself is fine — its marked damage was removed, and it ends the turn as a 9/9 (5/5, +2/+2 from Grafted Exoskeleton, +2/+2 from the counter).

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Withstand Death and Grafted Exoskeleton were already applied before combat damage, as stated. If Grafted Exoskeleton had been attached only after combat damage, Baron Sengir's damage would have been ordinary marked damage instead of -1/-1 counters, and Goblin Piker would simply shrink back to 2/1 and survive the turn.

This works the same whether the game has two players or more; the only multiplayer wrinkle in the provided rules is that trample damage goes to the defending player Goblin Piker was attacking.

question: Aubrey controls a [Necromancy] that was cast during their declare blockers step. During Aubrey's end step, Nikolai activates [Duskmantle Guildmage]'s first ability. Does Aubrey lose 1 life when the Necromancy is sacrificed?
answer:
Yes — Aubrey loses 1 life when Necromancy is put into their graveyard, and likely a second life if the reanimated creature card is also owned by Aubrey.

Why: Necromancy's own text says that because it was cast when a sorcery couldn't be cast (during the declare blockers step), "the controller of the permanent it becomes sacrifices it at the beginning of the next cleanup step." Sacrificing means Aubrey moves Necromancy from the battlefield directly to its owner's graveyard [701.21a] [Sacrifice]. That is a card being put into an opponent's graveyard from the standpoint of Nikolai, so Duskmantle Guildmage's first ability — which watches for cards put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere "this turn" — sees it and Aubrey loses 1 life. The cleanup step is still part of the same turn, and Duskmantle Guildmage's effect is not one that expires at the end of the end step [500.5], so it is still active in cleanup.

Second hit: Necromancy also reads "When this enchantment leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it." That leaves-the-battlefield trigger looks back in time and will trigger [603.10a]. When the reanimated creature is sacrificed it goes to its owner's graveyard and dies [Dies] [701.21a]. If that creature card is owned by Aubrey, Duskmantle Guildmage's effect triggers again and Aubrey loses another 1 life; if the creature card is owned by Nikolai or a third player, Duskmantle Guildmage's ability only cares about cards going to an opponent's graveyard, so it triggers for that owner instead (and not at all if that owner is Nikolai himself, since Nikolai is not his own opponent).

Assumed timing: I'm assuming Nikolai activated Duskmantle Guildmage's first ability and let it resolve during Aubrey's end step, before the cleanup step. If it somehow never resolved before the sacrifice, the delayed watcher wouldn't be in place and no life would be lost.

Multiplayer note: the provided rules are not two-player-specific here; Duskmantle Guildmage's ability applies to any of Nikolai's opponents, so at a bigger table the life loss follows whoever owns each card going to a graveyard, as long as that owner is an opponent of Nikolai.

question: Angelina controls [Ice Cauldron]. Noel controls [Suppression Field]. Angelina activates Ice Cauldron's first ability with X=1, paying {C}{C}{C}. On Angelina's next turn, they activate Ice Cauldron's second ability. How much mana do they add?
answer:
Angelina adds {C}{C}{C} — three colorless mana — and that mana can be spent only to cast the card exiled with Ice Cauldron.

Why: Ice Cauldron's first ability is an activated ability that is not a mana ability, so Suppression Field's "Activated abilities cost {2} more to activate unless they're mana abilities" applies. With X=1, the mana component became {1} plus {2} more, i.e. {3} generic in total. Angelina paid that {3} generic with three colorless mana ({C}{C}{C}) — generic costs can be paid with colorless mana. Ice Cauldron's own text tells you to "note the type and amount of mana spent to pay this activation cost," so what's noted is the mana actually spent, three colorless mana, not the {1} the printed {X} alone would have been; paying an increased cost still counts as paying the cost (118.7c/118.7d framing on cost modification, and rule 118.4 for {X} costs).

Ice Cauldron's second ability ({T}, remove a charge counter: add the last noted type and amount of mana) is a mana ability, so Suppression Field does not tax it, and it simply reproduces the noted mana: {C}{C}{C}. The restriction "Spend this mana only to cast the last card exiled with this artifact" limits how the mana can be used but does not change its type (106.6).

This works the same whether the game is two-player or multiplayer; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

An ability’s activation cost must be paid by the player who is activating it. The activation cost of an ability that reads “{2}, {T}: You gain 1 life” is two mana of any type plus tapping the permanent that has the ability.
gold_text.602.2b: To activate an ability is to put it onto the stack and pay its costs, so that it will eventually resolve and have its effect. Only an object’s controller (or its owner, if it doesn’t have a controller) can activate its activated ability unless the object specifically says otherwise. Activating an ability follows the steps listed below, in order. If, at any point during the activation of an ability, a player is unable to comply with any of those steps, the activation is illegal; the game returns to the moment before that ability started to be activated (see rule 733, “Handling Illegal Actions”). Announcements and payments can’t be altered after they’ve been made. The remainder of the process for activating an ability is identical to the process for casting a spell listed in rules 601.2b–i. Those rules apply to activating an ability just as they apply to casting a spell. An activated ability’s analog to a spell’s mana cost (as referenced in rule 601.2f) is its activation cost.

question: Ariel activates [Warped Landscape]. Before that resolves Noe casts [Aven Mindcensor]. When Ariel is resolving Warped Landscape's ability, they find [Panglacial Wurm] in the top four cards of their library. Can they cast it?
answer:
Yes — Ariel can cast Panglacial Wurm, because it is among the four cards Ariel is actually searching.

Why: Aven Mindcensor doesn't stop the search; it replaces "search your library" with "search the top four cards of that library." Under rule 701.23f, when searching a zone is replaced with searching a portion of that zone, all other instructions that refer to searching the zone still apply. Ariel is still searching their library, just a restricted portion of it, so Panglacial Wurm's ability ("While you're searching your library, you may cast this card from your library") is live during that search. Since Panglacial Wurm is one of the top four cards Ariel is looking at, Ariel may cast it from the library right then, paying {5}{G}{G} (five generic plus two green). Nothing in rule 601.3 prohibits it.

Timeline assumption: I'm assuming Aven Mindcensor (which has flash) resolved before Warped Landscape's activated ability began resolving, as stated. If Aven Mindcensor had instead entered the battlefield after the search was already underway, it wouldn't retroactively shrink a search in progress — but either way Panglacial Wurm would be castable, and if Aven Mindcensor had restricted the search to a top four that did *not* contain Panglacial Wurm, Ariel could not cast it, since Ariel would never see it.

Other notes: casting Panglacial Wurm happens during the resolution of Warped Landscape's ability; the search then continues and finishes, and per 701.23f Ariel still shuffles their entire library, not just the four cards. If a basic land was among those four, Ariel may still put it onto the battlefield tapped.

Two players vs. multiplayer: this works the same. Aven Mindcensor's replacement applies to every opponent of Noe, so at a multiplayer table any opponent of Noe searching a library is limited to the top four cards, and each such player could likewise cast a Panglacial Wurm found there.

question: Addison has cast a sideboard card from [Glittering Wish], which is now in their graveyard. Addison then restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]. What happens?
answer:
The multicolored card Addison brought in from outside the game with Glittering Wish becomes part of Addison's library in the new game — it does not go back to the sideboard.

Why: once a card is brought into the game from outside the game, it's involved in that game. Rule 727.2 says all Magic cards involved in the game that was restarted are involved in the new game, even if they weren't originally involved in the restarted game, and it gives exactly this example: a player casts a wish card to bring a card in from outside the game, then the game is restarted — that card is part of that player's library when the new game begins. Ownership doesn't change regardless of where the card was when the new game starts ([727.2]), so wherever the wished-for card sat (battlefield, graveyard, stack, hand), it's shuffled into Addison's starting deck.

Glittering Wish itself is exiled by its own text, but that doesn't matter here — the question notes it's in the graveyard, and in either case every Magic card involved in the ended game is involved in the new one ([727.2]). The only exception is cards an effect specifically exempts from the restart procedure; those are not in their owner's deck as the new game begins ([727.5]). That's relevant for Karn Liberated: its −14 leaves in exile all non-Aura permanent cards exiled with Karn Liberated and then puts them onto the battlefield under Addison's control, so only those cards skip the deck. A wished-for card that wasn't exiled with Karn Liberated gets no such exemption.

Timing: the restart effect from Karn Liberated finishes resolving just before the first turn's untap step, and that's when Karn Liberated's additional instruction (putting the exiled permanent cards onto the battlefield) is carried out; no player has priority then, and any resulting triggered abilities wait until a player next receives priority, usually in the first upkeep ([727.4]).

All players still in the game when Karn Liberated restarts it begin the new game together ([104.6], [727.1]), so this works the same whether the table has two players or more; the only difference in a multiplayer game is that every remaining player is in the new game, and a new starting player is determined per the normal starting-the-game procedure.

question: Alvin controls [Mycosynth Lattice], a [Dance of the Dead] attached to a [Streetbreaker Wurm] that it returned to the battlefield, and a [Mizzium Transreliquat] that is currently a copy of [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces] due to its second ability. Alvin casts [Eureka], choosing to put [March of the Machines] onto the battlefield, then putting [Copy Artifact] onto the battlefield, which copies the Mizzium Transreliquat and then copies the Dance of the Dead with its new copy ability. (The one from Sakashima of a Thousand Faces.) They choose for it to enchant a [Viashino Warrior] in their graveyard. As Eureka continues resolving, they put [Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked] onto the battlefield and sacrifice March of the Machines. After Copy Artifact's trigger resolves and returns the Viashino Warrior to the battlefield, Alvin activates the ability of the Copy Artifact to turn it into a copy of Streetbreaker Wurm. What happens?
answer:
Direct answer: the Copy Artifact stops being a Dance of the Dead and becomes a 6/4 permanent with Streetbreaker Wurm's copiable values plus the {1}{U}{R} "becomes a copy" ability, and the Viashino Warrior is *not* sacrificed. It simply stays on the battlefield, still tapped, with no +1/+1 bonus and no untap restriction.

Step by step:

1. Because Mycosynth Lattice makes all permanents artifacts in addition to their other types, both Dance of the Dead and Streetbreaker Wurm are legal targets for the artifact-targeting copy ability, and Mycosynth Lattice also lets Alvin pay the {1}{U}{R} (one generic, one blue, one red) with mana of any color.

2. When the Copy Artifact entered as a copy of the Mizzium Transreliquat, it picked up the Transreliquat's current copiable values (Sakashima of a Thousand Faces' values, plus the {1}{U}{R} ability the Transreliquat's own exception granted it), because a copy exception's granted ability becomes part of the copiable values [707.9a], and Copy Artifact's own exception made it an enchantment in addition to its other types [707.9b].

3. When the Copy Artifact then became a copy of Dance of the Dead "except it has this ability," that change happened while it was already on the battlefield. Rule [707.4] is explicit that this kind of change does **not** cause enters-the-battlefield or leaves-the-battlefield abilities to trigger, so Dance of the Dead's "When this Aura enters..." ability should not have triggered at all, and the Copy Artifact never legitimately gained "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura" or put the Viashino Warrior onto the battlefield. I'm answering the rest as the question frames it (assuming the Viashino Warrior did get returned and the Copy Artifact was attached to it), but flag that this premise is itself contrary to [707.4].

4. Activating the ability again to copy Streetbreaker Wurm replaces the Copy Artifact's copiable values wholesale with Streetbreaker Wurm's — name Streetbreaker Wurm, Creature — Wurm, 6/4 — plus the {1}{U}{R} ability from the exception [707.3] [707.9a]. Type-changing and color effects aren't copied [707.2], but Mycosynth Lattice applies to it anew, so it is a colorless artifact creature. It is no longer an Aura and no longer has Dance of the Dead's text, so it ceases to be attached to the Viashino Warrior.

5. Critically, the Copy Artifact never leaves the battlefield — it only changes what it copies [707.4] — and it no longer has "When this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it." That ability therefore never triggers, and the Viashino Warrior survives.

6. The Viashino Warrior loses the +1/+1 and the "doesn't untap during its controller's untap step" clauses (those were continuous effects from the Aura's now-gone text, applied in layers 7c and elsewhere [613.6]), so it's a plain 4/2. It stays tapped, since a permanent keeps its status until something changes it [110.5c] — but it will now untap normally in Alvin's next untap step.

7. March of the Machines being sacrificed matters only in that nothing is setting noncreature artifacts' power and toughness anymore; Mycosynth Lattice alone doesn't make anything a creature. The upkeep "pay {1}{B} to untap" ability is also gone with the Dance of the Dead text.

Note on names: effects that referred to the permanent by name would still track it through the copy changes [707.11], but here nothing is left pointing at it.

This answer is the same whether the game has two players or more; Eureka's "each player" loop had already finished before any of this.

Then all applicable continuous effects are applied in a series of layers in the following order:

Each permanent always has one of these values for each of these categories. A permanent retains its status until a spell, ability, or turn-based action changes it, even if that status is not relevant to it. This creature becomes a copy of that card, except it has this ability.” It becomes a copy of Jushi Apprentice, a flip card. question: Aspen controls a [Blood Tyrant] that they took control of from Briella using [Malevolent Whispers]. Aspen has 1 life. Cason casts [Volt Charge] targeting Aspen. After it resolves and Aspen loses the game, will Blood Tyrant get the +1/+1 counters?
answer:
Short answer: no — Blood Tyrant won't end up with the five +1/+1 counters in any practical sense.

Why:

1. The trigger does technically trigger. Blood Tyrant's "Whenever a player loses the game, put five +1/+1 counters on this creature" is one of the abilities that "looks back in time" [603.10f], and such abilities trigger whenever a player loses or leaves the game for any reason other than a draw [603.9]. Aspen at 1 life taking 3 damage from Volt Charge means Aspen has 0 or less life and loses the game as a state-based action [119.6].

2. But the controller of that triggered ability is Aspen, who is gone. In a multiplayer game, as soon as Aspen leaves, all objects Aspen owns leave the game, all control-changing effects giving Aspen control end (so Malevolent Whispers' effect ends and Blood Tyrant reverts to Briella's control), and any objects on the stack not represented by cards that Aspen controlled cease to exist [800.4a]. Blood Tyrant's triggered ability is exactly such an object — a stack object that isn't a card, controlled by Aspen at the moment it triggered — so it ceases to exist and never resolves. No counters are placed. (Blood Tyrant itself is safe: it's Briella's card, so it isn't exiled or removed; it just goes back to Briella untapped/attacking status aside, without the +2/+0 and haste from Malevolent Whispers, which also end.)

3. Two-player case: if Aspen and Cason were the only players, Aspen losing simply ends the game immediately — there's no one left to resolve Blood Tyrant's trigger, so again it contributes nothing.

Timing note: I'm assuming Volt Charge fully resolved (3 damage dealt, and its proliferate performed) before state-based actions were checked, which is the normal sequence — damage is processed into life loss as part of resolution [120.4c], and only afterward do state-based actions see Aspen at 0 or less life [119.6]. If instead you imagine Blood Tyrant somehow being back under Briella's control before the loss occurred, the trigger would be Briella's and she would get the five counters; but that isn't what happens here, since Aspen's loss and Aspen's departure are the same event.

However, some triggered abilities are exceptions to this rule; the game “looks back in time” to determine if those abilities trigger, using the existence of those abilities and the appearance of objects immediately prior to the event. The list of exceptions is as follows:
gold_text.603.10f: Normally, objects that exist immediately after an event are checked to see if the event matched any trigger conditions, and continuous effects that exist at that time are used to determine what the trigger conditions are and what the objects involved in the event look like. However, some triggered abilities are exceptions to this rule; the game “looks back in time” to determine if those abilities trigger, using the existence of those abilities and the appearance of objects immediately prior to the event. The list of exceptions is as follows: Abilities that trigger when a player loses the game look back in time.
gold_text.800.4a: Unlike two-player games, multiplayer games can continue after one or more players have left the game. When a player leaves the game, all objects (see rule 109) owned by that player leave the game and any effects which give that player control of any objects or players end. Then, if that player controlled any objects on the stack not represented by cards, those objects cease to exist. Then, if there are any objects still controlled by that player, those objects are exiled. This is not a state-based action. It happens as soon as the player leaves the game. If the player who left the game had priority at the time they left, priority passes to the next player in turn order who’s still in the game. question: Aspen, Brycen, and Collins begin a multiplayer game. In Aspen's upkeep, they use [Leyline of Anticipation], several [Simian Spirit Guide]s and [Desperate Ritual]s, and [Goblin Charbelcher] to kill Brycen. Does Aspen draw a card for the turn?
answer:
Yes. Aspen draws a card in their draw step.

Two points make this clear:

1. In multiplayer games, no player skips the draw step of their first turn — including the starting player [103.8c]. This differs from a two-player game, where the starting player skips that first draw.

2. Killing Brycen with Goblin Charbelcher during Aspen's upkeep doesn't interrupt Aspen's turn. Brycen loses the game and leaves the game [104.5], and a multiplayer game simply continues with the remaining players; the only turn-related consequence is that a turn that would begin for a player who has left the game doesn't begin [800.4k]. Aspen is still in the game, so Aspen's turn proceeds normally into the draw step.

When the draw step begins, the active player (Aspen) draws a card as a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack [703.4d, 504.1]. Leyline of Anticipation (letting Aspen cast the spells at upkeep as though they had flash), Simian Spirit Guide, and Desperate Ritual only affect how Aspen generated mana and cast during the upkeep; none of them alter the draw step.

Timing note: I'm assuming all of this happens during Aspen's upkeep step, as stated, so the draw step hasn't happened yet. If instead the Goblin Charbelcher activation had somehow been resolved after Aspen's draw step, Aspen would already have drawn — either way Aspen gets the draw.

In a two-player game this answer would be different: the starting player skips the draw step of their first turn, and killing the only opponent would end the game immediately with that player winning [104.2a].

question: Addison, Brixton, and Collins started playing a multiplayer game. Collins lost the game, and then Addison restarted the game with [Karn Liberated]. Will Addison draw a card on the first turn of the restarted game?
answer:
No — Addison skips the draw step of the first turn of the restarted game, so Addison does not draw.

Why: Karn Liberated's −14 restarts the game. When a game is restarted, it immediately ends and only the players still in the game at that moment begin the new game [104.6], [727.1]. Collins had already lost and left, so only Addison and Brixton begin the new game. Addison is the starting player, because the starting player in the new game is the player who controlled the ability that restarted the game [727.1a].

The new game is played by two players, and in a two-player game the player who plays first skips the draw step of their first turn [103.8a]. The multiplayer exception — that the starting player does not skip their first draw step [103.8c], [800.7] — applies to games with more than two players, which the restarted game no longer is (a multiplayer game can continue after players leave [800.4k]). So Addison, as starting player in what is now a two-player game, skips the draw step; Brixton draws normally on their own turn [504.1], [703.4d].

If instead a third player were still in the game at the moment of the restart, that player would be in the new game too, it would still be a multiplayer game, and Addison would not skip the draw step [103.8c], [800.7].

Two other things to watch on the first turn: all cards from the ended game are in the new game under their same owners [727.2], and any player who ends up with fewer than seven cards in their library loses when state-based actions are checked during the first turn's upkeep [727.3]. Also, Karn Liberated's own instruction — leaving in exile the non-Aura permanent cards exiled with it and then putting them onto the battlefield under Addison's control — is carried out just before the first turn's untap step as the effect finishes resolving [727.4], [727.5].
