question: Aniyah casts [Martyrdom], targeting their [Douser of Lights]. After it resolves, Nico takes control of Douser of Lights with [Act of Aggression]. Can Nico activate the ability it gained from Martyrdom?
answer:
No. Nico can't activate the ability that Martyrdom granted to Douser of Lights; only Aniyah can.

Martyrdom's granted ability comes with the activation instruction "Only you may activate this ability," where "you" is Martyrdom's controller, Aniyah. Under rule [113.10a], when an effect adds an activated ability it may include activation instructions, and those instructions become part of the ability that's added to the object — so the "only Aniyah may activate this" restriction is baked into the ability Douser of Lights now has.

Rule [602.5b] then confirms this survives the change of control: a player can't begin to activate an ability that's prohibited from being activated, and if an activated ability has a restriction on its use, that restriction continues to apply to that object even if its controller changes. Act of Aggression gives Nico control of Douser of Lights (untapped, with haste) until end of turn, but it does nothing to strip or rewrite the granted ability's restriction, and per [101.2a] a "can't" effect takes precedence over an effect that would otherwise allow the action.

So while Nico controls Douser of Lights, Aniyah remains the only player who may activate the {0} damage-redirection ability, and she may do so at any time she has priority ([117.1b]) even though she no longer controls the creature. Note the ability targets separately: the redirection sends the next 1 damage to Douser of Lights, which is now Nico's creature for the turn.

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players: in a multiplayer game the same restriction applies, and no third player could activate it either. One additional multiplayer-only caveat from [801.6]: a player can't activate abilities of an object outside their range of influence, so in formats with a limited range of influence Aniyah would also need Douser of Lights to be within her range.

question: Ashley has restarted the game with a [Karn Liberated] that exiled an [Ajani's Chosen]. Ashley chooses to begin the restarted game with a [Leyline of Anticipation] on the battlefield. Does Ajani's Chosen trigger?
answer:
No — Ajani's Chosen does not trigger.

Why: Karn Liberated's −14 restarts the game and then puts the exiled non‑Aura permanent cards (here, Ajani's Chosen) onto the battlefield under Ashley's control. Those additional instructions are carried out when the restart effect finishes resolving, which is just before the first turn's untap step of the new game [727.4]. Actions taken from opening hands — including Leyline of Anticipation's "If this card is in your opening hand, you may begin the game with it on the battlefield" — happen earlier, as part of the normal starting-the-game procedure after mulligans [103.6a], [727.1].

So Leyline of Anticipation is already on the battlefield before Ajani's Chosen ever arrives. Ajani's Chosen only triggers "whenever an enchantment you control enters," and it wasn't on the battlefield at the moment Leyline of Anticipation entered, so there is nothing for it to see. Note also that no player has priority while the restart effect finishes resolving; any abilities that did trigger from Ajani's Chosen entering would go on the stack at the first player's upkeep [727.4].

This answer is the same regardless of the number of players; the restart involves all players who were in the game when it ended [727.1], and in a multiplayer game using the limited range of influence option every player is involved [727.7].

If instead you're asking whether some other enchantment entering later in the new game would trigger Ajani's Chosen — yes, once Ajani's Chosen is on the battlefield, any enchantment Ashley controls entering afterward triggers it normally.

question: Nehemiah controls a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 2 +1/+1 counters on it. Ari casts [Bishop of Binding], exiling the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave. When Ari attacks with Bishop of Binding on their next turn, what will X equal in Bishop of Binding's triggered ability?
answer:
X will equal 3.

Skullbriar, the Walking Grave is printed as a 1/1, and it had two +1/+1 counters on it. Normally counters cease to exist when a permanent changes zones, but Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's own text says "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." Exile is neither a hand nor a library, so this card text overrides the general rule and the two +1/+1 counters stay on the exiled card.

A +1/+1 counter on a creature card in a zone other than the battlefield still adds to that object's power and toughness (rule 122.1a). So the exiled Skullbriar, the Walking Grave card is a 3/3 in exile, and Bishop of Binding's attack trigger — "target Vampire gets +X/+X until end of turn, where X is the power of the exiled card" — sees power 3.

Timing note: X is determined as the ability resolves, using the exiled card's power at that time. If something changed the counters on the exiled Skullbriar, the Walking Grave card before resolution, X would change to match. Also note that if Bishop of Binding leaves the battlefield first, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave returns and there is no exiled card to reference.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; Bishop of Binding's exile ability targets a creature an opponent controls, and at a multiplayer table Ari simply chooses which opponent's creature to exile.

question: Neriah controls a [Containment Priest] and has a [Knotvine Mystic] in their graveyard. Alan casts [Ghastly Conscription], targeting Neriah. What happens to the Knotvine Mystic?

Knotvine Mystic never actually enters the battlefield — Containment Priest exiles it instead.

Step by step: Ghastly Conscription exiles all creature cards from Neriah's graveyard face down, shuffles that pile, and then manifests those cards, meaning it tries to put Knotvine Mystic onto the battlefield face down as a 2/2 creature. Being manifested is not being cast, and Knotvine Mystic is a nontoken card, so Containment Priest's replacement ability ("If a nontoken creature would enter and it wasn't cast, exile it instead") applies. Containment Priest's printed text overrides the normal result of the manifest instruction, so Knotvine Mystic goes to exile rather than to the battlefield. Because it never entered the battlefield, it is not a face-down 2/2 permanent Neriah could later turn face up for {R}{G}{W}; it simply sits in exile.

This happens to every creature card Ghastly Conscription would manifest from Neriah's graveyard, not just Knotvine Mystic. Note that Ghastly Conscription's own exile of the graveyard cards into a face-down pile happens normally — Containment Priest only interacts with the manifest (entering the battlefield) part.

The number of players doesn't change this: Containment Priest's ability cares about any nontoken creature entering, regardless of controller or player count, so the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Niko has a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] in their graveyard with 2 +1/+1 counters on it. Ashley controls [Containment Priest], and casts [Ghastly Conscription], targeting Niko. What happens?
answer:
Skullbriar, the Walking Grave never makes it onto the battlefield — Containment Priest exiles it instead — and it keeps its two +1/+1 counters the whole time, ending up in exile.

Step by step:

1. Ghastly Conscription resolves and exiles all creature cards from Niko's graveyard in a face-down pile (including Skullbriar, the Walking Grave), shuffles that pile, then manifests those cards. Because Skullbriar, the Walking Grave says "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library," the two +1/+1 counters stay on it as it moves from the graveyard to exile — this card text overrides the general rule that counters cease to exist when a permanent/card changes zones.

2. Manifesting means putting a card onto the battlefield face down as a 2/2 creature. That is not casting it. Containment Priest reads "If a nontoken creature would enter and it wasn't cast, exile it instead," so as each manifested card would enter the battlefield, it is exiled instead. Skullbriar, the Walking Grave (and every other card Ghastly Conscription tried to manifest) is exiled rather than entering as a face-down 2/2.

3. Since exile is not a hand or a library, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's own replacement wording again preserves its counters: it sits in exile with two +1/+1 counters on it. Those counters would only vanish if it later went to a hand or library. If it ever returns to the battlefield later, it comes back as a 3/3 (1/1 plus two +1/+1 counters).

Note on Ghastly Conscription's controller: Ashley cast it targeting Niko's graveyard, so Ashley would have been the one to control the manifested permanents — which is why Ashley's own Containment Priest eats them. Ashley gets nothing out of the spell.

Multiplayer: this works identically with two players or more, since Ghastly Conscription targets one specific player's graveyard and Containment Priest applies to any nontoken creature that would enter, regardless of who controls it. The only difference at a bigger table is that any other Containment Priest or similar effect would also apply.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Containment Priest was already on the battlefield when Ghastly Conscription resolved. If Containment Priest instead entered (via its flash) only after the manifest had already happened, the face-down permanents would already be on the battlefield and would stay there — Containment Priest only replaces creatures that are in the act of entering.

question: Avery controls [Magnetic Web] and is attacking with two [Leatherback Baloth]s with magnet counters on them. Nayeli controls one [Imperial Moth] that also has a magnet counter on it. What are Nayeli's legal blocks?
answer:
Nayeli must block with Imperial Moth, and Imperial Moth must block one of the two Leatherback Baloths — Nayeli chooses which one. Declining to block at all is an illegal declaration.

Why: Magnetic Web's second ability reads "Whenever a creature with a magnet counter on it attacks, all creatures with magnet counters on them block that creature this turn if able." Each attacking Leatherback Baloth with a magnet counter triggers it separately, so two separate blocking requirements are created for Imperial Moth (which has a magnet counter): block Leatherback Baloth #1 if able, and block Leatherback Baloth #2 if able.

A single creature can be assigned to block only one attacking creature in the declaration (rule 509.1a lets the defending player choose one attacking creature for each blocker, absent an ability letting it block additional creatures). So Imperial Moth physically cannot satisfy both requirements. Rule 509.1c says the declaration is illegal if the number of requirements obeyed is fewer than the maximum possible number that could be obeyed without disobeying a restriction. The maximum here is one — so Imperial Moth must block exactly one of the two Leatherback Baloths, and either choice is equally legal. Blocking neither obeys zero requirements and is illegal.

Caveats: this assumes Imperial Moth is untapped (rule 509.1a — chosen blockers must be untapped) and that nothing restricts it from blocking. If Imperial Moth is tapped or otherwise unable to block, it's not "able" and no requirement is broken. Imperial Moth having flying doesn't restrict what it can block; flying only limits what can block a flier (rule 509.1b covers evasion as a restriction on blockers, and Leatherback Baloth has no evasion here).

Multiplayer: the answer is the same whether this is a two-player game or a larger table. Nayeli may only block with creatures she controls, and only creatures attacking her, her planeswalkers, or a battle she protects (rules 802.4a and 802.4b); if other players are also being attacked, each defending player declares blockers in APNAP order and Nayeli's blocks are judged ignoring creatures attacking other players and other players' blockers. Magnetic Web's requirement still only compels Imperial Moth with respect to attackers Nayeli is legally allowed to block.

question: Arden controls [Naga Vitalist] and a [Deathrite Shaman] that's currently a land due to [Xenograft] (naming "Saproling") and [Life and Limb]. Neither player has any land cards in their graveyards. If Arden taps Naga Vitalist, what type(s) of mana can it produce?
answer:
Naga Vitalist can produce only {G}.

Why: Xenograft (naming Saproling) makes each creature Arden controls a Saproling in addition to its other types, so Deathrite Shaman — and Naga Vitalist itself — are Saprolings. Life and Limb then makes all Saprolings 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types. Any land with the Forest subtype has the intrinsic ability "{T}: Add {G}" [305.6], [Forest], so Deathrite Shaman is a land Arden controls that could produce {G}.

Naga Vitalist's ability adds "one mana of any type that a land you control could produce." Under [106.7], the types a permanent "could produce" are the types its abilities would produce if they resolved now, taking replacement effects into account and ignoring whether the ability's costs could be paid. Deathrite Shaman's first ability ("{T}: Exile target land card from a graveyard. Add one mana of any color.") requires a target land card in a graveyard, and there are none — that's a targeting requirement, not a cost, so [106.7]'s "ignore costs" clause doesn't rescue it. That ability can't be activated or resolve to produce mana now, so it contributes no mana types. (It's still a mana ability regardless, per [605.2] — it just can't define a type here.)

That leaves the Forest ability as the only defined mana type, so Naga Vitalist produces {G} and nothing else. Note Naga Vitalist is itself also a Forest land via Xenograft plus Life and Limb, which independently gives the same {G} answer.

Multiplayer note: nothing here depends on opponents' permanents (unlike Exotic Orchard in [106.7]), so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a larger table — assuming no other lands Arden controls that could produce other types.

question: Ashley controls [Skill Borrower] and [Sensei's Divining Top]. The top card of their library is a [Putrid Leech]. Ashley activates Skill Borrower's ability, then activates Sensei's Divining Top's first ability, choosing to put Putrid Leech second from the top. Then they activate Sensei's Divining Top again, putting Putrid Leech back on top. Can Ashley activate Skill Borrower's ability again?
answer:
Yes — Ashley can activate the pumped-up ability a second time.

Why: Skill Borrower has no activated ability printed on it; it grants itself "all activated abilities" of the top card of Ashley's library while that card is an artifact or creature card. Here that card is Putrid Leech, so Skill Borrower has "Pay 2 life: This creature gets +2/+2 until end of turn. Activate only once each turn."

The key is rule 602.5c: when an object acquires an activated ability with a restriction on its use from another object, that restriction applies only to that ability as acquired from that object — it doesn't apply to other, identically worded abilities. And rule 401.6 says that if a player is playing with the top card of their library revealed and that card stops being revealed for any length of time before being revealed again, it becomes a new object. Using Sensei's Divining Top's first ability to bury Putrid Leech second from the top, then using Sensei's Divining Top again to put Putrid Leech back on top, makes Putrid Leech a new object. Skill Borrower therefore acquires a brand-new, identically worded ability from a different object, and the "only once each turn" restriction from the earlier instance doesn't carry over. Ashley pays 2 more life and Skill Borrower gets another +2/+2 until end of turn.

Timing note: rule 401.5 means the top card can't be looked at or be revealed mid-activation — the new top card only counts once the Sensei's Divining Top activation is complete. That's satisfied in your sequence, since both Sensei's Divining Top activations fully resolve before the second Skill Borrower-granted activation.

This interaction is purely between Ashley's own permanents and library, so the answer is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

question: Adelyn controls [Panharmonicon] and [Mycosynth Lattice] and has [Dwarven Trader] and [Staunch Shieldmate] in their graveyard. They cast [Animate Dead] targeting Dwarven Trader. What happens as it enters the battlefield?
answer:
Direct answer: Animate Dead's enters-the-battlefield triggered ability triggers twice instead of once, and only the first one actually does anything — Dwarven Trader comes back to the battlefield under Adelyn's control with Animate Dead attached to it (and getting -1/-0). Staunch Shieldmate stays in the graveyard.

Why it triggers twice: Mycosynth Lattice makes all permanents artifacts in addition to their other types, so Animate Dead itself is an artifact enchantment as it enters. Panharmonicon says that if an artifact or creature entering causes a triggered ability of a permanent you control to trigger, that ability triggers an additional time. Animate Dead's own "When this Aura enters..." ability is a triggered ability of a permanent Adelyn controls, and the entering object is an artifact, so Panharmonicon gives a second instance of that trigger.

What each instance does:
- First instance to resolve: the intervening-if is satisfied (Animate Dead is on the battlefield), so it loses "enchant creature card in a graveyard," gains "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura," returns Dwarven Trader from the graveyard to the battlefield under Adelyn's control, and attaches itself to Dwarven Trader.
- Second instance: the text-changing part is redundant (it already has the new enchant ability), and the return instruction looks for the enchanted creature card in the graveyard. That card is no longer there — Dwarven Trader is on the battlefield — so under rule 603.6a that part of the ability fails to do anything. It does not return Staunch Shieldmate or any other card; the ability only ever refers to the enchanted card.

Adelyn controls both triggers, so she orders them on the stack, but since they're identical the outcome is the same either way. Note also that Dwarven Trader entering is itself an artifact/creature entering (again via Mycosynth Lattice), so any other enters-triggers of permanents Adelyn controls would likewise be doubled by Panharmonicon; here there are none.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Panharmonicon and Mycosynth Lattice were both already on the battlefield when Animate Dead entered. If Mycosynth Lattice weren't there, Animate Dead (a non-artifact, non-creature enchantment) entering would not satisfy Panharmonicon, and the trigger would happen only once — same end result of returning Dwarven Trader, just without the extra do-nothing trigger.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count, so it's the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

Continuous effects that modify characteristics of permanents do so simultaneously with the permanent entering the battlefield. They don’t wait until the permanent is on the battlefield and then change it. Because such effects apply as the permanent enters the battlefield, they are applied before determining whether the permanent will cause an ability to trigger when it enters the battlefield. A permanent with the static ability “All white creatures get +1/+1” is on the battlefield. A creature spell that would normally create a 1/1 white creature instead creates a 2/2 white creature. The creature doesn’t enter the battlefield as 1/1 and then change to 2/2.

During resolution, these abilities look for the object in the zone that it moved to. If the object is unable to be found in the zone it went to, the part of the ability attempting to do something to the object will fail to do anything. The ability could be unable to find the object because the object never entered the specified zone, because it left the zone before the ability resolved, or because it is in a zone that is hidden from a player, such as a library or an opponent’s hand. (This rule applies even if the object leaves the zone and returns again before the ability resolves.) The most common zone-change triggers are enters-the-battlefield triggers and leaves-the-battlefield triggers. Enters-the-battlefield abilities trigger when a permanent enters the battlefield. These are written, “When [this object] enters, . . . “ or “Whenever a [type] enters, . . .” Each time an event puts one or more permanents onto the battlefield, all permanents on the battlefield (including the newcomers) are checked for any enters-the-battlefield triggers that match the event.

question: Armani controls a [Gaea's Liege] and 3 [Canopy Vista]s. Nico controls a [Reverence] and 1 Canopy Vista. Can Armani attack with the Gaea's Liege?
answer:
Yes — Armani can legally declare Gaea's Liege as an attacker against Nico, and it stays in combat even though it shrinks once it's attacking.

Why: Reverence says "Creatures with power 2 or less can't attack you." That's an attack restriction, and restrictions are checked only when the active player declares attackers (rule 508.1c). At that moment Gaea's Liege is not yet attacking, so its own text — "As long as Gaea's Liege isn't attacking, its power and toughness are each equal to the number of Forests you control" — makes it 3/3, since Armani's three Canopy Vistas are Forest Plains and therefore count as Forests. Power 3 is not "2 or less," so Reverence doesn't forbid the declaration and the declaration is legal.

After Gaea's Liege is declared, its other characteristic-defining clause takes over: "As long as Gaea's Liege is attacking, its power and toughness are each equal to the number of Forests defending player controls." Nico controls one Canopy Vista (a Forest), so Gaea's Liege becomes 1/1 while attacking. That does not undo the attack — rule 508.1c only tests restrictions at the time of declaration; there is no ongoing re-check that would remove Gaea's Liege from combat, and Reverence doesn't say to remove attacking creatures. So Gaea's Liege remains an attacking 1/1 (dealing 1 damage if unblocked).

Note the reverse case: if Nico had 3+ Forests and Armani only 1–2, Gaea's Liege would be power 2 or less at declaration and Reverence would then prevent the attack on Nico.

Multiplayer: this works the same with more than two players. Reverence only protects Nico ("can't attack you"), so Gaea's Liege could also attack a different opponent, and each attacking creature's defending player is determined individually (rule 802.2a). If Gaea's Liege attacks a different opponent, its attacking power equals that player's Forest count instead. Table variants such as attack-left/attack-right (rule 803.1a) or seating restrictions (rule 811.4) could further limit whom Armani may attack.

If any restrictions are being disobeyed, the declaration of attackers is illegal. question: Ariel attacks with [Wildfire Eternal], which isn't blocked. As the trigger resolves, can they choose to suspend [Charnel Serenade]?
answer:
No. Ariel can't suspend Charnel Serenade as the Wildfire Eternal trigger resolves.

Two independent reasons:

1. Suspending is a special action, not casting. Exiling a card with suspend from your hand is one of the twelve special actions [116.2f], and suspend's first ability explicitly says "This action doesn't use the stack" [702.62a]. Special actions don't use the stack and can only be taken when the player has priority [116.2f, 405.6d]. While the Wildfire Eternal triggered ability is resolving, no player has priority, so no special action can be taken at that moment.

2. Wildfire Eternal's trigger only offers casting. Its text is "you may cast an instant or sorcery spell from your hand without paying its mana cost" — that's a permission to cast, and paying suspend's {2}{B} cost to exile the card isn't casting it at all.

What Ariel can do: use the Wildfire Eternal trigger to cast Charnel Serenade itself from hand without paying its {4}{B}{B} mana cost. Charnel Serenade's own text then surveils 3, returns a creature card from the graveyard with a finality counter, and exiles Charnel Serenade with three time counters on it — so Ariel effectively gets it suspended anyway, as part of the spell's resolution rather than as a special action.

Alternatively, Ariel could take the suspend special action on Charnel Serenade at any other time they hold priority and could begin to cast it from hand (i.e., a sorcery-speed window on their own turn with an empty stack) [116.2f, 702.62a, 702.62c]. Note that after the Wildfire Eternal trigger has fully resolved, the stack isn't empty only if other things are on it; once it is empty and Ariel has priority in the declare-blockers step, that's still not a sorcery-speed window, so suspending then isn't legal either.

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players; it's the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Brynn has 1 life and controls a phased-out [Fairgrounds Warden] that exiled Coleman's [Alpha Tyrranax]. Aspen casts [Psychic Purge], targeting Brynn. What happens as Brynn loses the game?
answer:
Alpha Tyrranax stays in exile permanently. Brynn drops to 0 life from Psychic Purge's 1 damage and loses the game (this is a state-based action, and abilities that trigger on a player losing the game "look back in time"). Because there are at least three players (Aspen, Brynn, Coleman), the game continues.

When Brynn leaves the game, all objects Brynn owns leave the game, including phased-out permanents [800.4a] [702.26k]. "Phased out" means the permanent is treated as though it doesn't exist while still remaining on the battlefield zone-wise. Crucially, rule 702.26k says a phased-out permanent leaving the game this way doesn't cause zone-change abilities to trigger, and the definition of "leaves the battlefield" only covers a permanent leaving the game because its owner left if that permanent is phased in. Fairgrounds Warden was phased out, so it never "leaves the battlefield."

Fairgrounds Warden's exile lasts "until this creature leaves the battlefield." Since that condition can now never be met, Coleman's Alpha Tyrranax remains in the exile zone for the rest of the game.

Timing note: I'm assuming Psychic Purge resolved and dealt the damage before anything phased Fairgrounds Warden back in. If Fairgrounds Warden had been phased in at the moment Brynn left the game, it would leave the game and that would count as leaving the battlefield, returning Alpha Tyrranax to the battlefield under Coleman's control.

In a two-player game the point would be moot, since the game would simply end.

question: Avery controls [Caelorna, Coral Tyrant] and [Darksteel Garrison] that's fortifying [Spire Garden]. Avery casts [Bludgeon Brawl]. After that resolves they activate Darksteel Garrison's equip ability targeting Caelorna, Coral Tyrant. What does the battlefield look like after that ability has resolved and state-based actions have been checked?
answer:
After the equip ability resolves, Darksteel Garrison is attached to Caelorna, Coral Tyrant only — it is no longer fortifying Spire Garden — and Caelorna, Coral Tyrant is a 2/8 modified creature.

Why:

- Bludgeon Brawl makes each noncreature, non-Equipment artifact an Equipment with equip {X} and "Equipped creature gets +X/+0," where X is that artifact's mana value. Darksteel Garrison is a noncreature artifact whose only subtype is Fortification, not Equipment, so Bludgeon Brawl applies to it: Darksteel Garrison gains equip {2} and "Equipped creature gets +2/+0" (its mana value is 2). It keeps its own printed abilities and its Fortification subtype as well.
- Equip attaches Darksteel Garrison to the target creature. Caelorna, Coral Tyrant is a creature, so this is a legal attachment (301.5c). Because a permanent can only be attached to one object, attaching Darksteel Garrison to Caelorna, Coral Tyrant removes it from Spire Garden; Spire Garden is no longer a fortified land.
- Consequences: Spire Garden loses indestructible (that grant only applies to "fortified land," and there is none now), and the "whenever fortified land becomes tapped" trigger can't trigger off Spire Garden anymore.
- Caelorna, Coral Tyrant gets +2/+0 from the granted Bludgeon Brawl ability (applied in layer 7c per 613.6), making it 2/8. Since it is now equipped, it counts as modified (see the Modified entry, rule 700.9).
- State-based actions find nothing to fix: Darksteel Garrison is attached to a legal object (a creature it can equip), so it stays attached (301.5c, 801.9).

Note Darksteel Garrison is still also a Fortification, so it could later be re-attached to a land with its fortify {3} ability, which would then unattach it from Caelorna, Coral Tyrant.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; the only player-count-sensitive detail here is Spire Garden's own "enters tapped unless you have two or more opponents" clause, which was already settled when Spire Garden entered the battlefield.

question: Noah controls a [Mons's Goblin Raiders] enchanted with a [Spider Umbra]. Alexandra casts [Yamabushi's Flame], targeting Mons's Goblin Raiders. What happens?
answer:
Mons's Goblin Raiders survives. Spider Umbra makes it a 2/2 with reach, so Yamabushi's Flame's 3 damage is lethal damage and Mons's Goblin Raiders would be destroyed — but Spider Umbra's umbra armor replaces that destruction: instead, all damage marked on Mons's Goblin Raiders is removed and Spider Umbra is destroyed, going to Noah's graveyard [702.89a]. Mons's Goblin Raiders remains on the battlefield as a 1/1 with no damage marked on it.

Because Mons's Goblin Raiders is never destroyed and never dies, Yamabushi's Flame's replacement clause ("If a creature dealt damage this way would die this turn, exile it instead") does nothing here — it only applies to a creature that would actually die. Umbra armor is a static ability found on some Auras meaning "If enchanted permanent would be destroyed, instead remove all damage marked on it and destroy this Aura" [702.89a]; card text like this overrides the ordinary destruction outcome. Damage results are applied as modified by replacement effects that interact with those results [120.4c], and damage is only dealt to battles, creatures, planeswalkers, and players [120.1a].

Note that Yamabushi's Flame's exile substitution lasts the rest of the turn: if Mons's Goblin Raiders (now 1/1 with Spider Umbra gone) would die later this turn from something else, it would be exiled instead. Also, if some other effect had already reduced its toughness to 0 or less, it would be put into the graveyard as a state-based action and regeneration-style effects couldn't save it [704.5f]. This interaction is between two named players and doesn't change with more players at the table.

Spider Umbra is destroyed and Mons's Goblin Raiders remains on the battlefield.

There are two replacement effects trying to apply to the same event. Umbra armor is attempting to replace the destruction of the creature, while Yamabushi's Flame's effect is attempting to replace where the creature moves to. The "move to the graveyard" event is a part of the "destroy" event, so the umbra armor replacement effect must apply first. Once that effect has been applied, the creature is no longer about to die, so there are no more effects to apply.

If the Mons's Goblin Raiders would die later in the turn, the Yamabushi's Flame's replacement effect will apply at that time and cause it to move to exile instead of the graveyard.

question: Abel attacks with [Pristine Angel]. While it's tapped, Nico activates [Cephalid Snitch]'s ability targeting Pristine Angel. After that resolves, Abel casts a spell and untaps Pristine Angel. Can Nico now target the Pristine Angel with [Murder]?
answer:
Yes. Nico can target Pristine Angel with Murder, and Murder will destroy it.

Why: Cephalid Snitch's ability says "Target creature loses protection from black until end of turn." That is a continuous effect lasting the rest of the turn; it isn't tied to Pristine Angel being tapped. Pristine Angel's own static ability reads "As long as this creature is untapped, it has protection from artifacts and from each color," so when Abel casts a spell and untaps Pristine Angel with its "Whenever you cast a spell, you may untap this creature" trigger, Pristine Angel regains protection from artifacts and from each color — except that the later-timestamped Cephalid Snitch effect continues to strip protection from black for the rest of the turn. Note also that the Cephalid Snitch ability was legally targeted and resolved while Pristine Angel was tapped and had no protection, so it applied normally (608.2b: targets are rechecked on resolution, and Pristine Angel was a legal target then).

Murder is a black instant, so with protection from black gone, Pristine Angel is a legal target and Murder's destruction isn't prevented. Untapping Pristine Angel does not remove it from combat either (506.4b: tapping or untapping a creature already declared as an attacker doesn't remove it from combat), so it remains an attacking creature until Murder kills it.

Timing assumption: I'm reading the sequence as stated — Cephalid Snitch's ability fully resolved before Abel cast the spell. If instead Abel had cast the spell and untapped Pristine Angel while Cephalid Snitch's ability was still on the stack, Pristine Angel would have protection from black at that moment, the target would be illegal, and Cephalid Snitch's ability would be removed from the stack without effect (608.2b) — then Murder could not target Pristine Angel.

This works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; nothing here depends on the number of players.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.613.7a: Within a layer or sublayer, determining which order effects are applied in is usually done using a timestamp system. An effect with an earlier timestamp is applied before an effect with a later timestamp. A continuous effect generated by a static ability has the same timestamp as the object the static ability is on, or the timestamp of the effect that created the ability, whichever is later. If the effect that created the ability has the later timestamp and the object the ability is on receives a new timestamp, each continuous effect generated by static abilities of that object receives a new timestamp as well, but the relative order of those timestamps remains the same. question: At the beginning of the game, Alex announced [Kaheera, the Orphanguard] as their companion. During the game, Alex cast [Carrion Grub] from their sideboard with [Wish]. Later, Alex restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]. What happens?
answer:
Short answer: the new game begins with Karn Liberated's non-Aura exiled permanent cards left in exile and then put onto the battlefield under Alex's control, and Carrion Grub — even though it started outside the game in Alex's sideboard — is shuffled into Alex's library for the new game.

Details:

1. Restart itself: Karn Liberated's −14 ability ends the current game immediately; no one wins, loses, or draws it, and all players who were in the game start a new game using the normal starting-the-game procedure [727.1], [104.6]. The restart effect finishes resolving just before the first turn's untap step, and Karn Liberated's additional instruction (leaving the exiled non-Aura permanent cards in exile, then putting them onto the battlefield under Alex's control) is carried out at that time. No player has priority then, so anything that triggers — for example Carrion Grub's "when this creature enters, mill four cards" if Carrion Grub happened to be one of those cards — goes on the stack the next time a player gets priority, usually in the first turn's upkeep step [727.4].

2. Carrion Grub, cast off Wish from outside the game: every Magic card involved in the ended game is involved in the new game, even cards that weren't originally part of it, and ownership doesn't change. A card brought in from outside the game this way is part of its owner's library when the new game begins [727.2]. So Carrion Grub (assuming it is not among the cards exiled with Karn Liberated) is in Alex's starting library for the new game. Cards that an effect exempts from the restart procedure — here, the non-Aura permanent cards exiled with Karn Liberated — are not in their owner's deck as the new game begins [727.5], [727.5a].

3. Kaheera, the Orphanguard: if Alex had already paid {3} to put Kaheera, the Orphanguard into hand from outside the game, it stays in the game until the game ends [702.139c], and by [727.2] it likewise becomes part of Alex's library in the new game (again unless it was exiled with Karn Liberated). If Alex never took that special action, Kaheera, the Orphanguard was still outside the game and the provided rules don't state that it joins the new game.

4. What the provided rules do NOT settle: whether Alex still has Kaheera, the Orphanguard available as a companion in the restarted game, and whether the presence of Carrion Grub (an Insect, not a Cat/Elemental/Nightmare/Dinosaur/Beast) in the new game's starting deck breaks the companion condition. The only companion rule given is [702.139b], which says "starting deck" means your deck after setting aside sideboard cards — it doesn't address restarted games. Treat that part as unresolved by this context.

5. Multiplayer: the same answer applies with more than two players — all players in the game when it ended start the new game [727.1], and in a game using the limited range of influence option every player is involved regardless of the range of influence of Karn Liberated's controller [727.7].

question: Adelyn controls [Back from the Brink] and has [Shifting Wall] in their graveyard. Can Adelyn activate Back from the Brink's ability to create a token of Shifting Wall? Can they pay more than {0} to do so? If so, will it enter the battlefield with any +1/+1 counters?
answer:
Yes, Adelyn can activate Back from the Brink targeting Shifting Wall, but the mana cost they must pay is effectively {0}, and the token copy enters with zero +1/+1 counters — so it's a 0/0 and is put into the graveyard immediately as a state-based action.

Why: Back from the Brink says "Exile a creature card from your graveyard and pay its mana cost: Create a token that's a copy of that card. Activate only as a sorcery." Shifting Wall is a creature card in Adelyn's graveyard, so it's a legal choice. Its mana cost is {X}. Per the symbol reference for {X}, the value of X is chosen only when the card itself is cast or an ability is activated with X in its cost; here Shifting Wall isn't being cast, so there's no opportunity to announce a value for X and it is treated as 0. Adelyn therefore pays {0} and cannot choose to pay more (paying extra mana isn't allowed — you pay exactly the cost).

The token is a copy of Shifting Wall, so it has "This creature enters with X +1/+1 counters on it." Copy effects do carry over replacement effects like "enters with" counters, and they apply as the token enters rather than afterward [707.5]. But with X = 0 for the token, it enters with no counters, making it a 0/0 Wall with defender that dies right away.

Timing note: the ability can be activated only when Adelyn could cast a sorcery (their own main phase, stack empty). Nothing here changes between a two-player and a multiplayer game; the rules provided are not player-count dependent.

Caveat: the rules excerpt provided does not include the specific rule on how X is treated in a cost outside of casting/activation (normally rule 107.3), so the {0} conclusion rests on the symbol reference note supplied rather than a quoted numbered rule.

In that case, the value of X is the value chosen or determined for it as the spell was cast.

Also, any enters-the-battlefield triggered abilities of the copy will have a chance to trigger. Skyshroud Behemoth reads, “Fading 2 (This creature enters with two fade counters on it. question: Alex controls a [Krark-Clan Ironworks], a [Mycosynth Lattice], and a [Control Magic] that took control of a [Boris Devilboon] from Nico. Alex begins activating the ability of Boris Devilboon and sacrifices Control Magic to help pay the cost. Is this legal? If so, who will control the ability?
answer:
Yes, it's legal, and Alex controls the activated ability of Boris Devilboon.

Why it's legal:
- Only an object's controller may activate its activated ability, and that's checked when the activation begins [602.2], [701.2a]. At that moment Control Magic ("You control enchanted creature") is applying in the control-changing layer [613.1b], so Alex is the controller of Boris Devilboon and may legally begin activating {2}{B}{R}, {T}.
- During the payment step Alex may activate mana abilities. Mycosynth Lattice makes all permanents artifacts, so Control Magic is an artifact and can be sacrificed to Krark-Clan Ironworks to add {C}{C}. Mycosynth Lattice also says players may spend mana as though it were mana of any color, so that {C}{C} can pay the {B} and the {R} of Boris Devilboon's cost. The remaining {2} generic can be paid with any mana, and the {T} is paid by tapping Boris Devilboon.
- Nothing rewinds the activation when Control Magic leaves the battlefield: announcements and payments can't be altered once made, and the activation is only rewound if a player can't complete a step of activation [602.2]. Losing control of the source mid-payment isn't such a failure.

Who controls the ability: the controller of an activated ability on the stack is the player who activated it [113.8]. That's Alex. Once Control Magic is gone, Boris Devilboon reverts to Nico's control, but the ability on the stack stays Alex's, so Alex creates the 1/1 black and red Minor Demon token under Alex's control when it resolves.

Timing note: I'm assuming Alex sacrifices Control Magic while paying costs for the already-announced ability. If instead Alex sacrificed Control Magic first and only then tried to announce the ability, the activation would be illegal — Boris Devilboon would already be Nico's, and Alex couldn't begin activating it [602.2], [701.2a].

Player count doesn't matter here: the same answer holds in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Nico has cast a [Gather Specimens] earlier in the turn. Aiden controls a [Chronatog Totem] that is currently a creature due to its own ability, and casts an [Evil Twin], choosing to have it copy Chronatog Totem. What happens?
answer:
Evil Twin enters the battlefield under Aiden's control, not Nico's — and it enters as a noncreature artifact named Chronatog Totem.

Why: when copying a permanent, the copy gets only the copiable values (printed name, mana cost, types, rules text, P/T, etc., as modified by other copy effects, face-down status, and "as ~ enters" abilities that set P/T). Other effects — including type-changing effects — are not copied [707.2]. Chronatog Totem's own {1}{U} ability making it a 1/2 blue Atog artifact creature is exactly such a type-changing effect, so Evil Twin does not copy the "is currently a creature" part. It copies Chronatog Totem as a plain artifact with the {T}: Add {U} ability, the {1}{U} animation ability, and the {0} +3/+3 ability, plus the Evil Twin exception ability "{U}{B}, {T}: Destroy target creature with the same name as this creature," which becomes part of its copiable values [707.9a][707.9b].

Gather Specimens says "If a creature would enter the battlefield under an opponent's control this turn, it enters under your control instead." Both Evil Twin's copy effect and Gather Specimens are replacement effects modifying the same event, so the affected object's controller — Aiden — chooses the order [616.1f]. Applying the copy effect first (the same pattern as the Essence of the Wild / Rusted Sentinel example in [616.1f]) means the permanent entering is not a creature, so Gather Specimens no longer applies at all and does nothing. Even if Gather Specimens were considered first, the object that actually enters is a noncreature artifact, so Gather Specimens' condition isn't met.

Practical result for Aiden: he has a second "Chronatog Totem" that is an artifact only. He can pay {1}{U} to animate it into a 1/2 blue Atog artifact creature, and then, with the Evil Twin ability, pay {U}{B} and tap it to destroy target creature with the same name — which could be Aiden's original Chronatog Totem, if it's still a creature (the ability targets a creature with the same name).

Assumption on timing: I'm reading it as Gather Specimens having already resolved before Evil Twin was cast, as stated. If Gather Specimens were instead cast and resolved after Evil Twin was already on the battlefield, it wouldn't affect Evil Twin at all, since it only replaces creatures entering later that turn.

Two players vs. more: the outcome is the same at any table size. Gather Specimens applies to creatures entering under any opponent's control, so with more opponents it would still simply fail to apply here because no creature entered.

question: Albert and Nico are beginning the game and have just drawn 7 cards. Albert has [Serum Powder] in their hand. Does Albert get to know whether Nico is going to mulligan before deciding whether to use Serum Powder's ability?
answer:
It depends on who declares first. Serum Powder's ability works "any time you could mulligan," which means Albert may use it at the moment Albert would declare whether to take a mulligan. Mulligan declarations are made in turn order, beginning with the starting player, and all mulligans are then taken simultaneously [103.5b].

- If Albert is the starting player, Albert declares first, so Albert must decide about exiling their hand to Serum Powder before knowing whether Nico will mulligan.
- If Nico is the starting player, Nico declares first, and Albert therefore already knows Nico's declaration when Albert's turn to declare (and to use Serum Powder) comes up. Rule 103.5b explicitly notes that other players may have already made their mulligan declarations by the time a player has the option to perform such an action.

Note that Albert isn't limited to the first round of declarations: 103.5b says the action need not be taken in the first round of mulligans, so Albert could keep Serum Powder's ability in reserve for a later round (Serum Powder's own text also confirms Albert can use it in addition to taking mulligans). If Albert does use it, Albert exiles all cards in hand and draws that many, then declares whether to take a mulligan.

What Albert never learns in advance is the *content* of Nico's new hand — only whether Nico declared a mulligan, and only if Nico declared first.

Multiplayer: the same principle scales up. Declarations go in turn order from the starting player [103.5b], so Albert knows the declarations of every player who declares before Albert and none of those after. In a multiplayer game (and Brawl), the first mulligan doesn't count toward cards bottomed or mulligans allowed [103.5c], and with shared team turns teammates may consult and a player may mulligan even after a teammate has kept [805.3a].

question: Ariana controls [Sen Triplets], which targeted Nico. Nico's hand contains [Rift Sower]. Can either player suspend it? If so, who will cast it once the last time counter is removed?
answer:
Neither player can suspend Rift Sower this turn.

Why Nico can't: exiling a card with suspend is a special action, and a player may take it only if they have the card with suspend in hand and "could begin to cast that card by putting it onto the stack" right then [116.2f], [702.62a]. Determining that takes into account any effect prohibiting the card from being cast [702.62c], [601.3]. Sen Triplets' ability says the targeted player "can't cast spells or activate abilities" this turn, so Nico could not begin to cast Rift Sower and therefore cannot take the suspend special action for it. (Suspend 2—{G} would otherwise cost {G}, one green mana.)

Why Ariana can't: the suspend special action is available only to "a player who has a card with suspend in their hand" [116.2f], and suspend's first ability is a static ability that functions while the card is in a player's hand [702.62a]. Rift Sower is in Nico's hand, not Ariana's. Sen Triplets grants Ariana only the ability to play lands and cast spells from Nico's hand — it does not grant her Nico's special actions, and suspending doesn't use the stack, so it isn't casting a spell [702.62a].

On the hypothetical second part: if Rift Sower had already been suspended earlier (by Nico, before Sen Triplets' ability resolved), the exiled card's third ability triggers when the last time counter is removed and gives its controller — the player who suspended it, i.e. Nico — permission to cast it without paying its mana cost, with haste as a creature spell [702.62a], [702.62b], [112.2a], [702.62d]. But if that trigger resolves during a turn in which Sen Triplets' effect is still stopping Nico from casting spells, Nico can't cast it and it simply remains exiled [702.62a]. Sen Triplets lets Ariana cast spells from Nico's hand only, not from exile, so she couldn't cast it either.

Multiplayer: the answer is the same at any table size. Sen Triplets targets one opponent, so only that one player (Nico here) is locked out; other opponents' suspend actions are unaffected.

question: Ariella controls a manifested [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nathaniel casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. After that resolves, Ariella turns Wayward Angel face up. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics afterwards?
answer:
Wayward Angel ends up as a face-up 1/1 blue Frog creature named Wayward Angel with no abilities at all (no flying, no vigilance, no threshold ability), still with mana cost {4}{W}{W}, for the rest of the turn.

Why:

1. While manifested, Wayward Angel was a 2/2 face-down colorless creature with no name, no types, and no mana cost — those are the characteristics granted by the ability that let it be face down, and they are its copiable values while face down [708.2a] [613.2b].

2. Turn to Frog resolved on that face-down permanent: until end of turn it loses all abilities and becomes a blue Frog with base power and toughness 1/1. That's a continuous effect applying in the ability-removing and type/color/P-T layers, not a change to copiable values.

3. When Ariella turns Wayward Angel face up, its copiable values revert to its normal printed values (name Wayward Angel, mana cost {4}{W}{W}, printed 4/4, Angel Horror, flying/vigilance/threshold). But rule 708.8 says any effects that were already applied to the face-down permanent still apply to the face-up permanent. So Turn to Frog keeps applying on top of those reverted values [708.8] [613.1g].

4. Result: the printed abilities are stripped by Turn to Frog, so flying, vigilance, and the threshold ability are all gone — even though Ariella has seven cards in the graveyard, the threshold static ability isn't there to grant +3/+3, black, trample, or the upkeep sacrifice trigger. Its base power and toughness is set to 1/1 and its color is blue and its creature type is Frog. Turning face up only changes its face up/face down status [110.5c]; it doesn't remove Turn to Frog's effect.

When Turn to Frog wears off at end of turn, Wayward Angel is a normal face-up 4/4 white Angel Horror with flying and vigilance, and its threshold ability will then function (making it 7/7, black, trample, with the upkeep sacrifice trigger) as long as seven or more cards are in Ariella's graveyard.

Timing note: I'm assuming Turn to Frog fully resolved before the face-up turning, as stated. If instead Wayward Angel had been turned face up first and Turn to Frog resolved after, the end state this turn would be identical (1/1 blue Frog, no abilities), since Turn to Frog would still be the latest effect in the ability-removing and P/T-setting layers.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — it's the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Ahmad controls [Conspiracy] (naming "Ferret"), [Kormus Bell], [Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth], and a [Vastwood Zendikon] enchanting Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth that entered the battlefield in that order. Is Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth a creature? If so, what are its creature types?
answer:
Yes — Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is a creature, and its only creature type is Elemental (it is a green 6/4 Elemental creature that is still a legendary land with the land types it had plus Swamp).

How it stacks up:

1. Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth's own ability makes each land a Swamp in addition to its other land types — including itself. Swamp is a land type, not a creature type ([205.3c], [205.3b]).
2. Kormus Bell says "All Swamps are 1/1 black creatures that are still lands." Because Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is now a Swamp, Kormus Bell makes it a creature while it keeps the land card type ([205.1b] — "still a land" means all prior card types, supertypes and subtypes are retained). It gains no creature type from Kormus Bell, and it stays legendary ([205.4b]).
3. Conspiracy (naming Ferret) says creatures you control are the chosen type, which sets the creature type of Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth to Ferret at Conspiracy's timestamp.
4. Vastwood Zendikon, which entered last and therefore has the latest timestamp, says the enchanted land "is a 6/4 green Elemental creature. It's still a land." This is the same kind of type-setting effect described in [205.1b]: it lets Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth keep its other card types and its land types/supertype, but the creature type it specifies replaces the creature types the permanent had. Applied after Conspiracy's effect, it overwrites Ferret with Elemental.

So the final type line is effectively "Legendary Land Creature — Swamp (plus its other land types) Elemental," a 6/4 green creature (Vastwood Zendikon's power/toughness and color also apply after Kormus Bell's 1/1 black).

Timing note: this answer assumes the entry order you gave (Conspiracy before Vastwood Zendikon). If Vastwood Zendikon had entered before Conspiracy, Conspiracy's later timestamp would win and the creature type would be Ferret instead of Elemental.

Caveat: the context I was given doesn't include the full layer/timestamp rules (613), so the ordering step above rests on [205.1b] plus the entry order you specified. Nothing here depends on player count — the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

gold_text.613.7d: Within a layer or sublayer, determining which order effects are applied in is usually done using a timestamp system. An effect with an earlier timestamp is applied before an effect with a later timestamp. An object receives a timestamp at the time it enters a zone.
gold_text.613.8a: Within a layer or sublayer, determining which order effects are applied in is sometimes done using a dependency system. If a dependency exists, it will override the timestamp system. An effect is said to “depend on” another if (a) it’s applied in the same layer (and, if applicable, sublayer) as the other effect; (b) applying the other would change the text or the existence of the first effect, what it applies to, or what it does to any of the things it applies to; and (c) neither effect is from a characteristic-defining ability or both effects are from characteristic-defining abilities. Otherwise, the effect is considered to be independent of the other effect.
gold_text.613.8b: Within a layer or sublayer, determining which order effects are applied in is sometimes done using a dependency system. If a dependency exists, it will override the timestamp system. An effect dependent on one or more other effects waits to apply until just after all of those effects have been applied. If multiple dependent effects would apply simultaneously in this way, they’re applied in timestamp order relative to each other. If several dependent effects form a dependency loop, then this rule is ignored and the effects in the dependency loop are applied in timestamp order.
gold_text.613.8c: Within a layer or sublayer, determining which order effects are applied in is sometimes done using a dependency system. If a dependency exists, it will override the timestamp system. After each effect is applied, the order of remaining effects is reevaluated and may change if an effect that has not yet been applied becomes dependent on or independent of one or more other effects that have not yet been applied.

cited_text.205.1b: The type line is printed directly below the illustration. It contains the card’s card type(s). It also contains the card’s subtype(s) and supertype(s), if applicable. Some effects change an object’s card type, supertype, or subtype but specify that the object retains a prior card type, supertype, or subtype. In such cases, all the object’s prior card types, supertypes, and subtypes are retained. This rule applies to effects that use phrases such as “in addition to its other types” or that state that something is “still a [type, supertype, or subtype].” Some effects state that an object becomes an “artifact creature”; these effects also allow the object to retain all of its prior card types and subtypes. Some effects state that an object becomes a “[creature type or types] artifact creature”; these effects also allow the object to retain all of its prior card types and subtypes other than creature types, but replace any existing creature types. An ability reads, “All lands are 1/1 creatures that are still lands.” The affected lands now have two card types: creature and land. If there were any lands that were also artifacts before the ability’s effect applied to them, those lands would become “artifact land creatures,” not just “creatures,” or “land creatures.” The effect allows them to retain both the artifact and land card types. In addition, each land affected by the ability retains any land types and supertypes it had before the ability took effect. An ability reads, “All artifacts are 1/1 artifact creatures.” If a permanent is both an artifact and an enchantment, it will become an artifact enchantment creature.
cited_text.205.3b: Subtypes Subtypes of each card type except creature and plane are always single words and are listed after a long dash. Each word after the dash is a separate subtype. Subtypes of creature cards are one or two words and are listed after a long dash. Each word or two-word phrase, as listed in rule 205.3m, is a separate subtype. Objects other than planes may have multiple subtypes. Subtypes of planes are also listed after a long dash, but may be multiple words; all words after the dash are, collectively, a single subtype. “Basic Land — Mountain” means the card is a land with the subtype Mountain. “Creature — Goblin Wizard” means the card is a creature with the subtypes Goblin and Wizard. “Artifact — Equipment” means the card is an artifact with the subtype Equipment.
cited_text.205.3c: Subtypes If a card with multiple card types has one or more subtypes, each subtype is correlated to its appropriate card type. Dryad Arbor’s type line says “Land Creature — Forest Dryad.” Forest is a land type, and Dryad is a creature type.
cited_text.205.4b: Supertypes An object’s supertype is independent of its card type and subtype, even though some supertypes are closely identified with specific card types. Changing an object’s card types or subtypes won’t change its supertypes. Changing an object’s supertypes won’t change its card types or subtypes. When an object gains or loses a supertype, it retains any other supertypes it had. An ability reads, “All lands are 1/1 creatures that are still lands.” If any of the affected lands were legendary, they are still legendary.
cited_text.205.2b: Card Types Some objects have more than one card type (for example, an artifact creature). Such objects satisfy the criteria for any effect that applies to any of their card types.
